raw.summary:
Nobody has adopted the model's current trigger, and no academic, Fed or research-institute source I read sets a threshold for "AI labour shock has started". The trigger is "12-month average unemployment at least 3 points above the 2025 average while real GDP is at or above its previous peak".

What does exist comes in two families.

(A) AI-specific trackers that compare exposed and unexposed workers. All use exposure scores from Eloundou et al. or the Anthropic Economic Index, and all are updated regularly:
- Stanford Digital Economy Lab (DEL) and ADP's Canaries Dashboard, monthly. Employment for 22-25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations was 19% below its counterfactual in June 2026 data.
- The Yale Budget Lab's AI Labor Market Tracker, monthly on CPS data. It reports occupational dissimilarity, AI exposure of the unemployed, and a synthetic difference-in-differences.
- Anthropic's "observed exposure" CPS unemployment gap between the most and least exposed quartiles, updated periodically.

The rest are one-off studies:
- The Dallas Fed rebuilt the Canaries measure on CPS data.
- The St. Louis Fed, the Economic Innovation Group (EIG) and the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research (SIEPR) compared unemployment across occupations by exposure.
- The NY Fed and the Fed Board studied job postings.
- Humlum and Vestergaard studied Danish administrative records.

None of these sets a trigger threshold. The nearest thing is Anthropic's stated detection limit: a gap of about 1 percentage point in unemployment between the most and least exposed quartiles would show up. Anthropic also offers a benchmark it calls "a Great Recession for white-collar workers": the top-quartile unemployment rate doubling from 3% to 6%. The Stanford DEL Transformation Tracker does publish explicit classification rules: strong evidence at the 95th percentile of a bootstrap from an AR model fitted to data from about 1997 to 2019, mild evidence from the 80th to 95th. But its 12 indicators are macro measures of an AI growth takeoff, and the only labour-related one is the capital share.

(B) Established tools for telling structural from cyclical change. None is specific to AI:
- Groshen-Potter 2003 industry quadrants
- Jaimovich-Siu jobless recoveries and routine-job employment
- Okun's-law deviations
- The Abraham-Katz test of vacancies against sectoral dispersion (Beveridge-curve logic)
- The Şahin-Song-Topa-Violante mismatch index
- The Sahm rule (a 0.50-point recession threshold)
- The BLS Displaced Worker Survey
- BLS permanent job losers
- The BLS labour share

A key point for the model: the jobless-recovery literature itself says 1991, 2001 and 2009 were jobless recoveries, and Jaimovich-Siu tie them to automation of routine jobs. So a "high unemployment while GDP is at its peak" test fires after every recession since 1990 by construction. It cannot separate AI from ordinary cyclical and automation dynamics. Ball, Leigh and Loungani and the SF Fed both say deviations from Okun's law are normal.

The best established building block for separating AI from recessions is a comparison of exposed and unexposed groups. The Yale Budget Lab (Gimbel, Kendall and Nunn, May 2026) finds that AI-exposed occupations are less sensitive to the business cycle. In a recession the exposed-minus-unexposed unemployment gap therefore falls, as EIG found for 2022 to 2025 (+0.30 points for the most exposed against +0.94 for the least).

I ran a rough check of my own (not an established signal) on the 8 CPS major occupation groups published on FRED. The 24-month change in the exposed-minus-unexposed gap was negative in 2009-10 and 2020-21 but positive in recoveries, so the gap on its own fires during recoveries. Adding a second condition fixes most of that. The rule "exposed-group unemployment up at least 0.5 points over 24 months AND the gap rising" fired only in August-September 2011 and March-June 2026. The same rule at 1.0 point never fired from 2002 to August 2026.

Other findings to note:
- The prediction-market anchors the model uses (aggregate US unemployment above 10%) price the aggregate rate, not these differential measures.
- Stanford DEL, the NY Fed, the Budget Lab and SIEPR all conclude there is no economy-wide AI displacement so far, apart from early-career workers in exposed occupations. The NY Fed attributes 64% of the rise in unemployment among young graduates to remote work; I saw that only in search snippets and did not verify it.

The scratch computation and downloaded sources are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Applications/da707ee8-bdb9-43d0-bb83-c08c894e427d/scratchpad/wf-signal/academic/ (exposure_gap.py, fred/*.csv, and PDF text extracts).

candidates.name: Anthropic 'observed exposure' unemployment gap (Massenkoff and McCrory, 5 Mar 2026)
candidates.who_uses_it: Anthropic Economics research. The Anthropic Economic Index usage data it rests on is also used by Stanford DEL's Canaries Dashboard (automation-ratio split), the Yale Budget Lab tracker (usage metrics) and NY Fed Liberty Street (Audoly, Guerin, Topa, May 2026) as the exposure score for postings. No institution was found using the gap itself as a trigger.
candidates.definition: Occupation-level 'observed exposure' combines O*NET tasks, the Eloundou et al. task feasibility score and Claude usage. Automated uses get full weight and augmentative uses half weight; tasks are aggregated by time share. The outcome is the CPS unemployment rate, with the unemployed assigned to their previous occupation. The comparison is the top quartile of time-weighted coverage against the bottom quartile (alternatively the 30% of workers with zero coverage), in a difference-in-differences of the gap since the Nov 2022 ChatGPT release against 2016 onward. Stated benchmarks: a differential rise of about 1 percentage point would be detectable, and a 'Great Recession for white-collar workers' means top-quartile unemployment doubling from 3% to 6%. Result so far: the exposed group's rise is 'indistinguishable from zero'. It also reports a 14% drop in the job-finding rate for exposed 22-25-year-olds. These are benchmarks, not a declared trigger.
candidates.data_source: CPS monthly microdata (BLS/Census). The Employment Situation is released on the first Friday; public-use microdata follows about 2-3 weeks later. Anthropic Economic Index open dataset on Hugging Face (reports roughly quarterly, per the 24 Mar 2026 report). O*NET. Also UI claims. Update cadence: 'revisit these analyses periodically', with no schedule.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Yes, by the exposure differential: AI should raise unemployment in high-observed-exposure occupations relative to low-exposure ones, while a recession hits all. It does not itself model differing cyclical sensitivity (see the Yale synthetic DiD candidate).
candidates.evidence_quote: Differential increases in unemployment on the order of 1 percentage point (Anthropic)

candidates.name: Stanford Digital Economy Lab / ADP Canaries Dashboard (Brynjolfsson, Chandar, Chen)
candidates.who_uses_it: Stanford DEL AI Economic Indicators project, launched with ADP Research; monthly dashboard (updated 23 Sep 2026); paper revised Aug 2026. Widely cited: the Dallas Fed replicated it on CPS (Jan 2026); the SIEPR policy brief (Jul 2026) and Yale Budget Lab discuss it; Bank of England and World Bank event copies of the slides exist. It is the most-cited 'canary' statistic, but no one has adopted it as a threshold.
candidates.definition: A 5-year balanced ADP firm panel (25,000 firms; 4.6M workers matched to 730+ occupations in Nov 2022). Occupations are ranked into 5 quintiles by Eloundou et al. (2024) GPT-4 beta exposure; workers are split into ages 22-25, 26-30, 31-34, 35-44 and 45+. Employment indices are normalized to Oct/Nov 2022. Headline: employment of 22-25-year-olds in the most-exposed occupations relative to their less-exposed peers is 19% below parity (June 2026 data, up from 15% with July 2025 data). The paper version found a 13% relative decline after controlling for firm-time effects. The dashboard also reports year-on-year and annualized growth by age and exposure, and by Anthropic automation and augmentation ratios. No threshold is defined.
candidates.data_source: ADP payroll records (proprietary, not public). Monthly dashboard; the June 2026 data were released 12 Aug 2026, a lag of about 6-8 weeks. The exposure scores (Eloundou et al.) are public.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Partly. It compares age and exposure groups; firm-time fixed effects absorb firm-level shocks such as interest rates; results hold when tech firms and remote-amenable occupations are excluded; the automation versus augmentation split is used as a check. Critics: the NY Fed and Lambert and Schindler (2026) attribute the young-graduate pattern to remote work, and Kolko notes pre-trends and disagreement between exposure measures.
candidates.evidence_quote: We do not see widespread, economy-wide job displacement associated with AI. (Stanford DEL, Aug 2026)

candidates.name: Yale Budget Lab AI Labor Market Tracker (occupational dissimilarity index; AI exposure of the unemployed)
candidates.who_uses_it: The Budget Lab at Yale (Gimbel, Kinder, Kendall, Lee; first published 1 Oct 2025; tracker v1.0 published 16 Jul 2026 and updated 15 Sep 2026 with August 2026 CPS). Cited by Stanford DEL, SIEPR, PIIE/Brookings (Kolko) and the press. No threshold.
candidates.definition: (1) Duncan-style dissimilarity index: the percentage-point difference between the occupational distribution of employment in month t and a baseline month, i.e. the share of workers who would need to change occupation to match the baseline. It uses a 12-month moving average of CPS employment (3-month for the recent-graduate comparisons). Baselines: Jan 1984 (computers), Jan 1996 (internet), Jan 2016 (control), Nov 2022 (AI). Benchmark: the internet era reached about 7 percentage points by 2002, and the AI path was 'only about 1 percentage point higher' at the same horizon. (2) Average share of tasks exposed (Eloundou beta) among the unemployed, by unemployment duration; this has stayed in a 25-35% band with no upward trend. (3) Share of workers in low (quintiles 1-2), middle (3-4) and high (quintile 5) exposure groups. (4) Anthropic usage metrics. (5) Synthetic difference-in-differences (separate candidate). The verdict language is 'remain flat, lie within historical ranges, or continue along pre-AI trends'. The authors call for 'preregistering areas where we would expect to see the impact' but have not published thresholds.
candidates.data_source: CPS basic monthly microdata; monthly updates after each CPS release; data downloads provided. Eloundou et al. exposure; Anthropic Economic Index usage.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Weakly. Dissimilarity measures any reallocation, with no stance on cause; the authors say it 'does not take a stance on the cause'. Comparing with past technology episodes gives context, not attribution. Exposure of the unemployed is AI-specific but, per the Dallas Fed, misses never-hired entrants because the CPS records the last occupation.
candidates.evidence_quote: does not provide clear evidence of labor market disruption associated with AI (Budget Lab, Sep 2026)

candidates.name: Yale Budget Lab synthetic difference-in-differences of exposed versus unexposed occupations (Gimbel, Kendall, Nunn, 7 May 2026)
candidates.who_uses_it: Budget Lab tracker, as its third tab. Chen et al. (arXiv 2509.15510) use a similar synthetic DiD for unemployment and earnings. Stanford DEL cites it.
candidates.definition: Synthetic DiD (Arkhangelsky et al. 2021). Treated units are occupations in the top tercile of AI exposure; donors are bottom-tercile occupations, weighted into a synthetic control. The outcome is mean occupation employment share of the civilian population, plus wage outcomes, after removing quarter-of-year effects at the detailed occupation level. The event date is 2022Q4. Result: 'no clear evidence of AI effects'. Key documented fact: AI-exposed occupations are less procyclical than unexposed ones in pre-pandemic data. No threshold.
candidates.data_source: CPS-based occupation employment shares (the page links data and R code); periodic updates.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Yes, and this is the design most directly aimed at the cyclical confound. Because exposed occupations are less cyclical, an ordinary recession should move exposed minus unexposed the opposite way from an AI shock, which is the property the model's current trigger lacks.
candidates.evidence_quote: AI-exposed occupations are generally less sensitive to the business cycle (Budget Lab)

candidates.name: Dallas Fed CPS replication of the canaries measure (Atkinson and Yamco, 6 Jan 2026)
candidates.who_uses_it: Dallas Fed Economics article, one-off. It shows the Stanford measure can be rebuilt from public CPS data.
candidates.definition: CPS public microdata with Eloundou et al. 0-1 exposure. Occupations are split into least, moderate and most exposed by tertiles of the 2024 employment-weighted score distribution, held fixed over time. Workers are young (20-24) or prime age (25-55), and 12-month moving averages are used. Statistics: (a) employment share of the young, most-exposed group (16.4% in Nov 2022 to 15.5% in Sep 2025); (b) employment-to-unemployment flow rates; (c) job-finding rate of the unemployed; (d) job-finding rate of labour-market entrants, down more than 3 points since Nov 2023 for young, most-exposed workers. Upper bound on the aggregate effect: 0.1 point of unemployment since Nov 2022. No threshold. The authors refuse to use the occupation of the unemployed because the CPS records the last job held.
candidates.data_source: CPS basic monthly public-use microdata (Census/BLS), monthly with about a 3-week lag after the Employment Situation. Not maintained as a tracker.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Partly: age by exposure comparison, plus a check that the pattern is not a typical cyclical one against past business cycles. The authors say it may be driven by correlates such as education.
candidates.evidence_quote: This is an early sign to watch as AI's development continues. (Dallas Fed)

candidates.name: St. Louis Fed: cross-occupation correlation of AI exposure with the rise in unemployment (Ozkan and Sullivan, 26 Aug 2025)
candidates.who_uses_it: St. Louis Fed On the Economy blog, one-off; widely quoted in the press as the '0.47 correlation'.
candidates.definition: Correlation across occupations between the Eloundou-based exposure score and the change in the 3-month-average unemployment rate from May-Jul 2022 to May-Jul 2025: 0.47. Using Real-Time Population Survey adoption instead of exposure gives 0.57. No threshold; the authors call for monitoring.
candidates.data_source: CPS unemployment by occupation (BLS); Real-Time Population Survey (Bick, Blandin, Deming) for adoption; Eloundou et al. exposure.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Weakly: a cross-sectional correlation with no control for differing cyclical sensitivity. The authors flag it as correlation, not causation.
candidates.evidence_quote: occupations with higher AI exposure experienced larger unemployment rate increases (St. Louis Fed)

candidates.name: Unemployment rate by AI-exposure quintile (EIG, Eckhardt and Goldschlag, Aug 2025; SIEPR, Mahoney, McEntarfer and Wahal, Jul 2026)
candidates.who_uses_it: Economic Innovation Group ('AI and Jobs: The Final Word (Until the Next One)', with public code) and the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research (SIEPR) policy brief. Stanford DEL cites EIG. No threshold.
candidates.definition: Occupations split into five equal quintiles by an exposure score. EIG uses Felten AIOE, Eloundou et al., Eisfeldt et al. and Webb. The unemployment rate for each quintile is tracked from 2022. EIG: most exposed +0.30 point versus least exposed +0.94 point, 2022 to early 2025. SIEPR (IPUMS-CPS through 2026Q1): top quintile +0.77 point versus least +0.85 point. SIEPR also cites the Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS): 'only 5 percent of firms report any employment impact'.
candidates.data_source: CPS basic monthly, ASEC and ORG via IPUMS/EPI; BTOS. The EIG repo is a snapshot 'accurate as of' 10 Aug 2025 and is not updated.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Partly, by the exposure gradient. The result so far (least exposed rising more) is what a cyclical slowdown looks like, because exposed occupations are less cyclical.
candidates.evidence_quote: top quintile of AI-exposed workers has risen by 0.77 percentage points (SIEPR)

candidates.name: NY Fed 'Labor Market for Recent College Graduates' (unemployment and underemployment of 22-27-year-olds with a bachelor's degree or more)
candidates.who_uses_it: NY Fed web feature, a long-running series tracked since 1990. The SIEPR brief and the press use it as an AI canary (5.6% in early 2026, up 1.6 points in 3 years). Search snippets (not verified by reading the page) say NY Fed research attributes 64% of the rise for young graduates to remote work, not AI.
candidates.definition: Unemployment rate of recent college graduates (ages 22-27, bachelor's degree or more), compared on the page with other groups; the underemployment rate is 42% in 2026Q2. No threshold.
candidates.data_source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, from CPS microdata (source not stated on the page I read). Updated quarterly, 'generally in February, May, August, and November'; latest is 2026Q2.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It is a young-graduate labour-market measure that is sensitive to the cycle, remote work and graduate supply.
candidates.evidence_quote: updated quarterly, generally in February, May, August, and November (NY Fed)

candidates.name: Job postings by AI exposure (NY Fed Liberty Street, Audoly, Guerin and Topa, 14 May 2026; Fed Board FEDS Note, Liu and Webber, 27 Mar 2026)
candidates.who_uses_it: NY Fed (one-off). Fed Board staff, who say they 'plan to monitor it on an ongoing basis'. Earlier academic version: Acemoglu, Autor, Hazell and Restrepo (NBER w28257), using establishment AI vacancies.
candidates.definition: NY Fed: Lightcast postings growth for high- versus low-exposure occupations (Anthropic exposure), and junior versus senior within exposed fields. The divergence 'began before 2022' with no additional break after ChatGPT. Fed Board: Lightcast postings regressed on BTOS industry AI adoption (3-digit NAICS) and firm AI-skill postings, giving precisely estimated null effects. Acemoglu et al.: AI-exposed establishments reduce non-AI hiring, but there is 'no discernible relationship' with employment at occupation or industry level. No thresholds.
candidates.data_source: Lightcast (formerly Burning Glass) postings (proprietary); Census BTOS; O*NET.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Partly: timing of the break relative to Nov 2022 and the exposure differential. Pre-trends dominate so far.
candidates.evidence_quote: does not show a clear additional break in trajectory after 2022 (NY Fed)

candidates.name: Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS) AI-use rate and AI supplement (official adoption statistic)
candidates.who_uses_it: U.S. Census Bureau (official, biweekly). Fed Board staff note 'Monitoring AI Adoption in the U.S. Economy' (Allen, 3 Apr 2026) tracks it alongside the Real-Time Population Survey (quarterly) and the Survey of Business Uncertainty. It is used by Goldman, SIEPR and EIG.
candidates.definition: Share of firms using AI to produce goods or services (about 18% at end-2025 in the Fed note). The Nov 2025-Feb 2026 supplement adds AI use by business function (18% of firms, 32% employment-weighted) and questions on AI-related employment change. SIEPR reports about 5% of firms saying AI had any employment effect, split between gains and losses. This measures adoption, not displacement, and has no threshold.
candidates.data_source: Census BTOS; a sample of about 1.2M businesses in six panels; data released every two weeks.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Measures AI adoption directly, and the supplement asks about employment effects of AI. It does not measure aggregate displacement.
candidates.evidence_quote: about 18 percent of firms have adopted AI (Fed Board note)

candidates.name: Goldman Sachs AI Adoption Tracker (Briggs, Dong) and AI unemployment estimates (Mei)
candidates.who_uses_it: Goldman Sachs Research, a client product; reported in Fortune (1 Jun 2026) and Yahoo Finance (24 Feb 2026). I could not read Goldman's own report page: the PDF URL returned a script-only page, not the PDF.
candidates.definition: As reported: net job losses in AI-affected industries (displacement in marketing, graphic design, customer service, document processing and software, offset by data-centre construction), about 11,000 per month (down from about 16,000 two months earlier). A 'slight positive correlation' across industries between AI adoption and unemployment of workers under 30. BTOS-type adoption of 19.5% of establishments. The Feb 2026 scenario says faster adoption could add up to 0.3 point to 2026 unemployment. No threshold.
candidates.data_source: Proprietary Goldman compilation (method not public in what I read); cadence appears to be about every two months (not verified).
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Yes, by industry AI-readiness and adoption, but the methodology is not public.
candidates.evidence_quote: not yet a clean structural break (Fortune on Goldman tracker)

candidates.name: Revelio Labs AI Labor Market Tracker
candidates.who_uses_it: Revelio Labs (commercial); monthly editions (August 2026 seen).
candidates.definition: Employment headcount, postings and wages by occupation AI exposure. The exposure score (0-1) is assigned by LLM evaluation of work activities and benchmarked against Eloundou et al. and Felten et al. Baseline is Oct 2022. It also tracks firm-level 'AI integrator adoption' and WARN notices. No threshold found.
candidates.data_source: Proprietary online professional profiles, postings, reviews and WARN notices.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: By the exposure differential relative to the Oct 2022 baseline.
candidates.evidence_quote: AI exposure score between 0 and 1 (Revelio methodology)

candidates.name: Humlum and Vestergaard, Denmark: adoption surveys linked to administrative records (NBER w33777, 'Still Waters, Rapid Currents', revised Mar 2026)
candidates.who_uses_it: Academic (NBER; previously titled 'Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects'). Stanford DEL cites it for replicating the age-based pattern in Denmark. One-off.
candidates.definition: Difference-in-differences on worker- and workplace-level earnings and recorded hours, comparing chatbot adopters with non-adopters in 11 exposed occupations (25,000 workers, 7,000 workplaces), linked to Danish registers. Result: precise nulls ruling out effects larger than 2% two years after ChatGPT. There is occupational switching and task reorganization. No threshold.
candidates.data_source: Danish administrative registers plus the authors' surveys; not a published recurring series.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Yes, via measured adoption at worker and firm level rather than exposure. It is a template for countries with register data, not a trigger.
candidates.evidence_quote: ruling out effects larger than 2% two years after the launch of ChatGPT

candidates.name: Stanford DEL Transformation Tracker (formerly 'Takeoff Tracker'): percentile classification of 12 macro indicators
candidates.who_uses_it: Stanford Digital Economy Lab AI Economic Indicators (Research Note #1, Jun 2026; page updated 23 Sep 2026). This is the only AI tracker found with explicit, pre-stated evidence thresholds.
candidates.definition: For each indicator, an AR(p) model is fitted to data from the sample start (typically 1997) to 2019 and bootstrapped. The one-year moving average of realizations is compared with the one-year moving average of the simulated distribution: at or below the 20th percentile is contradictory; 80th-95th is mild evidence; at or above the 95th is strong evidence; otherwise neutral. Indicators: output growth, TFP, labour productivity, real 10-year rates, capital share (logit-transformed; classed 'strong'), network-adjusted capital shares, IT equipment share, software shares, energy and electricity. As of May 2026, 7 show no evidence, 3 mild and 2 strong. There is no unemployment or employment indicator; capital share is the only labour-related one.
candidates.data_source: BEA/BLS national accounts and fixed-asset data, TIPS yields, EIA energy (series codes not given on the page); updated monthly.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Designed around an AI 'explosive growth' scenario, not labour displacement. The percentile-of-simulated-counterfactual rule is a reusable, falsifiable template.
candidates.evidence_quote: any realization at the 95th percentile or higher is classified as strong evidence

candidates.name: BLS nonfarm business labor share (FRED PRS85006173)
candidates.who_uses_it: Official BLS Productivity and Costs statistic. Stanford DEL's Transformation Tracker uses the complementary capital share as a takeoff indicator. Not used as an AI trigger by anyone I read.
candidates.definition: Labour compensation share of nonfarm business output, index 2017=100, seasonally adjusted. It was 93.446 in 2026Q2, down from 94.843 in 2026Q1. No established AI threshold.
candidates.data_source: BLS Productivity and Costs, quarterly (Q2 2026 data updated 3 Sep 2026).
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It moves with the cycle and with many structural forces.
candidates.evidence_quote: Nonfarm Business Sector: Labor Share for All Workers (FRED title)

candidates.name: Groshen-Potter structural versus cyclical industry test for jobless recoveries (NY Fed Current Issues 9(8), Aug 2003)
candidates.who_uses_it: NY Fed. Cited by Jaimovich and Siu and by Bernanke (2003) in the jobless-recovery literature. It is a classic retrospective diagnostic, not a real-time series.
candidates.definition: Each of about 70 two-digit SIC industries is placed on a grid of job growth during the NBER recession against job growth in the 12 months of recovery after the trough. If recession losses (or gains) reversed in recovery, the change is cyclical; if they continued, it is structural. The shares of business-cycle-peak employment in the two structural quadrants are summed: mid-1970s 51%, early 1980s 51%, early 1990s 57%, 2001 79%. A second diagnostic is the contribution of temporary layoffs to unemployment, which was small in 1990-91 and 2001. No formal threshold.
candidates.data_source: BLS CES payroll employment by industry (monthly) and CPS reasons for unemployment; requires NBER peak and trough dates, which are announced with long lags.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It separates permanent reallocation, from any cause, from cyclical swings, and needs a recession to be defined.
candidates.evidence_quote: 79 percent of employees worked in industries affected more by structural shifts

candidates.name: Jaimovich-Siu jobless recoveries and routine-job employment (NBER w18334)
candidates.who_uses_it: Academic (NBER WP 2012, revised 2018; widely cited). Defines the modern 'jobless recovery' fact.
candidates.definition: A jobless recovery is when aggregate per-capita employment (CPS, ages 16+, band-pass filtered) keeps contracting after the NBER trough while GDP and GDI expand: 17 months after 1991, 23 after 2001 and 23 after 2009. Employment regained its peak about 5 years later after 1991, and never did before the next recession after 2001. Routine (middle-skill) per-capita employment fell 29 log points from 1990, 88% of it within a 12-month window around NBER recessions. No threshold.
candidates.data_source: BLS CPS Labor Force Statistics by occupation (monthly); NBER dates.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: It attributes jobless recoveries to routine-biased technological change, which is automation but not AI. So a 'high unemployment while GDP is at its peak' test fires after every recession since 1990 by design and cannot separate AI from earlier automation or the cycle.
candidates.evidence_quote: these recoveries were jobless: despite expansions in other measures of economic activity

candidates.name: Okun's-law deviations or residuals (Daly, Fernald, Jordà and Nechio, SF Fed 2014; Meyer and Tasci, Cleveland Fed 2012; Ball, Leigh and Loungani, NBER w18668)
candidates.who_uses_it: Fed and IMF research. It is used to discuss 'breakdowns' and jobless recoveries, but no one I read uses it as a technology-displacement trigger.
candidates.definition: SF Fed: four-quarter change in unemployment against four-quarter growth of real GDP per person aged 16-64 (1959-2013); about 2% lower output for each 1 point rise in unemployment; deviations trace normal 'counterclockwise loops'. Cleveland Fed: 10-year rolling regressions of the quarterly change in unemployment on real GDP growth show unstable coefficients. Ball, Leigh and Loungani: the law is 'strong and stable', and accounts of breakdowns via jobless recoveries are flawed.
candidates.data_source: BEA real GDP (quarterly), BLS unemployment (monthly).
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. The authors attribute deviations to normal lagged employment dynamics or measurement, not technology.
candidates.evidence_quote: temporary departures from the average relationship are part of the normal dynamic path

candidates.name: Abraham-Katz test of sectoral shifts versus aggregate demand (Lilien dispersion index plus vacancies; Beveridge-curve logic), NBER w1410
candidates.who_uses_it: Classic academic test (1986), the standard rebuttal to Lilien's (1982) sectoral-shift index. The Beveridge-curve logic is widely used, but I found no AI adoption.
candidates.definition: Lilien's G is the dispersion of employment growth across sectors. Under pure aggregate demand, G is negatively related to vacancies (help-wanted) and associated with the change in unemployment; under sectoral reallocation, unemployment and vacancies rise together. Abraham and Katz find the aggregate-demand interpretation fits, and build a demand-purged proxy for sectoral shifts. No threshold.
candidates.data_source: Modern analogues: BLS CES industry employment (monthly) and JOLTS job openings (monthly, about 5-week lag).
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Not AI-specific, but it is the established way to separate reallocation (which AI displacement would be) from a recession: reallocation shows up with vacancies not falling.
candidates.evidence_quote: pure sectoral shifts have not been an important source of cyclical fluctuations

candidates.name: Şahin-Song-Topa-Violante mismatch index (NY Fed Staff Report 566; published in the AER in 2014 per my prior knowledge, not re-verified)
candidates.who_uses_it: NY Fed research; the academic standard for structural 'mismatch' unemployment. Not found as a maintained official series (not verified).
candidates.definition: M_t = 1 - sum over i of (phi_it / phi-bar_t)(v_it/v_t)^alpha (u_it/u_t)^(1-alpha): the fraction of hires lost because unemployed workers are misallocated across sectors relative to vacancies. It is computed by industry (JOLTS) and 2- and 3-digit occupation (HWOL online postings), with counterfactual unemployment. Mismatch explained at most one-third of the Great Recession rise in unemployment (about 1.5 points at the 3-digit occupation level). No threshold.
candidates.data_source: JOLTS by industry; Conference Board Help Wanted OnLine by occupation; CPS unemployed by last occupation.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It measures structural reallocation from any cause.
candidates.evidence_quote: Mismatch across industries and occupations explains at most one-third

candidates.name: Sahm rule recession indicator (FRED SAHMREALTIME)
candidates.who_uses_it: A widely adopted real-time recession signal (Claudia Sahm; FRED). It is the clearest example of an established unemployment threshold rule, but it signals recessions, not AI.
candidates.definition: Fires when the 3-month moving average of U-3 unemployment rises 0.50 point or more above the minimum 3-month average of the previous 12 months. It was -0.07 in Aug 2026 (updated 4 Sep 2026).
candidates.data_source: BLS U-3 unemployment via FRED, monthly and real-time.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It could serve as the cyclical guard, e.g. do not count a period as AI while the Sahm rule or an NBER recession is active, or as a template for a threshold rule.
candidates.evidence_quote: rises by 0.50 percentage points or more relative to the minimum

candidates.name: BLS Displaced Worker Survey (biennial January CPS supplement) and CPS permanent job losers (LNS13026638)
candidates.who_uses_it: Official BLS statistics since 1984. Groshen and Potter used the split between permanent and temporary layoffs to diagnose structural change.
candidates.definition: DWS: workers displaced from jobs held 3 or more years, by reason: position or shift abolished, plant closed or moved, insufficient work. The 27 Aug 2026 release covers Jan 2023-Dec 2025: 3.3M long-tenured displaced workers (+746k on the prior survey); 44.4% position or shift abolished, 32.6% plant closed, 22.9% insufficient work. Permanent job losers: 1,777k unemployed in Aug 2026 (monthly). No AI threshold.
candidates.data_source: BLS CPS supplement, conducted every two January surveys and released in late summer. By that pattern the next survey is Jan 2028 with release around Aug 2028 (inferred, not verified). Permanent job losers: monthly with the Employment Situation.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. The reason codes do not identify technology; 'position or shift abolished' is the closest proxy.
candidates.evidence_quote: 44.4 percent of long-tenured displaced workers lost their job because their position

candidates.name: Occupational AI-exposure measures used as weights (Eloundou et al. 'GPTs are GPTs'; Felten-Raj-Seamans AIOE; Webb 2020 patents; ILO 2025 global index; IMF Cazzaniga et al. 2024)
candidates.who_uses_it: Eloundou beta is used by Stanford DEL, the Yale Budget Lab, the Dallas Fed, the St. Louis Fed and Anthropic. AIOE and Webb are used by EIG. The ILO index covers ISCO-08 occupations worldwide and is suitable for the model's non-US countries. The IMF index (known from search snippets only; the page returned 403) covers countries and adjusts for complementarity. Frank, Ahn and Moro (arXiv 2308.02624) find individual exposure models do not predict unemployment risk, but an ensemble does.
candidates.definition: Static scores, not signals. Eloundou: share of an occupation's tasks an LLM, alone or with tools, could speed up by at least 50%; about 80% of workers have at least 10% of tasks exposed. AIOE: relatedness of 10 AI applications to 52 O*NET abilities, by 6-digit SOC, with industry and county versions. Webb: overlap of patent text with task descriptions. ILO: four exposure gradients across nearly 30,000 tasks; one in four workers globally in an occupation with some exposure.
candidates.data_source: O*NET, patents, and ILO/ISCO task data; one-off releases with occasional updates.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: These supply the 'which occupations' weights that make a differential signal AI-specific. Kolko (PIIE, Mar 2026) notes the measures 'do not entirely agree', so results depend on which one is used.
candidates.evidence_quote: individual AI exposure models are not predictive of unemployment rates (Frank et al.)

Script: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Applications/da707ee8-bdb9-43d0-bb83-c08c894e427d/scratchpad/wf-signal/academic/exposure_gap.py, using FRED CSVs in fred/.

verified.summary:
I checked all 23 candidates against their cited sources, reopening them myself on 30 Sep 2026. I also reran the researcher's CPS gap script on fresh FRED downloads. The researcher's main conclusion holds: nobody has adopted the model's current trigger, and no Fed, academic or institute source I read sets a pre-stated threshold that says "an AI labour shock has started". The core facts of every candidate check out, so none is dropped entirely. A few specific claims were wrong or could not be confirmed and are corrected in the candidates below.

Corrections that matter for the model:

1. **The current trigger does not fire after every recession since 1990.** The researcher claimed it does "by construction"; that is overstated. I tested the stated rule (12-month average unemployment at least 7.3% while real GDP, GDPC1, is at or above its prior peak) on the repo's UNRATE.csv and GDPC1.csv.
   - **Where it fires:** Oct 1975-Sep 1977, parts of 1981, Apr 1983-Jul 1985, Jul 1992-Jun 1993, Oct 2010-Dec 2013 (intermittently), and Jan-May 2021.
   - **Where it does not:** after 2001, because the 12-month average peaked at 6.0% over 2001-2007.
   - **Why it misfires:** it fires after every deep recession, not only the "jobless" ones. The SF Fed's explanation fits: employment lags GDP in every cycle.

2. **Stanford DEL Transformation Tracker.** The model fitted is a linear trend with AR(p) residuals, fitted up to 2019. Post-2019 draws are centred on the 2010 fitted level. The latest page (23 Sep 2026) shows 6 indicators neutral, 4 mild and 2 strong. The "7 / 3 / 2" split was the May 2026 figure in Research Note 1.

3. **Canaries (Stanford DEL / ADP).** The 13% firm-controlled figure is from the 2025 version of the paper. The Aug 2026 revision says firm-hiring-adjusted estimates are now "more sensitive to specification choices". It also says the gaps shrink once education is accounted for, and that some differential trends predate generative AI.

4. **Yale Budget Lab synthetic DiD.** Its finding that exposed occupations are less cyclical is estimated for 1994-2019, against the CBO output gap. The authors say they "do not find the same pattern" of reduced cyclical sensitivity in the last few years. So the "a recession moves the exposed gap the opposite way" guard needs testing; it cannot be assumed.

5. **EIG.** The +0.30 vs +0.94 point result uses the Felten AIOE exposure measure. Under the Eloundou and Eisfeldt measures, the most-exposed group rose about 0.2-0.3 points *relative to* everyone else. Direction depends on which exposure measure is used.

6. **Anthropic observed-exposure measure.** The comparison group is the roughly 30% of workers with zero observed exposure. The researcher described it as "the bottom quartile".

7. **BTOS.** The 18% end-2025 adoption rate uses the Nov 2025 revised wording ("any of its business functions"), not "to produce goods or services".

8. **Now verified.** The NY Fed "64%" remote-work figure was only a search snippet before. It is Liberty Street Economics, 1 Jun 2026 (Emanuel, Harrington, Pallais): "remote work can explain 64 percent" of the rise in young-graduate unemployment.

9. **The researcher's own gap check reproduces exactly** on freshly downloaded FRED data:
   - The 0.5-point rule fires in Aug-Sep 2011 and Mar-Jun 2026.
   - The 1.0-point rule never fires.
   - Latest (Aug 2026): exposed group +0.43, low-exposure group +0.33, gap +0.10.
   - One number was misstated: the 2020-21 low point of the 24-month gap change was -2.86 (Mar 2021), not -2.11 (that is the Jun 2021 value).

**Bottom line for the model.** Established components exist, but no established trigger does. The components are:
- the CPS unemployment gap between AI-exposed and less-exposed occupations (the design used by Anthropic, EIG, SIEPR and Yale);
- Anthropic's stated benchmarks: a differential of about 1 point is detectable, and a "white-collar Great Recession" means top-quartile unemployment doubling from 3% to 6%;
- a cyclical guard such as the Sahm rule (FRED SAHMREALTIME, -0.07 in Aug 2026);
- the DEL percentile-of-simulated-counterfactual template.

A trigger assembled from these would be new; it could be built from established parts, but nobody has adopted it. My working files are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Applications/da707ee8-bdb9-43d0-bb83-c08c894e427d/scratchpad/wf-signal/verify-academic/v2/ (source texts, and gap/ for the rerun).

candidates.name: Anthropic 'observed exposure' unemployment gap (Massenkoff and McCrory, 5 Mar 2026)
candidates.who_uses_it: Anthropic Economic Research. The Anthropic Economic Index usage data it rests on is also used by the Stanford DEL Canaries Dashboard (split by automation and augmentation ratios), the Yale Budget Lab analyses (Anthropic usage metrics), and the NY Fed's Liberty Street post (Audoly, Guerin and Topa, 14 May 2026), which uses Anthropic's task-level exposure for job postings. No institution was found using the gap as a trigger.
candidates.definition: Occupation-level 'observed exposure'. A task counts as covered when it is theoretically feasible (Eloundou et al. beta: an LLM could make it at least twice as fast) and has enough work-related Claude usage. Fully automated use gets full weight and augmentative use half weight; tasks are averaged to occupations using time-share weights. The outcome is the CPS unemployment rate, using the unemployed's previous job. The treatment group is the top quartile of time-weighted coverage. The comparison group is the roughly 30% of workers with zero coverage (a correction: not 'the bottom quartile'). A difference-in-differences of the gap runs from 2016, with a post-ChatGPT (Nov 2022) break. Robustness checks vary the treatment cutoff from the median to the 95th percentile, look at ages 22-25, and use Department of Labor unemployment-insurance claimants. Stated benchmarks, not triggers: a differential rise of about 1 point would be detectable ('merely a ballpark'); a 'Great Recession for white-collar workers' would double top-quartile unemployment from 3% to 6%. Result as of Mar 2026: the rise is 'indistinguishable from zero'. The job-finding rate of 22-25-year-olds into exposed jobs is down 14% from 2022, which is 'just barely statistically significant'.
candidates.data_source: CPS monthly microdata; DOL unemployment-insurance claimant data; O*NET; Anthropic Economic Index samples. The last two index reports used Nov 2025 data (published Jan 2026) and Feb 2026 data (published 24 Mar 2026), so roughly quarterly. The authors say they will 'revisit these analyses periodically', with no schedule. Not verified: the Hugging Face hosting and the CPS microdata release lag.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Yes, by the exposure differential: AI should raise unemployment for high-exposure workers relative to zero-exposure workers. It does not model differing cyclical sensitivity. During COVID the zero-exposure group's unemployment rose much more, so the gap moves against a recession.
candidates.evidence_quote: differential increases in unemployment on the order of 1 percentage point would be detectable

candidates.name: Stanford Digital Economy Lab / ADP Canaries Dashboard (Brynjolfsson, Chandar, Chen)
candidates.who_uses_it: Stanford DEL AI Economic Indicators, run with ADP Research. The dashboard is 'updated monthly' (last updated 23 Sep 2026); the paper was revised 12 Aug 2026. The Dallas Fed rebuilt the analysis on CPS data (6 Jan 2026). The SIEPR brief, the Yale Budget Lab and PIIE (Kolko) discuss it. Nobody uses it as a threshold. Dropped: the claim about Bank of England and World Bank slide copies (not verified).
candidates.definition: A 5-year balanced panel of firms using ADP payroll, rolled forward monthly. At launch this was 25,000 firms, whose 4.6M workers matched to more than 730 occupations in Nov 2022. Occupations are grouped into quintiles by Eloundou et al. (2024) exposure; ages are 22-25, 26-30 and older bands. Employment trends are measured from Nov 2022. Headline (12 Aug 2026 revision): 22-25-year-olds in highly exposed occupations are about 19% below where they would be had they kept pace with less-exposed peers of the same age. The gap was 15% at the July 2025 data vintage and 19% as of June 2026. In levels, the two most-exposed quintiles fell about 11% from Nov 2022 to Jun 2026, while the three least-exposed grew about 10%. The dashboard also shows year-on-year and annualized growth, and splits by Anthropic automation and augmentation ratios. No threshold is defined. Correction: the '13% relative decline after controlling for firm-level shocks' is from the 2025 version (Nov 2025 slides). The 2026 revision says firm-hiring-adjusted estimates are 'directionally consistent' but 'more sensitive to specification choices'.
candidates.data_source: ADP payroll records (proprietary). The dashboard is updated monthly. The 19% figure uses data through June 2026, published 12 Aug 2026. The exposure scores (Eloundou et al.) are public.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Partly. It compares age and exposure groups. The divergence survives excluding tech firms and computer occupations, controlling for interest-rate and remote-work exposure, allowing firm entry and exit, and using other exposure measures. Declines are concentrated where AI use is automating. Caveats the authors give: the gaps shrink once education is accounted for, some differential trends predate generative AI, and the gaps are larger in the ADP sample than in national survey benchmarks. Critics: Lambert and Schindler (2026), as cited in Stanford DEL's Research Note 1, explain the junior-hiring pattern by remote-work exposure. The NY Fed's Emanuel, Harrington and Pallais (Jun 2026) attribute 64% of the rise in young-graduate unemployment to remote work.
candidates.evidence_quote: We do not see widespread, economy-wide job displacement associated with AI.

candidates.name: Yale Budget Lab AI Labor Market Tracker (occupational dissimilarity index; AI exposure of the unemployed)
candidates.who_uses_it: The Budget Lab at Yale. First analysis 1 Oct 2025 by Gimbel, Kinder (Brookings Metro), Kendall and Lee. A Nov/Dec CPS update followed on 28 Jan 2026. Tracker v1.0 was published 16 Jul 2026 and updated 15 Sep 2026 with August 2026 CPS. Cited by Stanford DEL (Research Note 1), SIEPR and PIIE (Kolko). Correction: the earlier 'PIIE/Brookings' label was wrong; Brookings is linked through co-author Kinder. No threshold.
candidates.definition: (1) Dissimilarity index: the sum of absolute differences between the occupational employment mix in month t and a baseline month. It is the share of workers who would have to change occupation to match the baseline. It uses a 12-month moving average of CPS employment (3-month for the recent-graduate comparisons). Baselines: Jan 1984 (computers), Jan 1996 (internet), Jan 2016 (control), Nov 2022 (AI). Benchmark: the internet era reached at most about 7 points by 2002, and the AI path was 'only about 1 percentage point higher' at the same horizon. (2) Average share of exposed tasks among the unemployed, by unemployment duration: about 25-35% with no clear upward trend. (3) Exposure-group employment shares. (4) Anthropic usage (automation and augmentation) measures. (5) Synthetic difference-in-differences (separate candidate). Verdict (Sep 2026): measures 'remain flat, lie within historical ranges, or continue along pre-AI trends'. The authors urge 'preregistering areas where we would expect to see the impact' but have published no thresholds.
candidates.data_source: CPS basic monthly microdata, with downloadable data. The Oct 2025 piece says they will monitor 'monthly'; the tracker says it will update 'regularly'. Actual cadence so far: Oct 2025, Jan 2026, Jul 2026, Sep 2026.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Weakly. The dissimilarity index 'does not take a stance on the cause' of reallocation, and historical comparison gives context, not attribution. The exposure-of-the-unemployed measure is AI-specific but misses never-hired entrants: the Dallas Fed notes that the CPS records the most recent occupation.
candidates.evidence_quote: does not provide clear evidence of labor market disruption associated with AI

candidates.name: Yale Budget Lab synthetic difference-in-differences of exposed versus unexposed occupations (Gimbel, Kendall, Nunn, 7 May 2026)
candidates.who_uses_it: The Budget Lab tracker (one of its three analytic sections). Stanford DEL (Research Note 1) cites it. Chen et al. (arXiv 2509.15510) use a similar synthetic DiD and find higher earnings and unchanged unemployment in highly exposed occupations.
candidates.definition: Synthetic DiD (Arkhangelsky et al. 2021). Treated units are the top tercile of occupations by AI exposure; donors are the bottom tercile. Terciles are unweighted. Quarter-of-year effects are removed at the detailed-occupation level. Outcome: an occupation's average employment share of the civilian population. Log real median hourly wages are also examined, and the appendix shows unemployment rates. The event date is 2022Q4. Result: 'no clear evidence of AI effects'. The appendix unemployment effect in the latest quarter is about +0.5 point overall and larger for ages 16-34, but not significant as of 2026Q1. Cyclicality fact: over 1994-2019, exposed occupations' employment is less procyclical against the CBO output gap. Important caveat the researcher omitted: the authors 'do not find the same pattern' of reduced cyclical sensitivity over the last few years. No threshold.
candidates.data_source: CPS (BLS) occupation-level quarterly data; the page links data and code. Periodic updates.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Yes. This is the design most directly aimed at the cyclical confound, because it builds a weighted comparison group that matches exposed occupations before 2022. The idea that 'a recession moves exposed minus unexposed opposite to an AI shock' rests on the 1994-2019 cyclicality pattern, which the authors say did not hold recently. So it needs testing and cannot be assumed.
candidates.evidence_quote: AI-exposed occupations are generally less sensitive to the business cycle than unexposed occupations

candidates.name: Dallas Fed CPS replication of the canaries measure (Atkinson and Yamco, 6 Jan 2026)
candidates.who_uses_it: Dallas Fed Economics article (one-off). It shows the Stanford pattern can be approximated with public CPS data.
candidates.definition: CPS public microdata with the same 0-1 exposure measure as Stanford. Occupations are split into least, moderate and most exposed by tertiles of the 2024 employment-weighted score distribution, held fixed over time. Ages: young (20-24) and prime (25-55). 12-month moving averages. Statistics: (a) employment share of the young, most-exposed group, 16.4% in Nov 2022 to 15.5% in Sep 2025; (b) flows from employment into unemployment, with no rise; (c) job-finding of the unemployed, tracking other groups; (d) job-finding of labour-market entrants, down more than 3 points since the Nov 2023 peak for young, most-exposed workers, 'not a typical cyclical phenomenon'. Upper bound: 0.1 point of aggregate unemployment since Nov 2022. The authors deliberately do not use the occupation of the unemployed, because the CPS records the most recent job. No threshold.
candidates.data_source: CPS basic monthly public-use microdata (Census/BLS). One-off, not maintained as a tracker. Release lag not verified.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Partly: an age-by-exposure comparison, plus a check against past business cycles. The authors caution it may not be causal and could reflect correlates such as education.
candidates.evidence_quote: This is an early sign to watch as AI's development continues.

candidates.name: St. Louis Fed: cross-occupation correlation of AI exposure with the rise in unemployment (Ozkan and Sullivan, 26 Aug 2025)
candidates.who_uses_it: St. Louis Fed On the Economy blog (one-off). Wide press citation not verified.
candidates.definition: Correlation across occupations between Eloundou et al. (2024) exposure and the change in the 3-month-average (May-July) unemployment rate from 2022 to 2025: 0.47. Using Real-Time Population Survey AI adoption instead gives 0.57. No threshold; the authors say monitoring 'becomes increasingly critical'.
candidates.data_source: CPS unemployment by occupation (BLS); the Real-Time Population Survey (Bick, Blandin and Deming, per the Fed Board note), whose GenAI module is quarterly since Aug 2024; Eloundou et al. exposure.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Weakly. It is a cross-sectional correlation with no control for differing cyclical sensitivity. The authors cite uncertainty, monetary tightening and chance timing as alternatives.
candidates.evidence_quote: The findings presented here represent correlation, not causation.

candidates.name: Unemployment rate by AI-exposure quintile (EIG, Eckhardt and Goldschlag, Aug 2025; SIEPR, Mahoney, McEntarfer and Wahal, mid-2026)
candidates.who_uses_it: Economic Innovation Group ('AI and Jobs: The Final Word (Until the Next One)', with public code, 'accurate as of' 10 Aug 2025). SIEPR's policy brief updates and extends it with the replication code. Stanford DEL (Research Note 1) cites EIG. No threshold.
candidates.definition: Occupations are split into five equal quintiles by exposure. EIG's primary measure is Felten et al. AIOE, with Eloundou et al., Eisfeldt et al. and Webb as robustness checks. Each quintile's unemployment rate is tracked. EIG (AIOE): from 2022 to early 2025 the most-exposed quintile rose 0.30 point and the least-exposed 0.94 point. Correction: under the Eloundou and Eisfeldt measures, the most exposed rose about 0.2 and 0.3 points relative to less-exposed workers (2022-23 vs 2024-25), so direction depends on the measure. SIEPR (IPUMS-CPS, quarterly to 2026): top quintile +0.77 point, least exposed +0.85 point since 2022. SIEPR also says that in Census (BTOS) data 'only 5 percent of firms report any employment impact', split equally between gains and losses.
candidates.data_source: CPS basic monthly, ASEC (via IPUMS) and ORG (via EPI); BTOS; exposure files. The EIG repo is a snapshot and is not updated.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Partly, via the exposure gradient. The AIOE result (least exposed rising more) looks like a general softening; SIEPR calls it 'a broadly softening labor market'. Other exposure measures show a small differential rise for the exposed.
candidates.evidence_quote: top quintile of AI-exposed workers has risen by 0.77 percentage points

candidates.name: NY Fed 'Labor Market for Recent College Graduates' (unemployment and underemployment of 22-27-year-olds with a bachelor's degree or more)
candidates.who_uses_it: NY Fed web feature, with data from 1990. SIEPR cites a new-graduate unemployment rate of 5.6% in early 2026, up 1.6 points in three years (SIEPR does not name the NY Fed series in the text I read). Now verified: a NY Fed Liberty Street post (Emanuel, Harrington and Pallais, 1 Jun 2026) estimates remote work 'can explain 64 percent' of the rise in young-graduate unemployment, and that remote work, 'not generative AI', explains most of it. Note that post uses its own age split (under 29, or 18-28 versus 29+).
candidates.definition: Unemployment and underemployment rates of early-career college graduates (ages 22-27, bachelor's degree or higher). 2026Q2: unemployment about 5.6%, underemployment 42%. No threshold.
candidates.data_source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York; the underlying survey is not stated on the page sections I read. Unemployment and underemployment are updated quarterly, 'generally in February, May, August, and November'; latest is 2026Q2.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It is sensitive to the cycle, to remote work (per the NY Fed's own June 2026 analysis) and to graduate supply.
candidates.evidence_quote: updated quarterly, generally in February, May, August, and November

candidates.name: Job postings by AI exposure (NY Fed Liberty Street, Audoly, Guerin and Topa, 14 May 2026; Fed Board FEDS Note, Liu and Webber, 27 Mar 2026)
candidates.who_uses_it: NY Fed (one-off). Fed Board staff say they 'plan to monitor it on an ongoing basis'. Earlier, pre-LLM academic version: Acemoglu, Autor, Hazell and Restrepo (NBER w28257, Dec 2020), using Burning Glass vacancies for 2010-2018.
candidates.definition: NY Fed: Lightcast postings for high- versus low-exposure occupations, using Anthropic's task-level exposure; an occupation is high exposure at 0.2 or above. A second event study compares junior and senior postings within exposed occupations. The divergence 'began before 2022' with no clear additional break after it, and junior versus senior shows no clear divergence. Fed Board: log Lightcast postings regressed on BTOS 3-digit-NAICS AI adoption and on firm-level AI/ML skill postings, lagged 1, 3, 6 and 12 months. Coefficients are generally positive; the authors call the firm-level results 'precisely-estimated null effects'. Acemoglu et al.: AI-exposed establishments cut non-AI hiring, but there is 'no discernible relationship' with employment or wages at occupation or industry level. No thresholds.
candidates.data_source: Lightcast (formerly Burning Glass) postings (proprietary); Census BTOS; O*NET; BLS OEWS.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Partly: timing of the break relative to Nov 2022, plus the exposure differential. Pre-trends dominate so far.
candidates.evidence_quote: does not show a clear additional break in trajectory after 2022

candidates.name: Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS) AI-use rate (official adoption statistic)
candidates.who_uses_it: U.S. Census Bureau (biweekly). Fed Board note 'Monitoring AI Adoption in the U.S. Economy' (Allen, 3 Apr 2026) tracks it alongside the Real-Time Population Survey and the Atlanta Fed Survey of Business Uncertainty. Also used by the Liu-Webber FEDS Note, SIEPR, EIG (repo data list) and Goldman ('Census Bureau data compiled by Goldman': 19.5% of establishments).
candidates.definition: Share of firms using AI. Correction: in Nov 2025 Census changed the question from 'to produce goods or services' to use in 'any of its business functions'. The roughly 18% at end-2025 in the Fed note is on the new wording; SIEPR cites about 20% currently. This measures adoption, not displacement, and has no threshold. Dropped as not verified: the '18% of firms, 32% employment-weighted' supplement figures. Census published a story on 26 May 2026 that AI use grew from Dec 2025 to May 2026.
candidates.data_source: Census BTOS. About 1.2M businesses in six panels of about 200,000; each firm reports every 12 weeks; data released every two weeks.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Measures AI adoption directly. SIEPR cites Census data showing about 5% of firms report any AI employment impact. It does not measure aggregate displacement.
candidates.evidence_quote: about 18 percent of firms have adopted AI as of year-end 2025

candidates.name: Goldman Sachs AI Adoption Tracker (Briggs, Dong) and AI unemployment estimates (Mei)
candidates.who_uses_it: Goldman Sachs Research, a client product, known here only through press: Fortune (1 Jun 2026) and Yahoo Finance (24 Feb 2026). Goldman's own report was not read.
candidates.definition: As reported by Fortune: net jobs lost to AI in AI-affected industries (marketing, graphic design, customer service, document processing, software), net of data-centre construction gains, are about 11,000 per month, down from about 16,000 two months earlier. Data centres add about 9,000 jobs a month. There is a 'slight positive correlation' across industries between AI adoption and unemployment of workers under 30. AI-attributed layoff announcements: about 21,900 in April, 136,000 over three years. Census-based adoption is 19.5% of establishments. Yahoo (Mei, Feb 2026): faster adoption 'could add up to an additional 0.3 percentage points' to 2026 unemployment. No threshold.
candidates.data_source: Proprietary Goldman compilation; the method is not public in what I read. Fortune's 'two months ago' suggests roughly bimonthly releases (not verified).
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Yes, by industry AI-readiness and adoption, but the method is not public, so it cannot anchor a falsifiable trigger.
candidates.evidence_quote: It is not yet a clean structural break

candidates.name: Revelio Labs AI Labor Market Tracker
candidates.who_uses_it: Revelio Labs (commercial). I read the August 2026 edition, which uses data through July 2026; monthly cadence not verified.
candidates.definition: Each work activity gets an AI exposure score of 0-1 from a large language model; occupation exposure aggregates its activities. The measure is benchmarked against Eloundou et al. (2023) and Felten et al. (2023), and headcount results are re-estimated with the Eloundou measure as a check. Event study, following the Brynjolfsson-Chandar-Chen design: top versus bottom exposure quintile, reference month Oct 2022, two-way fixed effects, 12-month centred rolling average, for postings and headcount. Also tracked: firm 'integrator' AI adoption (from postings for GenAI build roles), WARN-notice layoffs (a bootstrap DiD by quintile), posted wages, and an activity and occupation dissimilarity index. No threshold.
candidates.data_source: Proprietary professional profiles, deduplicated postings, sentiment data and state WARN notices.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: By the exposure differential relative to Oct 2022, plus adopter versus non-adopter firm comparisons.
candidates.evidence_quote: assigned an AI exposure score between 0 and 1 by a large language model

candidates.name: Humlum and Vestergaard, Denmark: adoption surveys linked to administrative records (NBER w33777, 'Still Waters, Rapid Currents', May 2025, revised Mar 2026)
candidates.who_uses_it: Academic (NBER; previously 'Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects'). Stanford DEL (Research Note 1) cites it as replicating the age pattern in Denmark, while noting firm-level changes are unrelated to whether firms encourage AI adoption. SIEPR also cites it. One-off.
candidates.definition: Difference-in-differences on earnings and recorded hours at worker and workplace level. Adoption surveys (about 25,000 workers in 7,000 workplaces, in 11 exposed occupations) are linked to Danish registers. Result: precise nulls, 'ruling out effects larger than 2%' two years after ChatGPT. The structure of work moves: task reorganization, and adopters moving to higher-paying occupations. No threshold.
candidates.data_source: Danish administrative registers plus the authors' surveys; not a recurring published series.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Yes, via measured worker and firm adoption rather than exposure. A template for countries with register data, not a trigger.
candidates.evidence_quote: ruling out effects larger than 2% two years after the launch of ChatGPT

candidates.name: Stanford DEL Transformation Tracker (called 'Takeoff Tracker' in Research Note 1): percentile classification of 12 macro indicators
candidates.who_uses_it: Stanford DEL AI Economic Indicators (Research Note 1, June 2026; page last updated 23 Sep 2026, 'updated on a monthly basis'). The only AI tracker found with explicit, pre-stated evidence thresholds.
candidates.definition: Share indicators are logit-transformed. Correction on the model: a linear time trend with AR(p) residuals is fitted from the sample start (typically 1997) to 2019 and bootstrapped with refitting. Post-2019 predictive draws are centred at each draw's refitted 2010 value, holding the trend flat after a 2010 kink. The one-year moving average of realizations is compared with the one-year moving average of simulated draws. At or below the 20th percentile is contradictory; the 80th to below the 95th is mild; the 95th or above is strong; otherwise neutral. Indicators: output growth, TFP growth, labour productivity growth, real rates (TIPS), capital share, two network-adjusted private capital shares, IT equipment share, software share of software and R&D, software and R&D share of fixed assets, primary energy, electricity generation. Correction on status: as of 23 Sep 2026, 6 are neutral, 4 mild (real rates, IT equipment share, software share, electricity) and 2 strong (capital share; software and R&D share). The '7 no evidence, 3 mild, 2 strong' split was the May 2026 status in Research Note 1. There is no unemployment or employment indicator; the capital share is the only labour-related one.
candidates.data_source: BEA fixed-asset and national-accounts data and TIPS yields are named on the page. The other sources (BLS productivity, EIA energy) and exact series codes are not verified. Monthly updates.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Built around an AI 'explosive growth' scenario, not labour displacement. The percentile-of-simulated-counterfactual rule is a reusable, pre-stated, falsifiable template.
candidates.evidence_quote: any realization at the 95th percentile or higher is classified as strong evidence

candidates.name: BLS nonfarm business labor share (FRED PRS85006173)
candidates.who_uses_it: Official BLS Productivity and Costs statistic. Stanford DEL's Transformation Tracker uses the complementary capital share (currently 'strong evidence'). Not used as an AI trigger by anyone I read.
candidates.definition: 'Nonfarm Business Sector: Labor Share for All Workers', index 2017=100, seasonally adjusted, quarterly. 2026Q2 93.446, down from 2026Q1 94.843 (2025Q3 95.999). No established AI threshold.
candidates.data_source: BLS Productivity and Costs via FRED, quarterly; last updated 3 Sep 2026.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It moves with the cycle and many structural forces.
candidates.evidence_quote: Nonfarm Business Sector: Labor Share for All Workers (FRED title)

candidates.name: Groshen-Potter structural versus cyclical industry test for jobless recoveries (NY Fed Current Issues 9(8), Aug 2003)
candidates.who_uses_it: NY Fed. Cited by Jaimovich and Siu (NBER w18334). A classic retrospective diagnostic, not a real-time series. Dropped: the Bernanke (2003) citation (not verified).
candidates.definition: About seventy two-digit SIC industries are plotted by job growth during the recession (NBER peak to trough) against job growth in the twelve months of recovery. Losses that reverse are cyclical; losses that continue are structural. Summing peak employment in the structural quadrants: the mid-1970s and early-1980s downturns were 'about half' structural (exact 51% figures not verified in the text), the early 1990s 57%, and 2001 79%. A second diagnostic: temporary layoffs contributed little to unemployment in 1990-91 and 2001. No formal threshold.
candidates.data_source: BLS CES payroll employment by industry (monthly); CPS reasons for unemployment; requires NBER peak and trough dates, which are announced with long lags.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It separates permanent reallocation (any cause) from cyclical swings, and needs a dated recession.
candidates.evidence_quote: 79 percent of employees worked in industries affected more by structural shifts

candidates.name: Jaimovich-Siu jobless recoveries and routine-job employment (NBER w18334)
candidates.who_uses_it: Academic (NBER WP Aug 2012, revised Nov 2018). The standard reference for the link between job polarization and jobless recoveries.
candidates.definition: Aggregate per-capita employment (band-pass filtered) kept falling after NBER troughs despite output recovery: for 17 months after 1991 (back to pre-recession level only in 1996), 23 months after 2001 (never back before the next recession) and 23 months after 2009. Routine per-capita employment fell 29 log points from 1990; 88% of the loss since the mid-1980s occurred within a 12-month window of NBER recessions. No threshold.
candidates.data_source: CPS employment by occupation (monthly); NBER dates; monthly real GDP (Stock-Watson).
candidates.attributes_to_ai: It attributes jobless recoveries to routine-biased technical change (automation, not AI). Correction to the researcher's inference: the model's trigger does not fire 'after every recession since 1990 by construction'. By my own calculation on the repo's UNRATE.csv and GDPC1.csv, it holds Oct 1975-Sep 1977, Feb-Mar and Jul-Sep 1981, Apr 1983-Jul 1985, Jul 1992-Jun 1993, Oct 2010-Dec 2013 (intermittently) and Jan-May 2021. It does not hold after 2001: the 12-month average peaked at 6.0% over 2001-2007, below 7.3%. The misfires also include the 1970s and 1980s recoveries, which were not jobless. So the root cause is the general lag of unemployment behind output (SF Fed Okun loops), not only jobless recoveries.
candidates.evidence_quote: these recoveries were jobless: despite expansions in other measures of economic activity

candidates.name: Okun's-law deviations or residuals (Daly, Fernald, Jordà and Nechio, SF Fed Economic Letter 2014-12; Meyer and Tasci, Cleveland Fed EC 2012-08; Ball, Leigh and Loungani, NBER w18668)
candidates.who_uses_it: Fed and IMF-affiliated research, used to discuss 'breakdowns' and jobless recoveries. Not used as a technology-displacement trigger in anything I read.
candidates.definition: SF Fed (21 Apr 2014): four-quarter change in unemployment against four-quarter growth of real GDP per person aged 16-64. From 1959 to 2013, each 1-point rise in unemployment goes with almost 2% lower output. Deviations trace counterclockwise loops in all four recessions examined, because employment lags GDP. Cleveland Fed (Jun 2012): 10-year rolling regressions of the quarterly change in unemployment on annualized GDP growth show unstable coefficients. Ball, Leigh and Loungani (Jan 2013): the law is 'strong and stable', and accounts of breakdowns via 'jobless recoveries' are flawed.
candidates.data_source: BEA real GDP (quarterly); BLS unemployment (monthly).
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. The authors attribute deviations to normal lagged dynamics and data revisions. This is also the mechanism behind the current trigger's false positives.
candidates.evidence_quote: temporary departures from the average relationship are part of the normal dynamic path

candidates.name: Abraham-Katz test of sectoral shifts versus aggregate demand (Lilien dispersion index plus help-wanted vacancies), NBER w1410
candidates.who_uses_it: Classic academic test (NBER WP July 1984; Journal of Political Economy, June 1986), the standard rebuttal to Lilien. I found no AI use.
candidates.definition: Lilien's G is the dispersion of employment growth across sectors. Abraham and Katz show aggregate demand alone can produce a positive G-unemployment correlation. Two tests: G is negatively related to help-wanted advertising, and G is tied to the change rather than the level of unemployment. Both support the aggregate-demand reading. They then build a demand-purged proxy for sectoral shifts. The 'reallocation shows up with vacancies not falling' reading is the implied Beveridge-curve logic, not a quoted rule. No threshold.
candidates.data_source: Modern analogues: BLS CES industry employment and JOLTS job openings, both monthly (JOLTS lag not verified).
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Not AI-specific, but it is the established way to tell reallocation (which AI displacement would be) from a demand recession.
candidates.evidence_quote: pure sectoral shifts have not been an important source of cyclical fluctuations

candidates.name: Şahin-Song-Topa-Violante mismatch index (NY Fed Staff Report 566, Aug 2012, revised Jun 2013)
candidates.who_uses_it: NY Fed research; the standard academic measure of structural 'mismatch' unemployment. Not verified: publication in the AER, and whether any maintained official series exists.
candidates.definition: M_t = 1 - sum_i (phi_it/phi-bar_t)(v_it/v_t)^alpha (u_it/u_t)^(1-alpha): the fraction of hires lost because job seekers are misallocated across sectors relative to vacancies. Computed by industry (JOLTS) and by 2- and 3-digit occupation (Conference Board HWOL), with counterfactual unemployment. Mismatch explains at most one-third of the Great Recession rise in unemployment; at the 3-digit occupation level its contribution is just over 1.5 points. No threshold.
candidates.data_source: JOLTS by industry; Conference Board Help Wanted OnLine by occupation; CPS unemployed by last occupation.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It measures structural reallocation from any cause.
candidates.evidence_quote: Mismatch across industries and occupations explains at most one-third

candidates.name: Sahm rule recession indicator (FRED SAHMREALTIME)
candidates.who_uses_it: A widely used real-time recession signal (Claudia Sahm; published on FRED). The clearest established unemployment-threshold rule, but it signals recessions, not AI.
candidates.definition: Signals a recession when the 3-month moving average of U-3 unemployment rises 0.50 point or more above the minimum 3-month average of the previous 12 months. Real-time vintage. Aug 2026: -0.07 (May 0.10, Jun 0.07, Jul -0.03).
candidates.data_source: BLS U-3 via FRED, monthly (last updated 4 Sep 2026).
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It could serve as the cyclical guard (do not count AI while the Sahm rule or an NBER recession is active) or as a template for a threshold rule.
candidates.evidence_quote: rises by 0.50 percentage points or more relative to the minimum

candidates.name: BLS Displaced Worker Survey (biennial January CPS supplement) and CPS permanent job losers (LNS13026638)
candidates.who_uses_it: Official BLS statistics; the survey has run 'biennially in January' since 1984. Groshen and Potter used the permanent versus temporary layoff split to diagnose structural change.
candidates.definition: DWS: workers aged 20 and over with 3 or more years' tenure who lost jobs to plant closure or move, insufficient work, or a position or shift being abolished. Release of 27 Aug 2026 (survey Jan 2026, covering Jan 2023-Dec 2025): 3.3M long-tenured displaced workers, up 746,000 from the prior survey. Shares: 44.4% position or shift abolished, 32.6% plant closed or moved, 22.9% insufficient work. Permanent job losers: 1,777k in Aug 2026 (seasonally adjusted, monthly). No AI threshold.
candidates.data_source: BLS CPS supplement, every other January, released in late summer. Next is Jan 2028 with release around Aug 2028 (inferred from the biennial pattern). Permanent job losers: monthly via FRED (last updated 4 Sep 2026).
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. The reason codes do not identify technology; 'position or shift abolished' is the closest proxy.
candidates.evidence_quote: 44.4 percent lost their job because their position or shift was abolished

candidates.name: Occupational AI-exposure measures used as weights (Eloundou et al. 'GPTs are GPTs'; Felten-Raj-Seamans AIOE; Webb 2020 patents; ILO 2025 global index)
candidates.who_uses_it: Eloundou et al. is used by Stanford DEL, the Yale Budget Lab, the Dallas Fed, the St. Louis Fed, Anthropic (as the feasibility input) and Revelio (as a benchmark). AIOE is EIG's primary measure; EIG also uses Webb and Eisfeldt et al. The ILO index covers ISCO-08 occupations worldwide, which suits the model's non-US countries. Frank et al. (arXiv 2308.02624) find individual exposure models do not predict unemployment risk but an ensemble does. Dropped: the IMF index (page returned 403 for the researcher; not read).
candidates.definition: Static scores, not signals. Eloundou et al.: tasks an LLM could make at least twice as fast (beta: 1 for the LLM alone, 0.5 with tools). About 80% of workers have at least 10% of tasks affected; about 19% have at least 50%. AIOE: AI application-to-ability relatedness (from an mTurk survey), by 6-digit SOC, with 4-digit NAICS industry and county versions (the '10 applications by 52 abilities' detail is not verified from the README). Webb: overlap between patent text and job-task text. ILO 2025: four exposure gradients at the 6-digit ISCO level, from nearly 30,000 tasks; one in four workers globally is in an occupation with some exposure.
candidates.data_source: O*NET, patents, and ILO/ISCO task data; one-off releases with occasional updates.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: These supply the 'which occupations' weights that make a differential signal AI-specific. Kolko (PIIE, 10 Mar 2026) says the measures 'do not entirely agree' and results 'can be sensitive to which AI measure is chosen'. EIG's sign flip across measures is an example.
candidates.evidence_quote: individual AI exposure models are not predictive of unemployment rates
