raw.summary:
Short answer: nobody has adopted a rule that separates AI displacement from a recession at the national level. I checked every automatic labour-market trigger I could find in law or in serious proposals, and all of them respond to unemployment of any cause. Some were designed to be cyclical on purpose (Sahm 2019 says the trigger should switch on during a cyclical downturn). These are the Sahm rule, the US Extended Benefits IUR/TUR triggers, Canada's EI regional rates and German Kurzarbeit.

Established rules that do assign a cause all work case by case, at the level of a firm or a worker. None of them is a single national reading that settles on a known date:
- US Trade Adjustment Assistance: the Labor Department certifies petitions where imports "contributed importantly". It lapsed in 2022.
- The EU Globalisation Adjustment Fund: it needs at least 200 redundancies, and since 2021 it can cover restructuring caused by automation or digitisation.
- Germany's Transfer-Kurzarbeitergeld (permanent job loss from restructuring) versus ordinary Kurzarbeitergeld (temporary loss).
- The New York WARN-notice checkbox (March 2025): zero of 160+ filers ticked it in its first year.
- The Challenger, Gray & Christmas layoff-reason tally: AI was cited for 116,175 announced cuts from January to August 2026, about 22%.

Proposals from 2025-26 show that legislators are running into the same attribution problem:
- S.3108 / H.R.9352 (Hawley-Warner) would make firms and agencies report each quarter the layoffs "substantially due to" AI, with BLS publishing within 60 days.
- S.5055 (Warner, July 2026) explicitly does not require proof that AI was the cause; it targets workers using labour-market indicators instead.
- S.3339 asks the Labor Department to work out what "thresholds of evidence" would decide who counts as displaced by AI.
- H.R.10044 (Casar, August 2026) sets an AI token tax whose rate rises with BLS U-4 unemployment. Its only AI-versus-other-causes test is Treasury's discretion to discount unemployment caused by war, pandemic or other shocks unrelated to AI.

The published framework closest to the model's trigger is Anthropic's Economic Policy Framework (June 2026). It uses the unemployment rate as the primary trigger, in tiers of about 5%, about 10%, and above historical peaks. The top tier is described as unemployment never before sustained alongside record output, which is the model's rule in words. Anthropic does not turn this into a formula: it names no series, averaging window or exact threshold, and it gives no test for AI versus a recession.

Computed this session (approximate, because it mixes real-time Sahm values with current-vintage GDP from the repo's GDPC1.csv): adding "real GDP at or above its previous peak" to the Sahm rule does not remove the false alarms after recessions. It still fires in 1961, 1971, 1992, 2002, 2008 and 2024.

What the model could adopt:
1. Use an established unemployment component with statutory wording. Options: the Sahm on/off rule as drafted in S.2312, which would also have BLS state the determination in each monthly jobs report; the Extended Benefits TUR thresholds (6.5% or 8% with a 110% lookback); or the Chodorow-Reich and Coglianese 9%/10% levels with no lookback.
2. Resolve the timing questions against Anthropic's published tiers, which are an adopted, citable framing, rather than a bespoke +3-point rule.
3. For attribution, add an established published cause-coded series. Challenger's AI-cited share is monthly and has run since 2023, but it counts self-reported announcements. BLS series under S.3108 would exist only if it is enacted. Say plainly that attribution is not established anywhere.

Several sources could not be checked: OpenAI and DOL pages (403), EUR-Lex (bot check), and BLS. The session-wide WebSearch budget ran out partway through, so later discovery used the GovInfo and Congress.gov APIs and known URLs. Scratch files are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Applications/da707ee8-bdb9-43d0-bb83-c08c894e427d/scratchpad/wf-signal/policy/.

candidates.name: Sahm rule (real-time recession indicator)
candidates.who_uses_it: Proposed by Claudia Sahm in the Hamilton Project's 'Recession Ready' (May 2019) as the trigger for automatic stimulus payments. St. Louis Fed publishes it daily-updated on FRED (SAHMREALTIME, source 'Claudia Sahm'). Written almost word for word into S.2312 / H.R.4439, the Unemployment Insurance Modernization and Recession Readiness Act (Wyden plus 6 cosponsors, July 16, 2025; still in Finance Committee per the Congress.gov API) as the 'Elevated National Unemployment Trigger'. That bill would make BLS print an on/off determination in every monthly Employment Situation report. Widely watched by markets; it is not an enacted policy trigger anywhere.
candidates.definition: On when the 3-month moving average of the national U-3 unemployment rate is at least 0.50 percentage points above the minimum 3-month average of the previous 12 months (FRED definition). The S.2312 version adds an off rule. It turns off when the 3-month average has fallen for at least 2 consecutive months, is below 5.5%, and is less than 1.5 points above its level in the first 'on' week. FRED uses the real-time unemployment data available in each month.
candidates.data_source: BLS Current Population Survey U-3 (UNRATE). FRED SAHMREALTIME, monthly, published with the Employment Situation release (usually the first Friday). Latest reading: August 2026 = -0.07 points, updated Sept 4, 2026. Computed from the FRED CSV this session, first crossings of 0.50 since 1960 were: 1959-12, 1960-08, 1969-10, 1970-02, 1974-03, 1974-07, 1976-11, 1980-04, 1981-11, 1990-11, 2001-06, 2008-04, 2020-04 and 2024-07 (0.53).
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. Sahm designed it to switch on during a cyclical downturn (paraphrased from Sahm 2019, p.78), and it uses changes rather than a fixed level so that it adapts to shifts in the natural rate. Computed check (approximate: real-time Sahm values against current-vintage GDPC1 from the repo, prior quarter): adding 'real GDP at or above its previous peak' still fires in 1961, 1970-71, 1974, 1976, 1980-81, 1990, 1992, 2001-02, 2008 and 2024. So it does not fix the problem that unemployment lags output in recoveries.
candidates.evidence_quote: is at least 0.5 percentage points higher than the lowest average rate (S.2312 sec.102(b))

candidates.name: Sahm (2019) automatic stimulus payment rule: an unemployment-triggered cash payment
candidates.who_uses_it: A Hamilton Project / Washington Center for Equitable Growth policy proposal, chapter 3 of 'Recession Ready' (2019). Not enacted. It is the best-known serious proposal that ties universal lump-sum cash payments to a published unemployment trigger.
candidates.definition: 1) First payment: when the Sahm trigger turns on, pay lump sums totalling 0.7% of GDP in year 1. 2) Second year: if unemployment rises a further 2.0 points or more from the rate at the initial trigger within the next four quarters, pay another 0.7% of pre-recession GDP. 3) Later years: payments continue each year until unemployment is no more than 2 points above its level at the first trigger. After the peak (or after year 2, whichever is later) they scale down by (current - prerecession - 2) / (peak - prerecession - 2). Sahm notes the trigger could either pay out automatically or start a congressional vote. In her back-test, second rounds would have occurred only in 1973-75, 1981-82 and 2008-09.
candidates.data_source: The same monthly BLS U-3 series (real-time), released with the Employment Situation report.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It is explicitly counter-cyclical. It is still a ready-made, published template for 'payment level as a function of the unemployment path', which the model's shock payment could borrow.

candidates.name: Federal-State Extended Benefits (EB) triggers: IUR/TUR
candidates.who_uses_it: US law since 1970 (Federal-State Extended Unemployment Compensation Act; regulation 20 CFR 615.12). The Labor Department (ETA/OUI) computes on/off status for every state each week and publishes it in a Trigger Notice. The mandatory IUR trigger applies in every state. The TUR option is written into law in only 12 jurisdictions, according to Trigger Notice 2026-37 (AK, CT, KS, ME, MN, NH, NJ, NM, OR, RI, VT, WA). Chodorow-Reich and Coglianese (Hamilton 2019) note that except during 2009-13 no more than 11 states ever adopted the optional triggers.
candidates.definition: Tier 1 (13 extra weeks) switches on in any of three ways. (a) Mandatory: the 13-week insured unemployment rate (not seasonally adjusted) is at least 5.0% and at least 120% of the average for the same 13-week periods in each of the two preceding years. (b) Optional: IUR at least 6.0%, with no lookback. (c) Optional: the 3-month average seasonally adjusted TUR is at least 6.5% and at least 110% of the same 3-month period in either or both of the prior two years. High-unemployment period, optional (20 weeks in total, which is 7 more): TUR at least 8.0%, with the same 110% lookback. Once on or off, a state stays that way for at least 13 weeks. Chodorow-Reich and Coglianese found the lookback forces states off EB precisely during long, lasting unemployment. They propose removing it and adding TUR triggers at 9% (60 total weeks) and 10% (73 weeks). S.2312 (2025) would instead set a 5.5% state/national TUR trigger with no lookback, plus tiers at 6.5, 7.5 and 8.5%.
candidates.data_source: DOL ETA weekly 'Trigger Notice Report' (oui.doleta.gov/unemploy/trigger/YYYY/trig_MMDDYY.html). The IUR covers the 13 weeks ending about 2 weeks before the notice; the TUR is the BLS LAUS seasonally adjusted 3-month average. Notice No. 2026-37, effective Sept 27, 2026: 'Total Number ON: 0'. The IUR covers the period ending Sept 12, 2026 and the TUR the 3 months ending August 2026; the highest TURs were Puerto Rico 6.0 and DC 5.9.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. Levels and year-on-year growth ratios only. The 2-year lookback would switch EB off during a persistent AI-driven rise, which is the opposite of what the model needs. The level-only variants (6% IUR, and the proposed 9%/10% TUR or 5.5% TUR with no lookback) avoid that.
candidates.evidence_quote: equals or exceeds 110 percent of the Trigger Value for either (or both) (20 CFR 615.12)

candidates.name: Anthropic Economic Policy Framework (June 2026): unemployment-rate tiers for an AI labour shock
candidates.who_uses_it: Published by Anthropic (an AI lab) as part of 'Policy on the AI Exponential', aimed at US federal policy. It comes with $350M of commitments ($200M Economic Futures Research Fund, $150M fellowship). This is the closest published analogue to the model's trigger. It is a company framework, not law, and I found no government that has adopted it. It builds on Anthropic's October 14, 2025 post, which sorted policy ideas into 'nearly all', 'moderate acceleration' and 'fast-moving' scenarios.
candidates.definition: The unemployment rate is the primary trigger, alongside labour force participation, underemployment, wages and labour's share of income. Tier 1: about 5% unemployment with churn. Tier 2: 'recession-level' disruption at about 10% unemployment, with expanded UI; it also proposes reforming the EB trigger so extensions become automatic and uniform across states. Tier 3: unemployment above historical peaks alongside record output, possibly calling for UBI, sovereign wealth funds or token/compute levies. Thresholds are approximate. The framework names no series (U-3 vs U-6), averaging window or duration. It proposes a government unit to flag the early signals that should trigger a policy response.
candidates.data_source: Not specified. The framework calls for new AI-specific survey instruments and reporting requirements, and cites the Anthropic Economic Index, Brynjolfsson et al. (2025, 'Canaries in the Coal Mine') and Massenkoff & McCrory (2026) as exposure-based evidence.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Only in concept. It separates a temporary shock from an enduring restructuring, and says unemployment alongside rapid productivity growth would be 'more structural than cyclical'. It gives no operational test, and its Tier 2 is explicitly 'recession-level', so a recession would satisfy it.
candidates.evidence_quote: unemployment at levels never before sustained alongside an economy generating record output

candidates.name: AI Tax and Work Protection Act (H.R.10044, 2026): AI token tax indexed to U-4
candidates.who_uses_it: Introduced August 6, 2026 by Rep. Casar with Reps. Foushee and Jacobs (4 cosponsors per the Congress.gov API). Referred to Education & Workforce and Ways & Means; no further action. Revenue goes to a trust fund and a Work Protection Administration / Office of Job Creation at the Labor Department. It is the only bill I found that ties an AI-specific tax to an unemployment measure.
candidates.definition: The excise tax on foundation-model developers or sellers is the greater of two amounts: token value times the token percentage, or AI-services consideration times the transaction percentage. Covered models are trained with at least 10^25 FLOP. Token percentage: 2% if the 'applicable unemployment rate' is at or below 5%; 2% plus the excess over 5% between 5% and 7%; 2% plus twice the excess over 5% above 7%. The transaction percentage has the same form from a 3% base. The applicable rate is BLS U-4, taken from the Employment Situation release for the highest calendar year in the 3 years before the transaction; years before enactment do not count. Sec.4491(c): Treasury, in consultation with Labor, may disregard the part of unemployment above 5% caused by war, pandemic or another shock unrelated to AI.
candidates.data_source: BLS U-4 (unemployed plus discouraged workers), annual averages from the monthly Employment Situation release.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Partly, through a discretionary Treasury carve-out rather than a formula. It is the only statutory text found that explicitly tries to exclude non-AI unemployment.
candidates.evidence_quote: any other massive economic shock unrelated to the use of artificial intelligence (H.R.10044 sec.101)

candidates.name: AI-Related Job Impacts Clarity Act (S.3108 / H.R.9352): proposed BLS series of AI-attributed layoffs
candidates.who_uses_it: Senate bill introduced November 5, 2025 by Sen. Hawley for himself and Sen. Warner (3 cosponsors per the Congress.gov API; referred to HELP). House companion H.R.9352 introduced June 18, 2026. Neither has moved past committee. Hawley's release says AI could push unemployment to 10-20% within five years. Not enacted.
candidates.definition: Publicly traded companies, federal agencies and non-public firms the Labor Department designates by rule must report within 30 days of each quarter's end. They report: layoffs 'substantially due to' AI replacing or automating the workers' functions; hires substantially due to AI; positions filled in the prior quarter but left unfilled because of AI; and workers being retrained because of AI; all with NAICS codes. The Labor Department must publish quarterly summaries, plus a net-impact analysis every other quarter, on the BLS website within 60 days of quarter end.
candidates.data_source: Would be a new quarterly Labor Department/BLS series, possibly collected through an existing DOL or Census survey. Does not exist yet.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Yes, if enacted: attribution by the employer's own report ('substantially due to'). It would give quarterly counts on known dates, but inherits the underreporting problem seen with New York's WARN checkbox.
candidates.evidence_quote: substantially due to the replacement or automation by artificial intelligence (S.3108 sec.2(a))

candidates.name: National Workforce Transition Fund Act of 2026 (S.5055) and AI Workforce PREPARE Act (S.3339): indicator-based eligibility instead of proving AI caused the job loss
candidates.who_uses_it: S.5055: Sen. Warner, July 21, 2026, referred to Finance with no cosponsors listed. It would replace WIOA Title III with a temporary fund financed through AI data-centre property rules. S.3339: Sens. Banks, Hassan, Hickenlooper and Husted, December 3, 2025, referred to HELP. It orders a Labor Department study of 'rapid AI adjustment assistance' modelled on TAA and adds AI questions to the CPS, Annual Business Survey, BTOS, Occupational Requirements Survey and ATUS. Neither is enacted.
candidates.definition: S.5055: no worker has to show that AI or emerging technology was the sole or primary cause of their disruption. The Secretary picks priority groups using UI claims, wage records, occupational employment trends, entry-level hiring trends, employer reports, sector disruption, regional displacement, wage losses, and exposure to AI or emerging technology. S.3339 asks how to 'rapidly and reliably determine' who counts as an AI-impacted worker, what thresholds of evidence to use, and whether a petition-based or tiered system fits.
candidates.data_source: A mix of existing administrative and survey data, chosen at the Secretary's discretion. There is no fixed formula or release date.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Deliberately not at the individual level. Legislators treat proving AI caused a job loss as unworkable and fall back on exposure-weighted labour-market indicators.
candidates.evidence_quote: rather than requiring individual workers to prove that artificial intelligence (S.5055 sec.301)

candidates.name: Trade Adjustment Assistance (TAA) group certification: the established cause-specific displacement test, and 'Automation Adjustment Assistance' proposals
candidates.who_uses_it: US law since 1974 (19 U.S.C. 2272). New certifications stopped when authority lapsed in 2022; Sen. Fetterman's release says 200,000 laid-off workers applied and received nothing. Reauthorization bills include the Sánchez TAA Modernization Act (March 4, 2026), which does not mention AI or automation. Anthropic's October 2025 post cites Marinescu's 'AI insurance' and a Mittal & Manning 'Automation Adjustment Assistance' idea funded at TAA-like levels (about $700M a year). I did not read the primary text of that idea.
candidates.definition: The Labor Department certifies a group of workers when a significant number or proportion of the firm's workers have been separated or threatened, and either (a) imports of like or directly competitive articles increased and contributed importantly to the separation, or (b) production shifted abroad. 'Contributed importantly' means a cause that is important but not necessarily more important than any other. The statute sets no number for 'significant number or proportion'. Certification is petition by petition, on no fixed schedule.
candidates.data_source: DOL ETA TAA petition determinations; the DOL pages returned 403 this session, so not verified.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Attributes cause (trade), case by case through administrative adjudication; it does not cover AI. It is the model most AI-adjustment proposals copy, and it gives no national on/off signal.
candidates.evidence_quote: a cause which is important but not necessarily more important than any other cause (19 U.S.C. 2272(c)(1))

candidates.name: European Globalisation Adjustment Fund for Displaced Workers (EGF 2021-2027): 200-redundancy restructuring test including automation
candidates.who_uses_it: EU law, Regulation (EU) 2021/691. The Commission decides each application from a member state and reports every two years (COM(2023) 482, August 11, 2023). Between 2007 and 2022 it received 177 applications, which it classifies as 91 crisis-related and 85 trade-related.
candidates.definition: At least 200 workers made redundant over a 4-month reference period in one enterprise, including suppliers and downstream producers (Art. 4(2)(a)); other reference periods apply for SMEs in a sector or region. There is a derogation for small labour markets with serious local impact. From 2021 the scope covers 'any major restructuring event', including globalisation, financial or economic crises, the low-carbon transition, digitisation or automation. The threshold was cut from 500 to 200 workers.
candidates.data_source: Commission EGF decisions and biennial reports, published at irregular dates. I read the report via a PDF copy on irshare.eu; EUR-Lex itself showed a bot check and was not bypassed.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Yes, at case level: each application must name the restructuring cause, and automation/digitisation became eligible in 2021. It is not a macro indicator, and I found no evidence of any application attributed to AI.

candidates.name: Germany: Kurzarbeitergeld (temporary) vs Transferkurzarbeitergeld (permanent restructuring), SGB III §96 and §111
candidates.who_uses_it: German federal law, administered by the Bundesagentur für Arbeit.
candidates.definition: Ordinary Kurzarbeitergeld (§96): the loss of work is significant if it rests on economic reasons or an unavoidable event, is temporary and unavoidable, and in the calendar month at least one-third of employees lose more than 10% of gross pay. §96(2) counts structural change caused by general economic development as an economic reason. Losses that are typical for the industry or firm, seasonal, or purely organisational count as avoidable. Transferkurzarbeitergeld (§111) applies when a restructuring (Betriebsänderung) permanently removes employment opportunities. Affected workers are grouped in a separate transfer unit, and the benefit lasts at most 12 months.
candidates.data_source: Bundesagentur für Arbeit monthly short-time work statistics (not fetched this session).
candidates.attributes_to_ai: It separates temporary (cyclical) from permanent (structural) loss at firm level, but not AI specifically. The ratio of Transfer-KuG to ordinary KuG counts could in principle be a structural-versus-cyclical component (untested).
candidates.evidence_quote: auf Grund einer Betriebsänderung ... die Beschäftigungsmöglichkeiten ... nicht nur vorübergehend entfallen (§111(2) SGB III)

candidates.name: Canada Employment Insurance: regional unemployment-rate entitlement
candidates.who_uses_it: Canadian federal EI program (Employment and Social Development Canada), with rates produced by Statistics Canada for about 60 EI economic regions.
candidates.definition: The hours needed to qualify and the maximum weeks of benefits depend on the regional unemployment rate, a seasonally adjusted 3-month moving average (territories use the greater of the 3-month and 12-month averages). Low-unemployment regions require 700 insured hours for fewer weeks; high-unemployment regions require as few as 420 hours for up to 45 weeks. Parameters are reset about every four weeks; the current period runs September 6 to October 10, 2026.
candidates.data_source: Statistics Canada Labour Force Survey regional rates, published on the ESDC 'EI program characteristics' page.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No; it responds to unemployment level only.

candidates.name: New York WARN notice AI/automation checkbox
candidates.who_uses_it: New York State Department of Labor, on the Governor's direction (January 2025); it is a change to the form, not the statute. It has been live since March 2025 and applies to WARN filers with 50 or more employees.
candidates.definition: Employers filing a WARN notice must tick whether the job losses relate to 'technological innovation or automation' and, if so, name the technology (for example AI or robotic process automation). A Hunton law-firm post (May 18, 2026) reports that none of 160+ filers ticked it in the first year.
candidates.data_source: NY DOL WARN notice filings, posted continuously. I did not read the NY DOL dashboard itself this session.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Yes, by employer self-report. The zero count after a year shows self-report badly undercounts, compared with Challenger's AI attributions in press announcements.

candidates.name: Challenger, Gray & Christmas job-cut reasons: 'Artificial Intelligence' category
candidates.who_uses_it: A private outplacement firm's monthly job-cuts report, widely reported in the press (I did not check the press coverage itself). It has tracked AI as a separate reason since 2023. It also uses a 'Technological Update (possibly AI)' category when AI is hinted at but not directly tied to the cuts (20,219 cuts in 2025).
candidates.definition: Announced US job cuts are coded by the reason the employer gives. July 2026 report (published Aug 6): AI led all reasons for the fifth straight month, with 10,970 of 33,429 cuts (33%); 184,538 AI-cited cuts since 2023. August 2026 report (published Sep 2): AI fell to fourth place with 3,462 cuts, but led year to date with 116,175 cuts (about 22% of all cuts).
candidates.data_source: Monthly, usually published in the first week of the following month.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Yes, by the employer's stated reason in announcements, as coded by Challenger. These are announced plans, not realised layoffs, so they are open to 'AI-washing' and are not an official statistic.

candidates.name: Altman 'American Equity Fund' (Moore's Law for Everything, March 16, 2021)
candidates.who_uses_it: An essay by Sam Altman, framed as a conversation starter. I found no legislation or OpenAI policy adopting it; OpenAI's policy pages returned 403, so not verified.
candidates.definition: An annual 2.5% tax on the market value of companies above a size threshold (paid in shares) and on privately held land (paid in dollars). Every adult citizen gets an annual distribution; Altman projects about $13,500 a year within a decade. The rate phases in, and the full 2.5% applies only once GDP has grown 50% from when the law passes.
candidates.data_source: None specified. The phase-in would resolve from BEA real GDP.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No displacement test at all. Payments are unconditional, and the only trigger is output growth (the abundance side), not unemployment.

candidates.name: Windfall Clause (O'Keefe, Cihon, Garfinkel, Flynn, Leung, Dafoe; 2019/2020)
candidates.who_uses_it: An academic proposal (arXiv 1912.11595, AIES 2020) for voluntary ex ante commitments by AI firms. I found no evidence that any firm has signed one (not verified).
candidates.definition: A firm donates a marginal share of profits that scales with its profits as a share of gross world product: 0% below 0.1% of GWP, 1% of marginal profits from 0.1% to 1%, 20% from 1% to 10%, and 50% from 10% to 100%.
candidates.data_source: Firm financial statements plus GWP (for example World Bank or IMF), reported annually.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Indirectly. It triggers on AI-firm windfall profits rather than unemployment, so a recession cannot set it off. That makes it an AI-specific signal on the output side, not a labour-displacement measure.

candidates.name: South Korea 2026: Basic Income Planning Team (planned 2027 pilot) and rural basic income pilot
candidates.who_uses_it: Korean Ministry of Health and Welfare, which set up a Basic Society Policy Task Force with a Basic Income Planning Team (reported April 10, 2026). Separately, the rural basic income pilot in selected depopulating counties (for example Okcheon and Yeoncheon) runs 2026-27; Okcheon started December 2025.
candidates.definition: The planned 2027 pilot is a conditional 'participation income' for young and middle-aged adults, justified by expected AI-driven structural unemployment. The article defines no measurable trigger. The rural pilot pays every registered resident 150,000 won a month in local vouchers regardless of income or job, again with no trigger.
candidates.data_source: None; no indicator is defined.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: AI appears only as the rationale; there is no operational test.

candidates.name: Robot or automation taxes (South Korea 2017, European Parliament 2017, de Blasio 2019)
candidates.who_uses_it: According to Wikipedia's 'Robot tax' article: South Korea cut tax breaks for automation investment (August 6, 2017), described as the first 'robot tax'. The European Parliament rejected the robot-tax part of the Delvaux robotics report in 2017. Bill de Blasio proposed in 2019 that large corporations pay five years of income tax for jobs automated away. I could not open the primary sources (The Hill returned 403).
candidates.definition: Korea: smaller investment incentives, with no displacement trigger. De Blasio: a per-job liability that needs someone to decide, case by case, which jobs were 'automated away'.
candidates.data_source: None published.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: De Blasio's version would need case-level attribution of automation; the others have no trigger.

Every rule that attributes a cause does it case by case: TAA, EGF, Transfer-KuG, NY WARN, Challenger, and the proposed S.3108.

verified.summary:
I re-checked all 16 candidates against their sources this session. Each claim was checked against the primary text where one exists: bill texts on govinfo, the CFR and U.S. Code on Cornell LII, SGB III on gesetze-im-internet.de, the FRED series and CSV, the Labor Department's Trigger Notice 2026-37, the Hamilton Project PDFs, and Anthropic's framework page and PDF. Where no primary text exists, I re-read the same secondary source the researcher cited: Hunton, Kaufman Dolowich, the Challenger posts, the Altman essay, arXiv, Asiae, the Korea Herald and Wikipedia. Bill status came from GovInfo BILLSTATUS XML, because the Congress.gov DEMO_KEY hit its rate limit partway through.

The researcher's main finding holds. No established indicator anywhere separates AI or technological unemployment from cyclical unemployment at the national level. Every automatic trigger that exists is cyclical by design: Sahm, Extended Benefits (EB) IUR/TUR, the S.2312 triggers, Canada's EI regional rates and German Kurzarbeit. Sahm 2019 says the trigger must "turn on during a cyclical downturn". Every rule that assigns a cause does it case by case: US Trade Adjustment Assistance (TAA), the EU Globalisation Adjustment Fund (EGF), German transfer short-time pay (Transfer-KuG), the NY WARN checkbox, Challenger's tally, and the proposed S.3108 and S.3339 section 204.

Anthropic's June 2026 Economic Policy Framework is confirmed as the closest published analogue to the model's trigger. It uses the unemployment rate as the "primary trigger", with tiers at about 5%, about 10% ("recession-level") and "unemployment exceeding historical peaks" alongside record output. It names no series, averaging window or duration, and gives no test for AI versus a recession.

All numeric claims checked out except the ones listed next. I corrected six factual errors:
1. SAHMREALTIME is updated monthly, not daily.
2. 1959-12 is where the series starts, not a crossing.
3. Okcheon was designated as a pilot site in December 2025; payments run 2026-27.
4. Altman's essay says only "GDP", not BEA real GDP.
5. The Canadian EI period shown is 5 weeks long, not "about four".
6. The Korean task force is the "Basic Social Policy Task Force".

I also added facts the researcher missed:
- H.R.9352's sponsor (Horsford) and cosponsors.
- S.3339's fifth cosponsor (Marshall).
- S.3339 sec. 204 would add a federal WARN statement requiring employers to say whether AI was a "substantial factor" and to estimate what percentage of the job loss it caused.
- TAA's regulatory threshold for a "significant number or proportion" of workers (20 CFR 618.110).
- H.R.10044's taxable transactions include a firm's own use of a foundation model when that use cuts its workforce.
- H.R.10044's token rate jumps discontinuously at a 7% unemployment rate (my own calculation from the bill text).

I reproduced the Sahm-plus-GDP-peak check. I used the repo's GDPC1.csv, taking the prior quarter as the latest available, against FRED SAHMREALTIME. The combined rule fires in 1961, 1969-71, 1974, 1976, 1980-81, 1990, 1992, 2001-02, 2008 and 2024. The researcher's list omitted 1969. It fires in two situations:
- at the start of recessions, because GDP has not yet fallen from its peak;
- in recoveries where jobs lag output (1961, 1971, 1992, 2002), and in the 2024 false alarm.

So adding a GDP condition does not fix the problem the review found.

Recommendation for the model: build the trigger from established parts, since there is no established AI-specific trigger to adopt.
- Unemployment component: use one with statutory wording that resolves on a published schedule. The candidates are FRED SAHMREALTIME (monthly, next release October 2, 2026), a level threshold with no lookback in the style of S.2312 or Chodorow-Reich and Coglianese (5.5%, 6.5%, 7.5%, 8.5% or 9%/10%), or the U-4 formula in H.R.10044.
- Attribution: label it plainly as not established anywhere. If a proxy is needed, Challenger's monthly AI-cited share is the only running cause-coded series, and it counts announcements, not realised layoffs.

I did not publish anything; the scratch files are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Applications/da707ee8-bdb9-43d0-bb83-c08c894e427d/scratchpad/wf-signal/verify-policy/fresh/.

candidates.name: Sahm rule (real-time recession indicator)
candidates.who_uses_it: Proposed by Claudia Sahm in the Hamilton Project's 'Recession Ready' (May 2019) as the trigger for automatic stimulus payments. FRED (St. Louis Fed) publishes it as SAHMREALTIME, source 'Sahm, Claudia', updated monthly. The FRED page shows 'Updated: Sep 4, 2026' and 'Next Release Date: Oct 2, 2026'. It is written almost word for word into S.2312, the Unemployment Insurance Modernization and Recession Readiness Act, as the 'Elevated National Unemployment Trigger'. S.2312 was introduced July 16, 2025 by Sen. Wyden with 6 cosponsors (Bennet, Reed, Warren, Sanders, Fetterman, Booker). Its latest action is referral to Finance on July 16, 2025, per the Congress.gov API. H.R.4439, sponsored by Rep. Beyer, has the same title and was introduced the same day; I did not compare the two texts. The S.2312 trigger would make the BLS Commissioner put an on/off determination in each monthly Employment Situation report. It is not an enacted policy trigger anywhere. The claim that it is 'widely watched by markets' was not verified this session.
candidates.definition: FRED: the rule signals when the 3-month moving average of the national U-3 unemployment rate rises by 0.50 percentage points or more above the minimum of the 3-month averages from the previous 12 months. FRED computes it from the real-time data available in each month. S.2312's version turns on when the average unemployment rate for all States (seasonally adjusted) over the latest 3 months is at least 0.5 points above the lowest 3-month average in the preceding 12 months. It turns off only when three conditions all hold: (i) the average has decreased for at least 2 consecutive months, (ii) it is below 5.5%, and (iii) it is less than 1.5 points above its level in the first 'on' week.
candidates.data_source: BLS Current Population Survey U-3, via FRED SAHMREALTIME. Monthly, released with the Employment Situation report. Latest value: August 2026 = -0.07 points (July -0.03, June 0.07). I recomputed first crossings of 0.50 from the FRED CSV this session: 1960-08, 1969-10, 1970-02, 1974-03, 1974-07, 1976-11, 1980-04, 1981-11, 1990-11, 2001-06, 2008-04, 2020-04 and 2024-07 (0.53). The series starts in 1959-12 at 0.77, so that first observation is not a crossing.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. Sahm 2019 (p.77) says the trigger must 'turn on during a cyclical downturn'. She uses changes rather than a fixed level so the trigger adapts to shifts in the natural rate. I reproduced a combined check using the repo's research/trigger/GDPC1.csv, taking the prior quarter as the latest available (approximate, because it mixes real-time Sahm values with current-vintage GDP). Requiring 'Sahm at or above 0.50 AND real GDP at its running peak' still fires in 1961, 1969-71, 1974, 1976, 1980-81, 1990, 1992, 2001-02, 2008 and 2024. That covers both recession onsets, where GDP has not yet fallen, and jobless recoveries, so it does not fix the recession false positives.
candidates.evidence_quote: is at least 0.5 percentage points higher than the lowest average rate (S.2312 sec.102(b))

candidates.name: Sahm (2019) automatic stimulus payment rule: an unemployment-triggered universal cash payment
candidates.who_uses_it: A policy proposal in the Hamilton Project's 'Recession Ready' (2019), in the chapter 'Direct Stimulus Payments to Individuals'. Not enacted. It is a serious published template that ties universal lump-sum payments to an unemployment trigger.
candidates.definition: 1) First year: when the 3-month average unemployment rate rises at least 0.50 points above its low in the prior 12 months, pay lump sums totalling 0.7% of GDP (about 1% of PCE). 2) Second year: if the unemployment rate rises 2.0 points or more above its level at the first trigger within the next four quarters, pay another 0.7% of pre-recession GDP. 3) Later years: payments continue until unemployment is no more than 2 points above its level at the first trigger. After the second year or the unemployment peak, whichever is later, the amount scales down by (current - prerecession - 2) / (peak - prerecession - 2). The paper's example: rates of 5%, 10% and 9% give 2/3 of the first-year amount (p.85). Sahm says the trigger could pay out automatically or instead start a congressional vote. In her back-test only the 1973-75, 1981-82 and 2008-09 recessions would have produced a second round.
candidates.data_source: The same national unemployment rate, monthly from the BLS Employment Situation release, using real-time data.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It is explicitly counter-cyclical. It is still a ready-made published schedule for 'payment size as a function of the unemployment path', which the model's shock payment could borrow.

candidates.name: Federal-State Extended Benefits (EB) triggers: IUR/TUR
candidates.who_uses_it: US law since 1970: the Federal-State Extended Unemployment Compensation Act, implemented by 20 CFR 615.12. The Labor Department's ETA/OUI publishes weekly Trigger Notices giving each state's on/off status. The IUR trigger is mandatory in every state. Trigger Notice 2026-37 shows the TUR option in the law of only 12 states: AK, CT, KS, ME, MN, NH, NJ, NM, OR, RI, VT and WA. Chodorow-Reich and Coglianese (Hamilton 2019) write that outside 2009-13, 'at no time have more than 11 states' adopted the optional triggers.
candidates.definition: 20 CFR 615.12 sets three routes to an 'on' indicator, which gives up to 13 extra weeks. (a) Mandatory: the 13-week insured unemployment rate (not seasonally adjusted) is at least 5.0% and at least 120% of the average of the same 13-week periods in each of the two preceding calendar years. (b) Optional: the IUR is at least 6.0%, with no 120% test. (e)(1) Optional: the 3-month TUR is at least 6.5% and at least 110% of the same 3-month period 'for either (or both)' of the two preceding years. (e)(2) Optional high-unemployment period: the same test at 8.0%, which gives up to 20 extra weeks in total (7 more). Per Chodorow-Reich and Coglianese, once a state triggers on or off a tier it stays there for at least 13 weeks. They propose removing the lookbacks and adding triggers at 9% (60 weeks of regular UI plus EB) and 10% (73 weeks). S.2312 would instead add a 5.5% state or national TUR trigger with no lookback, plus tiers at 6.5%, 7.5% and 8.5%.
candidates.data_source: DOL ETA weekly Trigger Notice (oui.doleta.gov/unemploy/trigger/YYYY/trig_MMDDYY.html). Notice No. 2026-37, effective Sept 27, 2026, shows 'Total Number ON: 0'. Its IUR covers the 13 weeks ending Sept 12, 2026, and its TUR is the seasonally adjusted average for the 3 months ending August 2026. The highest TURs are Puerto Rico 6.0 and DC 5.9.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It uses levels and ratios to prior years only. The 2-year lookback turns EB off during a long, persistent rise in unemployment, which is the opposite of what an AI-shock trigger needs. The level-only variants avoid this: the 6% IUR option, the S.2312 5.5% TUR, and the proposed 9%/10% TUR triggers.
candidates.evidence_quote: equals or exceeds 110 percent of the Trigger Value for either (or both) (20 CFR 615.12(e))

candidates.name: Anthropic Economic Policy Framework (June 2026): unemployment-rate tiers for AI labour disruption
candidates.who_uses_it: Published by Anthropic as part of 'Policy on the AI Exponential' and aimed at US federal policy. It comes with $350M of commitments: a $200M Economic Futures Research Fund and a $150M national fellowship. This is a company framework, not law; the researcher found no government that has adopted it. It follows Anthropic's Oct 14, 2025 post, 'Preparing for AI's economic impact: exploring policy responses', which grouped ideas into 'nearly all', 'moderate acceleration' and 'fast-moving' scenarios.
candidates.definition: The framework uses 'the unemployment rate as the primary trigger'. It also tells governments to watch labour force participation, underemployment, wages and labour's share of national income. Tier 1: 'Baseline economy (~5% unemployment with churn)'. Tier 2: 'Recession-level disruption (~10% unemployment)', which prioritises expanded UI. At this tier it proposes reforming the EB trigger 'so that extension is automatic and uniform across states'. Tier 3: 'Transformative disruption (unemployment exceeding historical peaks)', described as unemployment never before sustained while the economy produces record output. Tier 3 candidates include basic income, AI sovereign wealth funds, equity sharing, and levies on AI use measured by tokens, compute or revenue. Thresholds are approximate. The framework names no series (U-3 vs U-6), averaging window or duration. It calls for a small government unit to 'flag the early signals that should trigger a policy response'.
candidates.data_source: Not specified. It calls for more funding for statistical agencies, AI-specific survey instruments, and reporting requirements for AI labs and firms. It cites the Anthropic Economic Index, Brynjolfsson et al. (2025, 'Canaries in the Coal Mine') and Massenkoff and McCrory (2026).
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Only in concept. It says AI-driven unemployment alongside strong growth would be 'more structural than cyclical', and it contrasts temporary support with an 'enduring restructuring'. It gives no operational test. Its Tier 2 is labelled 'recession-level', so an ordinary recession would satisfy it.
candidates.evidence_quote: unemployment at levels never before sustained alongside an economy generating record output

candidates.name: AI Tax and Work Protection Act (H.R.10044, 2026): foundation-model excise tax indexed to U-4
candidates.who_uses_it: Introduced August 6, 2026 by Rep. Casar for himself, Rep. Foushee and Rep. Jacobs. The Congress.gov API now shows 4 cosponsors. Referred to Education and Workforce and to Ways and Means, with no further action. Revenue goes to a trust fund that pays for a Work Protection Administration and Office of Job Creation jobs-grant program at the Labor Department. Not enacted.
candidates.definition: New IRC sec. 4491 taxes each covered person on the greater of two amounts: (A) the fair market value of tokens processed in covered transactions times the token percentage, or (B) the consideration received for AI services, plus related-party transactions, times the transaction percentage. Covered transactions include providing a foundation model to unrelated parties. They also include the firm's own use of a model, or sale to a related party, if that use 'enables or results in a reduction in the workforce'. A foundation model is one trained with at least 10^25 integer or floating-point operations, or a Secretary-set equivalent. Token percentage: 2% if the applicable unemployment rate is at or below 5%; 2% plus the excess over 5% between 5% and 7%; 2% plus twice the excess over 5% above 7%. The transaction percentage has the same form from a 3% base. Computed from that text, the token rate jumps from 4% to about 6% as the rate crosses 7%. The applicable rate is BLS U-4, as published in the monthly Employment Situation release, for the highest calendar year among the 3 years before the transaction; years that began before enactment are ignored. Sec. 4491(c), 'Suspension of Higher Rates': Treasury, in consultation with Labor, may disregard the part of unemployment above 5% that results from war, pandemic or another shock unrelated to AI.
candidates.data_source: BLS U-4 (unemployed plus discouraged workers), from the monthly Employment Situation release.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Partly. Treasury has discretion to exclude unemployment it judges to have non-AI causes, and there is no formula for doing so. There is also a firm-level test: a firm's own AI use counts if it reduces the firm's workforce. This is the only statutory text found that explicitly tries to exclude non-AI unemployment from a national measure.
candidates.evidence_quote: any other massive economic shock unrelated to the use of artificial intelligence (H.R.10044 sec.101, new IRC 4491(c))

candidates.name: AI-Related Job Impacts Clarity Act (S.3108 / H.R.9352): proposed BLS series of employer-reported AI layoffs
candidates.who_uses_it: S.3108 was introduced November 5, 2025 by Sen. Hawley and referred to HELP. Its cosponsors are Warner (Nov 5, 2025), Kaine (Jan 29, 2026) and Blackburn (Mar 19, 2026). The House companion, H.R.9352, was introduced June 18, 2026 by Rep. Horsford and referred to Education and Workforce. Its cosponsors are Del. Moylan, Rep. Sara Jacobs and Rep. Walkinshaw (added Sep 2, 2026). Neither bill has moved past committee, and neither is enacted. Hawley's release says 'experts project AI could drive unemployment up to 10-20%' within five years.
candidates.definition: Covered entities must report within 30 days after each quarter ends. Covered entities are publicly traded companies, federal agencies (as defined in 5 U.S.C. 551), and non-public companies the Labor Department brings in by regulation within 180 days. They report: layoffs 'substantially due to' AI replacing or automating the workers' functions; hires substantially due to AI; positions filled in the prior quarter that the firm decided not to refill for that reason; and workers being retrained because of AI. Each item carries NAICS codes. The Labor Department may collect these through an existing DOL or Census survey. It must publish quarterly summaries, a net-impact analysis every other quarter, and the underlying data on the BLS website within 60 days of quarter end.
candidates.data_source: Would be a new quarterly Labor Department series on the BLS website, 60 days after quarter end. It does not exist yet.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Yes, if enacted. Attribution would come from employers' own reports ('substantially due to'). It would give quarterly counts on known dates but has the same self-report weakness shown by New York's WARN checkbox.
candidates.evidence_quote: substantially due to the replacement or automation by artificial intelligence (S.3108 sec.2(a)(1)(A))

candidates.name: National Workforce Transition Fund Act of 2026 (S.5055) and AI Workforce PREPARE Act (S.3339): indicator-based eligibility instead of individual proof of AI cause, plus a proposed federal WARN AI statement
candidates.who_uses_it: S.5055: introduced by Sen. Warner on July 21, 2026, with no cosponsors, and referred to Finance. It would replace WIOA Title III with a temporary National Workforce Transition Fund. The fund would receive an amount equal to the revenue raised by ending bonus depreciation for AI data-centre property, and would expire after 5 years. S.3339: introduced December 3, 2025 by Sen. Banks with Sens. Hassan, Hickenlooper and Husted; Sen. Marshall joined on March 10, 2026. Referred to HELP. Neither bill is enacted.
candidates.definition: S.5055 (new WIOA sec. 301 and 305): 'no worker shall be required to show' that AI or emerging technology was the sole or primary cause of their disruption. The Secretary picks priority populations using labour-market indicators: UI claims, wage records, occupational employment trends, entry-level hiring trends, employer reports, sectoral disruption, regional displacement, wage losses, and exposure to AI or emerging technology. S.3339 sec. 402 orders a study of a 'Rapid AI Adjustment Assistance Program' that draws on TAA. The study asks how to 'rapidly and reliably determine' who counts as an impacted worker, what 'thresholds of evidence' fit, and whether to use tiered approval or petitions. Other sections add AI questions to five surveys: the Annual Business Survey, CPS and BTOS (Census), and the Occupational Requirements Survey and ATUS (BLS). S.3339 sec. 204 would amend the federal WARN Act. When AI was a 'substantial factor' in a mass layoff, the notice would have to say so, name the AI, and give a good-faith estimate of the percentage of the job loss it caused. Labor would issue guidance within 300 days, and the requirement would apply 1 year after enactment.
candidates.data_source: S.5055: existing administrative and survey data, at the Secretary's discretion, with no fixed formula or release date. S.3339: new survey questions and WARN notice statements, if enacted.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: S.5055 deliberately avoids individual attribution and falls back on labour-market indicators weighted by AI exposure. S.3339 studies the attribution question and would add employer-estimated AI shares to federal WARN notices, which is self-reported attribution at the level of each layoff.
candidates.evidence_quote: rather than requiring individual workers to prove that artificial intelligence (S.5055, new WIOA sec.301)

candidates.name: Trade Adjustment Assistance (TAA) group certification: the established cause-specific displacement test, and 'Automation Adjustment Assistance' proposals
candidates.who_uses_it: US law since 1974 (19 U.S.C. 2272). Authority lapsed in 2022. Sen. Fetterman's release says '200,000 laid-off workers have applied for help but received none'. Rep. Sánchez's March 4, 2026 release, introducing the TAA Modernization Act, says nearly 200,000 petitions are pending; the release does not mention AI or automation, and I did not read the bill text. Anthropic's Oct 14, 2025 post cites Ioana Marinescu's TAA-like 'AI insurance'. It also cites Suchet Mittal and Sam Manning's 'Automation Adjustment Assistance', funded at TAA-like levels of about $700 million a year and scaled with the pace of AI displacement. I did not read the primary Mittal/Manning text.
candidates.definition: The Labor Department certifies a group of workers when two conditions hold. First, a 'significant number or proportion' of the firm's workers have been separated or threatened with separation. Second, either imports of like or directly competitive articles increased and 'contributed importantly' to the separations and to the fall in sales or production, or production shifted abroad. 'Contributed importantly' means a cause that is important but not necessarily more important than any other (19 U.S.C. 2272(c)(1)). The statute sets no number. The regulation (20 CFR 618.110) defines a significant number or proportion as the lesser of 50 workers or 5% of the firm's workers, or at least 2 workers in a firm with fewer than 50. Certification is decided petition by petition, on no fixed schedule.
candidates.data_source: DOL ETA TAA petition determinations. The DOL petition pages were not re-opened this session (the researcher got 403), so they are not verified.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: It attributes a cause (trade), case by case through administrative adjudication, and does not cover AI. It is the model that AI-adjustment proposals copy (S.3339 sec. 402, Mittal/Manning), and it gives no national on/off signal.
candidates.evidence_quote: a cause which is important but not necessarily more important than any other cause (19 U.S.C. 2272(c)(1))

candidates.name: European Globalisation Adjustment Fund for Displaced Workers (EGF 2021-2027): 200-redundancy restructuring test including automation
candidates.who_uses_it: EU law, Regulation (EU) 2021/691. The Commission decides each member-state application and reports under Article 21. The most recent report read was COM(2023) 482, dated 11.8.2023, covering 2021-2022. Between 2007 and 2022 it received 177 applications (excluding withdrawn or rejected ones), which the report splits into 91 crisis-related and 85 trade-related. Those two numbers sum to 176, a discrepancy that is in the source.
candidates.definition: Article 4(2)(a), as summarised in the report: at least 200 workers made redundant over a 4-month reference period in one enterprise, counting suppliers, downstream producers and self-employed people whose activity has ceased. Article 4(3) allows a derogation for small labour markets where the redundancies seriously affect the local and regional economy. From 2021 the scope covers 'any major restructuring event', including globalisation, financial or economic crises, the low-carbon transition, 'digitisation or automation'. The threshold fell from 500 (2014-2020) to 200. I did not see the researcher's claim about other reference periods for SMEs in a sector or region in the text I read, so it is not verified.
candidates.data_source: Commission EGF decisions and biennial activity reports, published at irregular dates. Read via a PDF print of EUR-Lex CELEX:52023DC0482 hosted on irshare.eu. EUR-Lex itself was not accessed.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Yes, at case level: each application names the restructuring cause, and automation and digitisation have been eligible since 2021. It is not a macro indicator. The 2021-22 report does not mention artificial intelligence.

candidates.name: Germany: Kurzarbeitergeld (temporary) vs Transferkurzarbeitergeld (permanent restructuring), SGB III §96 and §111
candidates.who_uses_it: German federal law (SGB III), administered by the Bundesagentur für Arbeit.
candidates.definition: Ordinary Kurzarbeitergeld (§96(1)): the loss of work is significant if four conditions hold. It rests on economic reasons or an unavoidable event; it is temporary; it is unavoidable; and in the calendar month at least one-third of employees each lose more than 10% of gross monthly pay. §96(2) counts a change in the firm's structures caused by general economic development as an economic reason. §96(4) treats as avoidable any loss that is mainly typical for the industry or firm, seasonal, or purely organisational. Transferkurzarbeitergeld (§111) applies when a restructuring (Betriebsänderung) removes employment opportunities not just temporarily, that is, a permanent loss. Affected workers are grouped in a separate organisational unit, the loss must be reported to the Agentur, and the benefit lasts at most 12 months. So the legal line is temporary versus permanent loss, not cyclical versus structural cause.
candidates.data_source: Bundesagentur für Arbeit short-time work statistics (not fetched this session).
candidates.attributes_to_ai: It separates temporary from permanent loss at firm level, but not AI specifically. The ratio of Transfer-KuG to ordinary KuG counts could in principle be a structural-versus-cyclical indicator; that is untested.
candidates.evidence_quote: auf Grund einer Betriebsänderung ... die Beschäftigungsmöglichkeiten ... nicht nur vorübergehend entfallen (§111(2) SGB III)

candidates.name: Canada Employment Insurance: regional unemployment-rate entitlement
candidates.who_uses_it: Canada's federal EI program. The current table lists 62 EI economic regions, with boundaries set by ESDC and rates produced by Statistics Canada.
candidates.definition: The hours needed to qualify and the minimum and maximum weeks of regular benefits depend on each region's unemployment rate. Outside the territories, that rate is a seasonally adjusted 3-month moving average. The territories use the greater of the 3-month and 12-month moving averages. In the table for September 6 to October 10, 2026, low-unemployment regions need 700 hours for 14-36 weeks. High-unemployment regions, such as Northern Manitoba at 28.7%, need 420 hours for 32-45 weeks. The table is refreshed each monthly period, and this one runs 5 weeks; the researcher's 'about every four weeks' is imprecise.
candidates.data_source: Regional rates produced by Statistics Canada for EI purposes and published on the ESDC 'EI Program Characteristics' page. The page does not name the Labour Force Survey.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It responds to the level of unemployment only.

candidates.name: New York WARN notice AI/automation checkbox
candidates.who_uses_it: The New York State Department of Labor, following Governor Hochul's January 2025 direction, added the disclosure in March 2025. Hunton says the statutory text was not amended. It applies to employers covered by NY WARN, which Kaufman Dolowich describes as private businesses with 50 or more full-time employees in New York.
candidates.definition: Employers filing a WARN notice must say, by checkbox, whether 'technological innovation or automation' contributed to the layoffs. If they tick it, they select the technology involved, such as AI or robotic processes. Kaufman Dolowich calls the checkbox mandatory; Hunton says employers lack guidance on whether it is optional. Hunton (May 18, 2026) reports that none of the notices from more than 160 companies in the first year attributed layoffs to AI or automation.
candidates.data_source: NY DOL WARN notice filings, posted as they arrive. I did not read the NY DOL WARN dashboard itself this session.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Yes, by employer self-report. A zero count after a year shows self-report undercounts badly, compared with Challenger's AI attributions drawn from announcements.

candidates.name: Challenger, Gray & Christmas job-cut reasons: 'Artificial Intelligence' category
candidates.who_uses_it: A monthly report on announced US job cuts from a private outplacement firm. It has tracked AI as a distinct reason since 2023. It also uses a 'Technological Update (possibly AI)' category when a company names new technology as the main reason and AI is alluded to but not directly tied to the cuts: 20,219 cuts in 2025. Press uptake was not checked.
candidates.definition: Announced US job cuts are coded by the reason the employer gives. July 2026 report (published Aug 6): AI led all reasons for the fifth straight month, with 10,970 of 33,429 cuts (33%). Year to date that was 112,713 (about 24%), and 184,538 since 2023. August 2026 report (published Sep 2): AI fell to fourth with 3,462 cuts, but still led year to date with 116,175 (about 22% of all cuts). Restructuring led August with 16,173 cuts.
candidates.data_source: Monthly blog report, published in the first week of the following month.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Yes, by the employer's stated reason as coded by Challenger. These are announced plans, not realised layoffs; they are open to 'AI-washing' and are not an official statistic. The July report itself flags ambiguous coding cases.

candidates.name: Altman 'American Equity Fund' (Moore's Law for Everything, March 16, 2021)
candidates.who_uses_it: An essay by Sam Altman, offered 'in the spirit of a conversation starter'. No legislation or OpenAI policy adopting it was found; the OpenAI policy pages returned 403 earlier and were not re-checked.
candidates.definition: An annual 2.5% tax on the market value of companies above an unspecified valuation threshold, paid in shares, and 2.5% on privately held land, paid in dollars. All citizens over 18 get an annual distribution; Altman projects about $13,500 per adult a decade out. The rate phases in, and the full 2.5% applies only once 'GDP increases by 50%' from when the law passes.
candidates.data_source: None specified. The phase-in keys to 'GDP'; the essay does not say real or nominal, or which series. The researcher's 'BEA real GDP' is an inference.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No displacement test at all. Payments are unconditional, and the only trigger is output growth (the abundance side), not unemployment.

candidates.name: Windfall Clause (O'Keefe, Cihon, Garfinkel, Flynn, Leung, Dafoe; 2019/2020)
candidates.who_uses_it: An academic proposal, arXiv 1912.11595, posted Dec 25, 2019. The arXiv comment says a short version was 'to be published in proceedings of AIES'. It proposes voluntary ex ante commitments by AI firms. No firm is known to have signed one; not verified.
candidates.definition: A firm commits a share of its marginal profits that scales with those profits as a share of gross world product (Table 2): 0% below 0.1% of GWP, 1% from 0.1% to 1%, 20% from 1% to 10%, and 50% from 10% to 100%.
candidates.data_source: Firm profits plus a GWP estimate, annually. The paper does not fix a data series.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Indirectly. It triggers on AI-firm windfall profits rather than unemployment, so a recession cannot set it off. That makes it an AI-specific signal on the output side, not a measure of labour displacement.

candidates.name: South Korea 2026: Basic Income Planning Team (planned 2027 pilot) and rural basic income pilot
candidates.who_uses_it: Korea's Ministry of Health and Welfare set up a 'Basic Social Policy Task Force' with a 'Basic Income Planning Team' under it, reported by The Asia Business Daily on April 10, 2026. It aims to put a pilot into the 2027 budget. Separately, the rural basic income pilot covers 10 designated depopulating counties, including Okcheon and Yeoncheon. The Korea Herald (Dec 25, 2025) says the regions were named in December 2025, the program runs 2026-2027, and the central government pays 40% of the cost.
candidates.definition: The planned 2027 pilot favours a conditional 'participation income', tied to socially contributive activity, for young and middle-aged adults. It is justified by structural unemployment expected from AI, with no measurable trigger. The rural pilot pays every registered resident of the chosen regions 150,000 won a month in local vouchers for two years, regardless of income or job, also with no trigger.
candidates.data_source: None; no indicator is defined.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: AI appears only as the rationale; there is no operational test.

candidates.name: Robot or automation taxes (South Korea 2017, European Parliament/Delvaux, de Blasio 2019)
candidates.who_uses_it: Per Wikipedia's 'Robot tax' article: on August 6, 2017, South Korea passed what has been called the first robot tax, which reduces tax breaks for robotics investment. The European Parliament rejected the robot-tax part of Mady Delvaux's robotics report; the article gives no year. In 2019 Bill de Blasio proposed that large corporations pay five years of income tax for jobs 'automated away'. The primary sources were not opened this session.
candidates.definition: Korea: smaller investment incentives, with no displacement trigger. De Blasio: a per-job liability that requires deciding, case by case, which jobs were automated away.
candidates.data_source: None published.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: De Blasio's version would need automation attributed case by case; the others have no trigger.

verified.none_found_notes:
Verification method: I re-downloaded each cited source this session into /private/tmp/claude-501/-Applications/da707ee8-bdb9-43d0-bb83-c08c894e427d/scratchpad/wf-signal/verify-policy/fresh/ and converted it to text with bs4 or pdftotext. I did not rely on the researcher's local copies. The Congress.gov DEMO_KEY hit its rate limit after two calls, so bill status came from GovInfo BILLSTATUS XML. I dropped no candidates; every one is supported by at least one source I re-opened.

Corrections made:
1. Sahm: FRED updates SAHMREALTIME monthly, not daily. 1959-12 is the first observation (0.77), not a crossing, so I removed it from the list of first crossings. Page cite for 'turn on during a cyclical downturn' is p.77.
2. Sahm-plus-GDP-peak computation: I reproduced it with the repo GDPC1.csv (prior quarter) against FRED SAHMREALTIME. The researcher's candidate list omitted 1969 (1969-10); the summary's shorter list (1961, 1971, 1992, 2002, 2008, 2024) also left out the recession-onset years. The rule fires at recession onsets (GDP still at peak) and in jobless recoveries.
3. Korea: the task force is the 'Basic Social Policy Task Force' in the Asiae translation. Okcheon was designated in December 2025, not 'started'. The program runs 2026-27 across 10 regions.
4. Altman: the phase-in keys to 'GDP' without specifying real or BEA; 'BEA real GDP' was an inference.
5. Canada EI: the period shown (Sept 6 to Oct 10, 2026) is 5 weeks, so 'about every four weeks' is wrong. The page says rates are 'produced by Statistics Canada' and does not name the LFS. 62 regions are listed.
6. H.R.9352: the sponsor is Rep. Horsford, with cosponsors Moylan, Jacobs and Walkinshaw; the researcher gave no sponsor. S.3339 has a fifth cosponsor, Sen. Marshall (Mar 10, 2026). S.3108's cosponsors are Warner, Kaine and Blackburn, which confirms the count of 3.
7. EGF: 91 + 85 = 176, not 177; the discrepancy is in the Commission report itself. The claim about other reference periods for SMEs in a sector or region is not in the text read, so it is marked not verified. The 2021-22 report does not mention AI.
8. Robot tax: the Wikipedia extract gives no year for the European Parliament's rejection.

Additions the researcher missed:
(a) S.3339 sec. 204 would require federal WARN notices to state whether AI was a 'substantial factor', with a good-faith estimate of the percentage of job loss attributable to it. This is a proposed federal analogue of the NY checkbox with a quantitative share.
(b) TAA's regulatory threshold for a significant number or proportion of workers (20 CFR 618.110): the lesser of 50 workers or 5%, or at least 2 workers in firms with fewer than 50.
(c) H.R.10044 covers a firm's own foundation-model use if it 'enables or results in a reduction in the workforce', which is a firm-level AI attribution hook. The token rate jumps from 4% to about 6% at 7% U-4 (my calculation from the bill text).

Still not verified (unchanged from the researcher):
- OpenAI policy pages (403).
- EUR-Lex (bot check, not bypassed) and the 'Regulation (EU) 2026/1139' hit.
- DOL TAA petition pages and the BLS Displaced Worker Supplement.
- Korea's employment-crisis-region rules.
- Primary texts of Mittal and Manning, Sanders, Kelly and de Blasio.
- NBER recession dating as a component.
- The Sahm rule being 'widely watched by markets'.
- Press coverage of Challenger.
- Whether H.R.4439's text matches S.2312.
- The TAA Modernization Act bill text: only Sánchez's release was read, and it does not mention AI or automation.

Bottom line for the model: no established signal separates AI displacement from a recession. Adoptable established components that resolve on known dates are:
- FRED SAHMREALTIME (monthly; next release Oct 2, 2026).
- S.2312-style level triggers with no lookback (5.5%, 6.5%, 7.5%, 8.5%) or Chodorow-Reich and Coglianese's 9%/10%.
- The H.R.10044 U-4 formula, whose applicable rate is the highest calendar-year U-4 over the prior 3 years.
- Anthropic's EPF tiers (~5%, ~10%, above historical peaks), which are a citable framing but not a formula.

Any AI-attribution layer must be labelled non-established. Challenger's monthly AI-cited counts are the only running cause-coded series, and they count announcements.

raw.summary:
Short answer to the owner's question: no. None of the six platforms uses the model's rule (unemployment 3 points above its 2025 level while real GDP is at its peak). No platform has a shared operational definition of "an AI labour shock has started". The questions I read fall into three groups.

(1) Pure BLS/BEA thresholds with no attribution. These are the most liquid and fully reproducible:
- Kalshi KXU3MAX-30: U-3 above 10% between June 2025 and January 2030, bid 0.36 / ask 0.49.
- Metaculus 18664: U-3 of 10% before 2031, 55%, 58 forecasters.
- Polymarket 2026 U-3 ladder.
- Manifold 10%-before-2030 markets at about 28-30%.
- Metaculus questions on the employment-population ratio (EPOP) and labour force participation (LFPR).
Several say "due to AI or otherwise" outright.

(2) Attribution by judgment, all on Manifold. This includes both markets the model cites:
- The 175-trader "AI causes US unemployment above 10% before 2030" market (23%) needs UNRATE above 10% AND AI "directly responsible for at least 3 percentage points", judged by the creator. It explicitly lets a recession spike count if AI stops the jobs coming back.
- The 643-trader ACX market (30%) resolves on the creator's impression of economist consensus that a visible break in trend is directly due to AI.
- Smaller markets use a credible poll of economists (Bldrt), "BLS or two credible sources, not downturns" (Vorak), or mainstream media (AitchKay, bens).
None of these resolves mechanically from published data.

(3) Proxies and counterfactuals:
- **Challenger.** Challenger, Gray & Christmas has tracked "Artificial Intelligence" as a stated reason for announced job cuts since 2023: 116,175 AI-cited cuts from January to August 2026, about 22% of all cuts, and the top reason from March to July 2026. Kalshi trades a monthly market on it (KXCHAICUTS, resolved from Table 4 of the first-published report).
- **Metaculus Labor Automation Hub.** It resolves on OEWS all-occupation employment and states that its questions "aren't explicitly posed as being dependent on AI". It attributes to AI by comparing against the BLS projections baseline and through conditional questions:
  - 43025 is conditional on positive real GDP growth (GDPCA) in the year and the year before; forecasts are -1.05% for 2030 and -3.19% for 2035.
  - 43292 is conditional on AI-funding stagnation; forecasts are +1.1% and +1.86%.
  - Against the unconditional -0.54% and -3.62%, that implies an AI effect of about -1.6 points by 2030 and -5.5 points by 2035 (my subtraction).
- **MacAskill–Moll bet on Kalshi.** It uses a published peak-relative rule (real GDP per capita, A939RX, at least 15% above the peak through quarter Q-4) to stop recession rebounds from counting. It does not require AI causation.

What this means for the model:

- **The cited market is a different event.** Its level bar is above 10%, not 7.3%, and its attribution is not reproducible.

- **Borrowing Metaculus's cycle filter is not enough.** I ran this on the repo's FRED CSVs: annual average UNRATE at or above 7.26 with positive real GDP growth in the year and the year before. It still fires in 1984 and 2011-2013 (jobless recoveries).

- **A rule built from established components had no false fires.** Take a Sahm-style rise: the 12-month average UNRATE at least 3 points above its minimum over the prior 36 months. Add a MacAskill–Moll-style peak-relative output test: GDPC1 at or above its previous peak in every quarter since the unemployment trough. That fired in no month since 1948 on the repo's FRED CSVs. It is my own construction, not an adopted standard, and it would miss an AI shock that coincides with any dip in output.

- **Proxies and counterfactuals:**

**What I corrected** (details in none_found_notes):
- Some live prices had moved: KXU3MAX-27-7, KXRECSSNBER-26, KXCHAICUTS for September, and the Polymarket 10% bucket.
- KXRECSSNBER's definition was overstated: its rules do not say "annualised" or "advance estimate data".

**For the model:**
- The cited 23% market is a different event: above 10%, plus at least 3 points attributable to AI by the creator's judgment. The model's rule is a 7.3% level test.
- The most defensible falsifiable design built from established parts is:
  - a cause-agnostic BLS level or rise test (Kalshi- or Sahm-style);
  - a published peak-relative output condition (MacAskill–Moll style) to exclude recession rebounds;
  - optionally, Challenger's AI-cited share of announced cuts as a monthly attribution add-on.

4. **Wrong Manifold slug for the AGI-before-2035 market.** The RemNi market (131 traders, 63.3%) sits at 'will-we-get-agi-before-2033-34ec8e1d00fd'. The slug 'will-we-get-agi-before-2035' is a different 3-trader JasonMendoza2008 market. The 2025-11-02 moderator edit appears in the 2030 market's text only, not the 2040 one.
5. **Metaculus 11416.** I removed "0-100 scale"; it is not in the resolution text I read. The occupation list (15) and the 30.6 baseline are confirmed.
6. **Kalshi series metadata lists template settlement links.** KXCHAICUTS shows BLS links, KXAIGROWTHBET shows NY Fed SOFR. The market rules name the real sources (Challenger Table 4; BEA A939RX).

**Caveats I added**
- **Metaculus subtraction.** The -1.6 / -5.5 point "AI effect" compares medians from different forecaster pools (60 vs 30). The Hub's methodology says a same-cohort comparison will come later.
- **The Hub mislabels its stagnation condition.** It calls it "AI benchmark stagnation" at roughly 2026-level capabilities, but Q43292 actually conditions on corporate AI investment staying below $1T before 2030 (Stanford AI Index Fig 4.2.1).

**Own computations (re-run on the repo's research/trigger/UNRATE.csv and GDPC1.csv)**
- **2025 baseline confirmed:** 11 months, average 4.264, so the level is 7.26.
- **Metaculus-43025-style filter reproduced.** Annual-average UNRATE of at least 7.26 with positive real GDP growth in the year and the year before (annual GDP taken as the mean of the quarterly GDPC1 values, not GDPCA itself) fires in:
  - 1984: 7.51%
  - 2011: 8.93%
  - 2012: 8.07%
  - 2013: 7.36%
- **Peak-relative rule reproduced:** zero firing months since 1948. Rule: a 3-point rise in 12-month-average UNRATE above its prior 36-month minimum, with GDPC1 at a new peak in every quarter since that minimum. This held in all four variants: minimum of the 12-month average or of monthly values, trough quarter included or excluded.
- **Why zero fires is weak evidence:**
  - The rise condition alone was met in only four episodes (1975-09 to 1976-08, 1982-08 to 1983-10, 2009-06 to 2011-12, 2020-08 to 2021-06), all with output declines. So the result shows specificity against four recessions and says nothing about sensitivity.
  - The rule never fired, so it has no true positive to validate against.
- **"Sahm-style" is only an analogy.** The Sahm rule compares a 3-month average with its 12-month low at a 0.5 threshold; this construction uses a 12-month average, a 36-month low and a 3.0 threshold.
- **Look-ahead in the historical test.** It dates each quarter's GDP from the quarter's first month, before BEA publishes it. A real-time version resolves only after the BEA advance estimate, about 4 weeks after quarter end, and on first-print rather than latest-vintage data.

**Method**
- Manifold, Kalshi and Polymarket: re-read through their public APIs.
- Challenger: blog pages fetched with curl; the timestamps 2026-08-06 and 2026-09-02 are the pages' datePublished.
- Metaculus: the Claude-in-Chrome extension was not connected, so I read the pages in the desktop app's built-in browser. No challenge appeared and none was bypassed. Numeric medians were computed from embedded aggregation data (linear scaling; zero_point null).
- The repo was read, not modified. Scratch files are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Applications/da707ee8-bdb9-43d0-bb83-c08c894e427d/scratchpad/wf-signal/verify-forecasting/ (m/, k/, pm_*.json, ch_*.txt, recheck.py).
