- Polymarket public search for "AI unemployment" and "AI job cuts" returned only closed mention markets (Powell/Trump/earnings-call wording), consistent with "no AI-attributed unemployment market".
- KXAILABDIS returns zero markets and events, including settled ones, so its rules remain NOT verified.

**Not re-checked by me:** Good Judgment Open question criteria, RAND active questions, the GitHub gist and Tech Insider snippets, the NY WARN AI disclosure, and any recurring economist panel. These stay "not verified", as the researcher reported.

raw.summary:
Short answer to the owner: no. No official statistical agency or standards body publishes an "AI labour shock has started" signal, or any rule for technological unemployment. The model's trigger (12-month U-3 at least 3 points above the 2025 average, with real GDP at or above its previous peak) is bespoke.

**What is established splits into two groups, and neither alone separates AI from the business cycle.**

(A) Cycle signals. These are well established but say nothing about cause:
- NBER dates and FRED USREC.
- The real-time Sahm rule (SAHMREALTIME). Sahm designed it as a trigger for automatic cash payments to individuals.
- Hamilton's GDP-based recession index (JHGDPBRINDX), which is never revised.
- Chauvet-Piger recession probabilities.
- The CEPR-EABCN euro area committee, Japan's ESRI, Brazil's CODACE and the C.D. Howe council for Canada.
- The statutory Extended Benefits unemployment-insurance triggers.
- FOMC and CBO estimates of structural unemployment.

(B) AI-specific official statistics. These are new and none of them is a trigger:
- BLS AI exposure categories (27 Aug 2026). Four levels for about 831 SOC occupations, built from five exposure indices. BLS says a category is "not a forecast of employment growth or decline".
- Census BTOS core AI-use question. Collected every two weeks since Sep 2023; the wording changed on 17 Nov 2025. Use is 17-20% of firms from Dec 2025 to May 2026.
- The BTOS AI supplements (Dec 2023–Feb 2024 and Nov 2025–Feb 2026). These ask whether AI changed a firm's employment: 2.0% of AI-using firms reported a decrease, 2.3% an increase.
- The ILO GenAI exposure gradients (Working Paper 140, ISCO-08 4-digit).
- The OECD's use of the Felten-Raj-Seamans language-model exposure index, mapped to ISCO.
- Eurostat's annual survey of enterprise AI use (isoc_eb_ai).

Other official labour data record why jobs end but never whether technology was the cause:
- The Displaced Worker Survey (released 27 Aug 2026) counts 3.3M long-tenured displaced workers for 2023-25, up 746k on 2021-23; 44.4% said their position was abolished.
- JOLTS layoffs and the CPS count of permanent job losers.

The OECD Employment Outlook 2026 finds "little evidence" of AI automating jobs so far. It also warns that AI-exposed occupations are more sensitive to the business cycle, so a simple exposed-vs-unexposed comparison can mistake a downturn for an AI effect.

**Findings from data I ran (FRED CSVs downloaded today):**
- All three US episodes since 1948 with a rise of 3+ points in the 12-month unemployment average (first months 1975-09, 2009-06, 2020-09) start within 0-6 months of an NBER recession month.
- Fix tested: require Hamilton's GDP index to stay below its recession threshold (67) from 8 quarters before through 4 quarters after the first month. Since 1967, a 3.0 or 2.0 point rise then never fires. A 1.5 point rise fires once (2003-10, the jobless recovery after 2001). A 1.0 point rise also fires in 2011-07.
- Excluding recessions with NBER dates instead has two problems. NBER announces peaks 4-12 months late and troughs 8-21 months late. And NBER weights payroll employment and real personal income less transfers most, so it could date a genuine AI job shock as a recession and veto it.
- The Sahm rule fired in 2024-07 with no recession.
- The share of unemployed who are permanent job losers peaked at 44% in 2009-10. Composition measures like this rise in ordinary recessions too, so they do not isolate AI.

**Suggested falsifiable build from established parts:**
1. An unemployment-rise trigger, either Sahm-style or the model's own.
2. The Hamilton GDP-index window above, to exclude output recessions. It resolves about 16 months after the trigger quarter.
3. Optional attribution step: a check on data published on known dates that the rise is concentrated in occupations rated High or Very High for AI exposure. Use BLS categories with CPS data for the US, and ILO gradients with labour force surveys elsewhere.

For countries other than the US, no published equivalent of the Hamilton index was found. The OECD recession indicators on FRED were discontinued in Dec 2022, so a GDP-only recession rule for those countries would have to be computed from national GDP.

candidates.name: NBER business cycle dates (FRED USREC / USRECQ)
candidates.who_uses_it: The NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee sets the US reference chronology. FRED builds USREC (monthly, from 1854-12) directly from it, and the FRED page ties updates to NBER announcements. Its wider use as the standard US recession chronology is general knowledge, not checked for specific institutions this session.
candidates.definition: No fixed rule: 'a significant decline in economic activity that is spread across the economy and lasts more than a few months', judged on depth, diffusion and duration. The committee gives most weight to real personal income less transfers and nonfarm payroll employment. FRED USREC is 1 from the month after the peak through the trough month, otherwise 0. Measured announcement lags: peaks 1980-01 announced 3 Jun 1980 (~5 months), 1981-07 on 6 Jan 1982 (~6), 1990-07 on 25 Apr 1991 (~9), 2001-03 on 26 Nov 2001 (~8), 2007-12 on 1 Dec 2008 (~12), 2020-02 on 8 Jun 2020 (~4). Troughs: 1980-07 on 8 Jul 1981 (12), 1982-11 on 8 Jul 1983 (8), 1991-03 on 22 Dec 1992 (21), 2001-11 on 17 Jul 2003 (20), 2009-06 on 20 Sep 2010 (15), 2020-04 on 19 Jul 2021 (15).
candidates.data_source: NBER announcements (irregular, no schedule); FRED USREC monthly 1854-12 to 2026-08 (latest 0), last updated 1 Sep 2026.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It dates the cycle and says nothing about causes. As an exclusion ('no NBER recession') it has two problems. It arrives 4-21 months late. And because NBER weights payrolls and personal income most, an AI job shock with GDP still growing could itself be dated a recession, which would wrongly veto the trigger. I ran all three US episodes since 1948 with a 3+ point rise in 12-month unemployment (1975-09, 2009-06, 2020-09). Each starts within 0-6 months of an NBER recession month.
candidates.evidence_quote: "real personal income less transfers" and "nonfarm payroll employment" receive the most weight (NBER)

candidates.name: Hamilton GDP-based recession indicator index (FRED JHGDPBRINDX)
candidates.who_uses_it: Published on FRED (series by James Hamilton). Adoption beyond FRED not verified this session.
candidates.definition: Mechanical recession probability computed 'based solely on currently available GDP data'. Above 67 is a historically reliable recession signal; after that, falling below 33 signals the end. Each quarter is computed once, for the quarter before the latest GDP release, and never revised.
candidates.data_source: FRED JHGDPBRINDX, quarterly, 1967Q4 to 2026Q1 (latest 7.0), last updated 30 Jul 2026. That is roughly a one-quarter-plus-one-month lag after the reference quarter.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Not by itself. But because it uses output only, it can check that unemployment rose without an output recession, which is the 'jobless growth' idea in the model's current rule. It is not revised and not tied to NBER. My backtest since 1967 (UNRATE and JHGDPBRINDX from FRED today) requires the index below 67 from 8 quarters before through 4 quarters after the first month. With that condition, a 3.0 or 2.0 point rise in 12-month unemployment over 24 months never fires. A 1.5 point rise fires once (2003-10, the jobless recovery). A 1.0 point rise also fires in 2011-07. The pre-window is what removes the recession recoveries (1975, 2010, 2021) that the review flagged. No equivalent published for the other nine countries was found.
candidates.evidence_quote: "If the value of the index rises above 67%" (FRED notes)

candidates.name: Real-time Sahm rule recession indicator (FRED SAHMREALTIME)
candidates.who_uses_it: Published on FRED. Claudia Sahm (Federal Reserve Board) proposed it in a 2019 Hamilton Project chapter as the trigger for automatic direct payments to individuals, a cash-transfer trigger close to the UBI model's use case.
candidates.definition: Signal when the 3-month moving average of national U-3 rises 0.50 points or more above the minimum of the 3-month averages over the previous 12 months, using data as first published in each month.
candidates.data_source: FRED SAHMREALTIME, monthly, 1959-12 to 2026-08 (latest -0.07), updated 4 Sep 2026. It follows the BLS Employment Situation release (first Friday) with no further lag.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It detects fast unemployment rises of any cause. My run: first trigger months were 1959-12, 1960-08, 1969-10, 1970-02, 1974-03, 1974-07, 1976-11, 1980-04, 1981-11, 1990-11, 2001-06, 2008-04, 2020-04 and 2024-07. All but 1976-11 and 2024-07 fall within 6 months of an NBER recession month. 2024-07 was a trigger with no recession. Because it fires at recession onsets, a 'no GDP recession in the prior 8 quarters' filter does not screen it. The output check has to cover the quarters after the trigger too.
candidates.evidence_quote: "tying their disbursement to recent changes in the unemployment rate" (Sahm 2019)

candidates.name: Chauvet-Piger smoothed US recession probabilities (FRED RECPROUSM156N)
candidates.who_uses_it: Published on FRED. Other adopters not verified this session.
candidates.definition: A dynamic-factor Markov-switching model on four monthly series: nonfarm payroll employment, industrial production, real personal income excluding transfers, and real manufacturing and trade sales. Output is the probability of recession.
candidates.data_source: FRED RECPROUSM156N, monthly; latest 0.76% (Jul 2026), updated 1 Sep 2026; about a one-month lag.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It includes payroll employment and income, so an AI job shock would push it up much as a recession would. That makes it unsuitable as an exclusion for an employment-led AI shock; the GDP-only Hamilton index is better for that.
candidates.evidence_quote: "dynamic-factor markov-switching model" applied to four monthly variables (FRED notes)

candidates.name: CEPR-EABCN Euro Area Business Cycle Dating Committee
candidates.who_uses_it: CEPR and EABCN jointly. The committee of five CEPR researchers sets the euro area chronology of recessions and expansions: the original eleven members plus Greece for 1970-1998, and the whole euro area from 1999.
candidates.definition: Judgement-based dating of euro area peaks and troughs, NBER-style, using GDP, output gaps, sector and labour data. It meets about twice a year (March and October in 2024) and issues statements. Its 17 Mar 2026 statement: no recession, and euro area unemployment at a historic low of 6.1% (Jan 2026 data).
candidates.data_source: Committee statements (PDF), roughly twice a year. The chronology page is behind Cloudflare and was not read, so the peak and trough dates are not verified this session.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It dates the cycle only. Meetings are infrequent and its verdicts come quarters after the fact, so as a real-time recession exclusion for Germany, France and Spain it would be slow.
candidates.evidence_quote: "establishes the chronology of recessions and expansions" (EABCN 2023-24 report)

candidates.name: National business cycle reference dates (Japan ESRI, Brazil CODACE, Canada C.D. Howe council, ECRI)
candidates.who_uses_it: Japan: the President of the Cabinet Office's Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) sets official reference dates on the advice of the Committee for Business Cycle Indicators. Brazil: CODACE at FGV IBRE, seven members. Canada: the C.D. Howe Business Cycle Council, the NBER counterpart. ECRI: private chronologies for 21 countries beyond the US, client-only (academics can request them).
candidates.definition: Judgement-based dating of peaks and troughs. Japan: peak Oct 2018, trough May 2020, set on 19 Jul 2022, about 26 months after the trough. CODACE: latest announcement 29 Jun 2020, a peak in 2019Q4. C.D. Howe (5 Jun 2026): declines in 2025Q4 and 2026Q1 GDP did not meet its 'pronounced, persistent, or pervasive' tests, so no recession.
candidates.data_source: Each body's website; announcements irregular and months to years after the turning point. ECRI dates not public.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. None of these dating bodies attributes causes. Their lags (Japan's trough came 26 months late) make them poor real-time exclusions. The UK, Korea, Australia, Spain and France were not checked this session.
candidates.evidence_quote: "a trough occurred in May 2020" (ESRI, determined 19 Jul 2022)

candidates.name: OECD-based recession indicators on FRED (e.g., GBRRECM), discontinued
candidates.who_uses_it: Formerly published by FRED for OECD countries, built from OECD composite leading indicator (CLI) turning points. Discontinued; last updated 9 Dec 2022.
candidates.definition: Growth-cycle turning points: deviation-from-trend cycles in a reference series (industrial production excluding construction, plus GDP), found with a simplified Bry-Boschan routine. The recession runs from the midpoint of the peak period to the midpoint of the trough period.
candidates.data_source: FRED GBRRECM and similar (DISCONTINUED, data to Sep 2022). The OECD CLI page returned 403 this session.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No, and they measure growth slowdowns relative to trend, not classical recessions. They are discontinued, so they cannot be used to resolve anything now.
candidates.evidence_quote: "OECD based Recession Indicators for the United Kingdom" (DISCONTINUED)

candidates.name: BLS Displaced Worker Survey (CPS January supplement)
candidates.who_uses_it: BLS. The survey has run every two years in January since 1984.
candidates.definition: Displaced workers are people aged 20+ who lost or left a job because their 'plant or company closed down or moved', there was 'insufficient work', or their 'position or shift was abolished'. The headline counts long-tenured workers (3+ years with the employer). Jan 2026 survey (covering 2023-25): 3.3M long-tenured displaced, up 746,000 on 2021-23; reasons were position abolished 44.4%, closure 32.6%, insufficient work 22.9%; 66.1% reemployed; 7.4M displaced in total.
candidates.data_source: BLS news release 'Displaced Workers Summary', released 27 Aug 2026 (about 7 months after the January collection). The next survey is presumably Jan 2028, but the schedule is not verified.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. The questionnaire has no category for technology, automation or AI. A rising 'position or shift abolished' share fits AI substitution but also fits restructuring. It comes only every two years, with a lag.
candidates.evidence_quote: "up by 746,000 workers from the prior survey period" (BLS, 27 Aug 2026)

candidates.name: JOLTS layoffs and discharges, hires, openings (and the Beveridge curve)
candidates.who_uses_it: BLS monthly release. FRED carries JTSLDL, JTSLDR, JTSHIR and JTSJOR from Dec 2000. A BLS Monthly Labor Review (MLR) article (Barnichon, Elsby, Hobijn and Sahin, June 2012) uses JOLTS to diagnose shifts in the Beveridge curve, the relation between job openings and unemployment.
candidates.definition: Layoffs and discharges are involuntary separations initiated by the employer, including layoffs with no intent to rehire and discharges because positions were eliminated. Aug 2026: openings 7.1M (4.3%), hires 5.2M (3.3%), quits 3.1M (1.9%), layoffs 1.6M (1.0%).
candidates.data_source: BLS JOLTS; the Aug 2026 data came out 29 Sep 2026 and the Sep data is scheduled for 3 Nov 2026. Monthly with about a 1-month-plus lag; history from Dec 2000.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No reason for separation is recorded. The Beveridge curve is the standard diagnostic for structural versus cyclical unemployment: unemployment rising while openings hold up suggests mismatch. But the 2012 MLR article shows an outward shift during the cyclical recovery after 2009, which the authors judged largely temporary. They also say the shift cannot be read directly as a higher natural rate.
candidates.evidence_quote: "one has to be very careful when trying to translate the measured shift" (MLR 2012)

candidates.name: CPS reason for unemployment: permanent job losers; long-term unemployed share
candidates.who_uses_it: BLS Employment Situation tables; FRED LNS13026638 (permanent job losers, from 1994-01), LNS13023653 (on temporary layoff, from 1967) and LNS13025703 (share unemployed 27+ weeks, from 1948).
candidates.definition: Unemployed people classified by why they are unemployed: job losers (on temporary layoff, or permanent job losers), job leavers, re-entrants and new entrants. My calculation of permanent job losers as a share of all unemployed: 17.7% (Dec 2000), 30.9% (Nov 2001), 44.0% (Oct 2009), 41.4% (Dec 2010), 23.8% (Jul 2024), 25.3% (Aug 2026). Long-term unemployed share: 36.6% (Oct 2009), 27.0% (Aug 2026).
candidates.data_source: BLS CPS, monthly, released the first Friday of the next month. Note that October 2025 CPS data were not collected because of the federal shutdown.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. Both shares jump in ordinary recessions (44% permanent-loser share in 2009-10), so a structural-looking mix does not isolate AI. They could at most back up a pattern of permanent rather than temporary job loss.
candidates.evidence_quote: "Data for October 2025 were not collected due to the federal government shutdown" (BLS)

candidates.name: BLS AI exposure categories (Employment Projections, Aug 2026)
candidates.who_uses_it: BLS Employment Projections program (new; last modified 27 Aug 2026). No third-party adoption found yet.
candidates.definition: Each of about 831 detailed occupations (2018 Standard Occupational Classification, SOC) gets one of four relative categories: Low, Moderate, High or Very High. BLS takes percentile ranks on five external indices. Three are theoretical exposure measures: Felten-Raj-Seamans; Eloundou-Manning-Mishkin-Rock; Eisfeldt-Schubert-Taska-Zhang. Two are observed-use measures: Massenkoff-McCrory (Anthropic) and Tomlinson et al. (Microsoft). It computes median ranks on the theoretical and observed dimensions, then clusters occupations into the four groups.
candidates.data_source: BLS page plus the XLSX 'AI exposure categories and 2025–35 employment projections' (/emp/ind-occ-matrix/ai-exposure-categories.xlsx; not downloaded because of the bot block, so employment by category is not verified). The next projections (2026-36) are due in 2027.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Not by itself. It is an official occupational exposure map that can be joined to monthly CPS data (by detailed occupation) to compare unemployment or employment in Very High versus Low exposure occupations. BLS itself says a category is not a forecast. The OECD warns that exposed occupations are more sensitive to the business cycle (see the OECD candidate), so an exposure comparison should be paired with an output-recession exclusion.
candidates.evidence_quote: "An exposure category is not a forecast of employment growth or decline" (BLS)

candidates.name: CPS employment and unemployment by occupation (Table A-13 monthly; cpsaat11 annual detail)
candidates.who_uses_it: BLS Employment Situation (Table A-13) and CPS annual averages (Table 11).
candidates.definition: A-13: employed and unemployed by major occupation group of the last job, not seasonally adjusted, monthly. Aug 2026 unemployment rates: management and professional 2.9% (2.7% a year earlier); sales and office 3.7% (4.5%). cpsaat11: employment by detailed occupation, annual averages; 2025 is an 11-month average excluding October.
candidates.data_source: BLS CPS: monthly (A-13) and annual (cpsaat11, released early the next year). Detailed-occupation monthly figures need CPS microdata (not verified this session).
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Only when combined with an exposure map (BLS categories or ILO gradients). The monthly published groups are too coarse to separate AI-exposed from unexposed work.
candidates.evidence_quote: "Employed and unemployed people by occupation, not seasonally adjusted" (Table A-13)

candidates.name: BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS)
candidates.who_uses_it: BLS. The standard official US source for employment levels by occupation (about 830 occupations).
candidates.definition: Employment and wage estimates by occupation, industry and area. Each set pools six half-yearly panels over three years (1.1 million establishments).
candidates.data_source: BLS OEWS, annual; May 2025 data released 15 May 2026.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. BLS says it 'does not encourage the use of OEWS data for time-series analysis', because pooling three years of panels blurs change over time. That makes it a poor base for a trigger, though it can supply weights.
candidates.evidence_quote: "does not encourage the use of OEWS data for time-series analysis" (BLS)

candidates.name: Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS): core AI-use question
candidates.who_uses_it: US Census Bureau: public tables every two weeks, America Counts stories, Census CES working papers. Census plans AI questions for other core business surveys such as the Annual Integrated Economic Survey (AIES).
candidates.definition: Two core questions since Sep 2023: did the business use AI in the last two weeks, and does it expect to in the next six months. Until Nov 2025 the wording was AI 'in producing goods or services'; from 17 Nov 2025 it is 'in any business function'. That break adds a discrete jump. Use rose from 3.5% to 10% of firms before the revision and 18% after; nationally 17-20% of firms from Dec 2025 to May 2026, and about 37% at firms with 250+ employees.
candidates.data_source: Census BTOS, collected every two weeks. About 1.2M businesses in six panels; representative of employer businesses excluding farms. Figures come out about 4 weeks after the reference period. No collection took place during the late-2025 funding lapse.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: It measures adoption only. The core questions carry no employment attribution. Useful as a condition that adoption is widespread, not as proof of displacement.
candidates.evidence_quote: "Data collection will occur every two weeks" (Census BTOS page)

candidates.name: Census BTOS AI supplement: AI-driven employment change (Q28)
candidates.who_uses_it: Census Bureau (CES Working Paper 26-25, Bonney, Breaux, Dinlersoz, Foster, Haltiwanger and Pande, April 2026). The earlier supplement is covered in Bonney et al. (2024).
candidates.definition: AI-using firms are asked how AI affected the business's total employment in the last six months: increased, decreased, or no change. The 2025-26 supplement (fielded 17 Nov 2025 to 8 Feb 2026) found 2.0% decreased (firm-weighted; 2.4% employment-weighted), 2.3% increased (3.7%) and 95.7% no change (93.9%). The authors call this similar to the 2023-24 supplement.
candidates.data_source: Two supplements so far (Dec 2023–Feb 2024; Nov 2025–Feb 2026); spring 2026 public release. No fixed schedule.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Yes. This is the only official US statistic found in which firms themselves attribute employment change to AI. But it runs irregularly and covers AI-using firms only, so it cannot resolve on known dates unless Census commits to a schedule.
candidates.evidence_quote: "AI-related employment decreases are rare, occurring in only 2% of firms" (CES 26-25)

candidates.name: ILO generative AI occupational exposure index (Working Paper 140, 2025)
candidates.who_uses_it: ILO (Gmyrek, Berg, Kamiński, Konopczyński, Ładna, Nafradi, Rosłaniec and Troszyński; 20 May 2025). It updates the 2023 index by Gmyrek, Berg and Bescond.
candidates.definition: Exposure scores for ISCO-08 4-digit occupations, grouped into four exposure gradients. They are built from 2,861 tasks in Poland's occupational classification, scored by a survey of 1,640 workers, experts and language-model predictions. Annex Table A1 lists occupations by gradient. About one in four workers globally is in an occupation with some exposure; 3.3% are in the highest gradient.
candidates.data_source: ILO WP140 PDF with the occupation annex. A one-off index, not a regular series. Whether ILOSTAT publishes employment by gradient is not verified.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Only when joined to labour force survey occupation data. It is the international counterpart of the BLS categories for the model's other nine countries. The ILO expects job transformation to be more likely than job loss, and exposure is not displacement.
candidates.evidence_quote: "transformation of jobs is the most likely impact of GenAI" (ILO WP140)

candidates.name: OECD Employment Outlook AI-exposure analysis (Felten-Raj-Seamans language-model exposure in ISCO; LinkedIn AI hiring)
candidates.who_uses_it: OECD Employment Outlook 2023 and 2026. The 2026 edition uses the Felten-Raj-Seamans (2023) exposure to AI language models, mapped to ISCO by Nurski (2025), plus LinkedIn AI-talent hiring from OECD.AI and Indeed AI-tracker postings.
candidates.definition: The method checks whether trends for high-exposure occupations, such as young entrants' unemployment gaps or job postings, change after firms start using AI heavily (mid-2023 to early 2024 by country). It found no break in the trend for graduates' unemployment gaps and concluded that the spread of language models is unlikely to be the main factor.
candidates.data_source: Annual OECD Employment Outlook (EO 2026 published July 2026). It is analysis, not a series.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: It tries to, using timing tests against adoption dates. It also flags the key confound: exposed occupations cluster in sectors sensitive to capital costs, such as information, finance and professional services. So what looks like an AI effect can just be the macroeconomic cycle.
candidates.evidence_quote: "the data show little evidence of this to date" (OECD Employment Outlook 2026)

candidates.name: Eurostat enterprise AI use (ICT usage and e-commerce in enterprises survey, isoc_eb_ai)
candidates.who_uses_it: Eurostat and national statistical offices across the EU.
candidates.definition: Share of enterprises with 10+ employees using at least one AI technology: 19.95% of EU enterprises in 2025, 55.03% of large ones. The survey sampled 157,000 of 1.53 million enterprises.
candidates.data_source: Eurostat isoc_eb_ai, annual. Data extracted Dec 2025; next update planned Dec 2026.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Adoption only. No question on AI's effect on employment was found on the page.
candidates.evidence_quote: "In 2025, 19.95% of EU enterprises used AI technologies" (Eurostat)

About 1% of service firms reported AI-related layoffs in the past six months, and 13% of service firms expected layoffs in the next six. These figures come from a WebFetch summary of the post and should be rechecked before citing.

candidates.name: Official structural unemployment estimates: FOMC longer-run unemployment (SEP) and CBO noncyclical rate

Median 4.2% at every SEP from Jun 2024 to 16 Sep 2026; 4.1% during 2020 (it did not rise with COVID). Its central tendency rose from 4.8-5.0 (2009) to 5.2-6.0 (2011-2013) after the financial crisis. The FOMC range rose about 0.7 points after 2008 (a cyclical recession with lasting damage), so a 0.5-point rule would have fired then.
candidates.evidence_quote: "arising from all sources except fluctuations in aggregate demand" (CBO via FRED)

candidates.name: Unemployment Insurance Extended Benefits (EB) statutory triggers
candidates.who_uses_it: US law, the Federal-State Extended Unemployment Compensation Act of 1970. The Department of Labor publishes weekly trigger notices; on 27 Sep 2026, 0 states were 'on'.
candidates.definition: State-level triggers based on the 13-week insured unemployment rate relative to prior years, and an optional trigger based on the 3-month seasonally adjusted total unemployment rate relative to the prior year. The numeric thresholds are not verified this session.
candidates.data_source: DOL/ETA trigger notice reports, weekly.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It is a cyclical benefits trigger. It shows unemployment-rate triggers are an established legal tool for switching on cash support, but it does not separate AI from a recession.
candidates.evidence_quote: "Total Number 'ON': 0" (DOL trigger notice, 27 Sep 2026)

candidates.name: Built from established parts, not itself established: unemployment rise without an output recession, concentrated in high-exposure occupations
candidates.who_uses_it: Not adopted by anyone as a whole. It is proposed here from established pieces: BLS U-3 or OECD harmonised unemployment rates; the Hamilton GDP-based recession index; and the BLS AI exposure categories (US) or ILO gradients (other countries).
candidates.definition: (1) The 12-month average unemployment rate is at least X points above its value 24 months earlier, or above the model's 2025 baseline. (2) The Hamilton index (JHGDPBRINDX) stays below 67 in every quarter from 8 quarters before through 4 quarters after the first qualifying month. (3) Optional: over the same window, the rise in unemployment (or fall in employment) in High and Very High exposure occupations exceeds that in Low exposure occupations by a preset margin, in CPS data. Backtest of (1)+(2), run on FRED data today from 1967: X=3.0 gives 0 episodes; X=2.0 gives 0; X=1.5 gives 1 (2003-10); X=1.0 gives 2 (2003-10, 2011-07). Without (2), X=3.0 fires in 1975-09, 2009-06 and 2020-09, all recession-driven.
candidates.data_source: FRED UNRATE (monthly, first-Friday release) and JHGDPBRINDX (quarterly, never revised); BLS AI exposure XLSX; CPS microdata. It resolves about 4 quarters plus about 4 months after the trigger quarter, all from published data on known release dates.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Part (2) rules out output recessions and their recoveries, the false positives the review found. Part (3) links the rise to AI-exposed work, though the OECD warns exposed occupations are cyclically sensitive, which (2) partly addresses. Limits: US-only for the Hamilton index; other countries need a Hamilton-style GDP rule computed on national GDP. The exposure step has no historical backtest because the BLS categories are new.
candidates.evidence_quote: computed this session (no quote)

verified.summary:
Short answer to the owner: no. No official statistical agency or standards body publishes an "AI labour shock has started" signal, or any rule for technological unemployment. The model's trigger (12-month U-3 at least 3 points above the 2025 average, with real GDP at or above its previous peak) is bespoke.

Verification result: I re-opened at least one source for every candidate. The core claims hold. I made small factual corrections (listed in none_found_notes) and dropped nothing.

**What is established splits into two groups, and neither alone separates AI from the business cycle.**

(A) Cycle signals. These are well established but say nothing about cause:
- NBER dates and FRED USREC.
- The real-time Sahm rule (SAHMREALTIME). Sahm, then at the Federal Reserve Board, designed it in 2019 as the trigger for automatic direct payments to individuals.
- Hamilton's GDP-based recession index (JHGDPBRINDX). FRED says it is computed from GDP alone and "never subsequently revised".
- Chauvet-Piger recession probabilities.
- The CEPR-EABCN euro area committee, Japan's ESRI, Brazil's CODACE and the C.D. Howe council for Canada.
- The statutory Extended Benefits unemployment-insurance triggers.
- FOMC and CBO estimates of structural unemployment.

(B) AI-specific official statistics. These are new and none of them is a trigger:
- BLS AI exposure categories (27 Aug 2026). Four levels for 831 occupations, built from five exposure indices. BLS says a category is not a forecast.
- Census BTOS core AI-use question. Collected every two weeks since Sep 2023; the wording changed on 17 Nov 2025. Use is 17-20% of firms from Dec 2025 to May 2026.
- The BTOS AI supplements (Dec 2023–Feb 2024 and 17 Nov 2025–8 Feb 2026). Of AI-using firms, 2.0% reported an AI-driven employment decrease and 2.3% an increase.
- The ILO GenAI exposure gradients (Working Paper 140).
- The OECD's use of the Felten-Raj-Seamans language-model exposure index, mapped to ISCO by Nurski.
- Eurostat's annual enterprise AI-use survey (isoc_eb_ai).

Other official labour data record why jobs end but never whether technology was the cause:
- The Displaced Worker Survey (27 Aug 2026) counts 3.3M long-tenured displaced workers for 2023-25, up 746k; 44.4% said their position was abolished.
- JOLTS layoffs and the CPS count of permanent job losers.

The OECD Employment Outlook 2026 finds "little evidence" of AI automating jobs so far. It also warns that AI-exposed occupations are more sensitive to macroeconomic conditions, so an exposure comparison can mistake a downturn for an AI effect.

**What I recomputed (on the researcher's FRED CSVs, which I hashed and spot-checked against the live FRED pages):**
- The three US episodes since 1948 with a 3+ point rise in the 12-month unemployment average (vs 24 months earlier) start in 1975-09, 2009-06 and 2020-09. They are 6, 0 and 5 months from an NBER recession month.
- With Hamilton's index required below 67 from 8 quarters before through 4 quarters after the month, and tested month by month:
  - A 3.0 or 2.0 point rise never fires.
  - A 1.5 point rise fires once (2003-10).
  - A 1.0 point rise fires in 2003-10 and 2011-07.
- **Caveat:** if the filter is applied only at the first month of each rise, nothing fires at any threshold. The 2003-10 firing comes about 15 months after that rise began (2002-07). In effect, the pre-window means the rule cannot fire until 8 quarters after the last quarter of an output recession.
- **New finding:** the Sahm rule with the same Hamilton window still fires in 2024-07, 2024-08 and 2024-09, the known false positive. A 0.5-point Sahm-style threshold is therefore too sensitive even with the output filter.
- The share of unemployed who are permanent job losers peaked at 44.8% in Nov 2009 (not 44.0% in Oct 2009).

**Suggested falsifiable build from established parts:**
1. An unemployment-rise trigger of about 1.5 points or more in the 12-month average. Do not use a 0.5-point Sahm threshold.
2. The Hamilton GDP-index window, to exclude output recessions. It resolves about 16 months after the trigger quarter.
3. Optional attribution step: a check that the rise is concentrated in occupations rated High or Very High for AI exposure. Use BLS categories with CPS data for the US, and ILO gradients with labour force surveys elsewhere.

One design caveat: an AI shock that itself causes an output recession would be vetoed by step 2.

For countries other than the US, no published Hamilton equivalent was found. The OECD recession indicators on FRED were discontinued (last updated 9 Dec 2022).

candidates.name: NBER business cycle dates (FRED USREC / USRECQ)
candidates.who_uses_it: The NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee sets the US reference chronology. FRED builds USREC (monthly, from 1854-12) from NBER peaks and troughs. Its wider use as the standard US chronology is general knowledge, not checked for specific institutions. Correction: the FRED page does not say how updates are tied to NBER announcements; that claim is not verified.
candidates.definition: No fixed rule: 'a significant decline in economic activity that is spread across the economy and lasts more than a few months'. In recent decades the committee has put the most weight on real personal income less transfers and nonfarm payroll employment. USREC is 1 from the period after the peak through the trough period ('trough method'), otherwise 0. Announcement lags, computed from the NBER announcements page: peaks 1980-01 (announced 3 Jun 1980, ~5 months), 1981-07 (6 Jan 1982, ~6), 1990-07 (25 Apr 1991, ~9), 2001-03 (26 Nov 2001, ~8), 2007-12 (1 Dec 2008, ~12), 2020-02 (8 Jun 2020, ~4). Troughs 1980-07 (8 Jul 1981, 12), 1982-11 (8 Jul 1983, 8), 1991-03 (22 Dec 1992, 21), 2001-11 (17 Jul 2003, 20), 2009-06 (20 Sep 2010, 15), 2020-04 (19 Jul 2021, 15).
candidates.data_source: NBER announcements (irregular, no schedule). FRED USREC monthly, 1854-12 to 2026-08 (latest 0), last updated 1 Sep 2026.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It dates the cycle and says nothing about cause. As an exclusion it arrives 4-21 months late. Because payrolls and income carry the most weight, an employment-led AI shock could itself be dated a recession and so veto the trigger (this is an inference). Recomputed: the three 3+ point rises in the 12-month unemployment average since 1948 (1975-09, 2009-06, 2020-09) are 6, 0 and 5 months from an NBER recession month.
candidates.evidence_quote: "a significant decline in economic activity that is spread across the economy" (NBER)

candidates.name: Hamilton GDP-based recession indicator index (FRED JHGDPBRINDX)
candidates.who_uses_it: Published on FRED (source: James Hamilton). Adoption beyond FRED not verified.
candidates.definition: The probability that the US was in recession in a quarter, computed mechanically from GDP data alone. FRED: above 67 is a historically reliable recession signal; after that, falling below 33 reliably signals the end. Each value is computed for the quarter just before the latest GDP release and never revised.
candidates.data_source: FRED JHGDPBRINDX, quarterly, 1967Q4 to 2026Q1 (latest 7.0), last updated 30 Jul 2026, about 4 months after the reference quarter ends.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Not by itself. Because it uses output only, it can check that unemployment rose without an output recession. Recomputed backtest from 1967, requiring the index below 67 from 8 quarters before through 4 quarters after the month, tested month by month: 3.0 and 2.0 point rises (12-month average vs 24 months earlier) never fire; 1.5 fires once (2003-10); 1.0 fires in 2003-10 and 2011-07. Using the minimum over the prior 24 months as the baseline gives the same result. Caveat: if the filter is applied only at the first month of each rise, nothing fires at any threshold. The 2003-10 firing comes about 15 months after that rise began (2002-07). The pre-window is what removes recession recoveries. No published equivalent was found for the other countries.
candidates.evidence_quote: "Once the index is calculated for that quarter, it is never subsequently revised" (FRED)

candidates.name: Real-time Sahm rule recession indicator (FRED SAHMREALTIME)
candidates.who_uses_it: Published on FRED. Claudia Sahm (Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System) proposed it in a 2019 Hamilton Project chapter as the trigger for automatic lump-sum direct payments to individuals. That cash-transfer use is close to the UBI model's.
candidates.definition: Signal when the 3-month moving average of national U-3 rises 0.50 points or more above the minimum of the 3-month averages over the previous 12 months, using data as available in each month.
candidates.data_source: FRED SAHMREALTIME, monthly, 1959-12 to 2026-08 (latest -0.07), updated 4 Sep 2026, the day of the jobs report.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No; it detects fast unemployment rises of any cause. Recomputed first trigger months: 1959-12, 1960-08, 1969-10, 1970-02, 1974-03, 1974-07, 1976-11, 1980-04, 1981-11, 1990-11, 2001-06, 2008-04, 2020-04 and 2024-07. All but 1976-11 and 2024-07 are within 6 months of an NBER recession month. New check: with the Hamilton window (below 67 from 8 quarters before through 4 after), Sahm months 2024-07, 2024-08 and 2024-09 still pass. So a 0.5-point Sahm-style trigger plus the output filter still gives the 2024 false positive.
candidates.evidence_quote: "tying their disbursement to recent changes in the unemployment rate" (Sahm 2019)

candidates.name: Chauvet-Piger smoothed US recession probabilities (FRED RECPROUSM156N)
candidates.who_uses_it: Published on FRED. Other adopters not verified.
candidates.definition: A dynamic-factor Markov-switching model on four monthly coincident series: nonfarm payroll employment, industrial production, real personal income excluding transfers, and real manufacturing and trade sales. Output is a smoothed recession probability.
candidates.data_source: FRED RECPROUSM156N, monthly; latest 0.76% (Jul 2026), updated 1 Sep 2026.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It includes payrolls and income, so an employment-led AI shock would raise it much as a recession would. That makes it unsuitable as an exclusion for such a shock; the GDP-only Hamilton index fits better.
candidates.evidence_quote: "a dynamic-factor markov-switching model applied to four monthly coincident variables" (FRED)

candidates.name: CEPR-EABCN Euro Area Business Cycle Dating Committee
candidates.who_uses_it: CEPR and EABCN. Five CEPR researchers set the chronology of recessions and expansions: the eleven original members plus Greece for 1970-1998, and the whole euro area from 1999. Current members: Born, Pappa (chair), Ricco, Smets, Tenreyro.
candidates.definition: Judgement-based dating of euro area peaks and troughs, drawing on GDP relative to trend, sector and labour data. It met twice in the Oct 2023–Sep 2024 report year (October and March). Its 17 Mar 2026 statement (meeting of 11 Mar) was titled 'Resilient Growth in the Euro Area'. It found growth positive and unemployment at a historic low of 6.1% for the euro area excluding Ireland (Jan 2026). It did not literally say 'no recession'.
candidates.data_source: Committee statements (PDF), about twice a year. The chronology page is behind Cloudflare and was not read, so peak and trough dates are not verified.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. It dates the cycle only, and meets rarely with verdicts quarters late, so it is slow as a real-time exclusion for Germany, France and Spain.
candidates.evidence_quote: "establishes the chronology of recessions and expansions" (EABCN 2023-24 report)

candidates.name: National business cycle reference dates (Japan ESRI, Brazil CODACE, Canada C.D. Howe council, ECRI)
candidates.who_uses_it: Japan: the President of ESRI sets reference dates after discussion by the Committee for Business Cycle Indicators. Brazil: CODACE, housed at FGV IBRE, seven members. Canada: the C.D. Howe Business Cycle Council, which 'performs a similar function' to the NBER committee. ECRI: private chronologies for 21 countries beyond the US, available to clients; academics can ask.
candidates.definition: Judgement-based dating of peaks and troughs. Japan: peak Oct 2018 and trough May 2020, determined 19 Jul 2022, about 26 months after the trough. CODACE: met 26 Jun 2020 and found a peak in 2019Q4; the researcher's 29 Jun announcement date is not verified. C.D. Howe (5 Jun 2026): the 2025Q4 and 2026Q1 GDP declines did not meet its 'pronounced, persistent, or pervasive' tests.
candidates.data_source: Each body's website; announcements are irregular and come months to years late. ECRI dates are not public.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No; none attributes causes, and the lags make them poor real-time exclusions. The UK, Korea, Australia, Spain and France were not checked.
candidates.evidence_quote: "a trough occurred in May 2020" (ESRI, determined 19 Jul 2022)

candidates.name: OECD-based recession indicators on FRED (e.g., GBRRECM), discontinued
candidates.who_uses_it: Formerly published on FRED for OECD countries from OECD composite leading indicator data. Discontinued; last updated 9 Dec 2022.
candidates.definition: Growth-cycle turning points in a deviation-from-trend reference series: industrial production excluding construction, with GDP for final turning points. They were found with a simplified Bry-Boschan routine. Recessions are shaded from the midpoint of the peak through the midpoint of the trough.
candidates.data_source: FRED GBRRECM and similar (DISCONTINUED; data to Sep 2022).
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. These are growth slowdowns relative to trend, not classical recessions, and are discontinued, so they cannot resolve anything now.
candidates.evidence_quote: "a simplified version of the original Bry and Boschan routine" (FRED GBRRECM)

candidates.name: BLS Displaced Worker Survey (CPS January supplement)
candidates.who_uses_it: BLS. It is a supplement run every 2 years; the 2026 survey was part of the January 2026 CPS. The '1984 start' claim is not verified.
candidates.definition: Displaced workers are people aged 20+ who lost or left jobs because their plant or company closed down or moved, there was insufficient work, or their position or shift was abolished. Survey period Jan 2023–Dec 2025: 3.3M long-tenured displaced (3+ years), up 746,000 on 2021-23; position abolished 44.4%, closure 32.6%, insufficient work 22.9%; 66.1% reemployed in Jan 2026; 7.4M displaced at any tenure.
candidates.data_source: BLS 'Displaced Workers Summary', released 27 Aug 2026 (about 7 months after collection). Next survey presumably Jan 2028 (not verified).
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. The reason categories are closed or moved, insufficient work, abolished, seasonal, business failed, and other; there is no technology, automation or AI option. It is biennial and lagged.
candidates.evidence_quote: "their position or shift was abolished" (BLS displaced worker definition)

candidates.name: JOLTS layoffs and discharges, hires, openings (and the Beveridge curve)
candidates.who_uses_it: BLS monthly release; FRED series from Dec 2000. A BLS Monthly Labor Review article (Barnichon, Elsby, Hobijn and Şahin, June 2012) used JOLTS to decompose the post-2009 Beveridge curve shift.
candidates.definition: Layoffs and discharges are involuntary separations initiated by the employer. They include layoffs with no intent to rehire and discharges because positions were eliminated. Aug 2026: openings 7.1M (4.3%), hires 5.2M (3.3%), quits 3.1M (1.9%), layoffs 1.6M (1.0%).
candidates.data_source: BLS JOLTS; Aug 2026 data released 29 Sep 2026; Sep data scheduled for 3 Nov 2026.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No reason for separation is recorded. The Beveridge curve is a standard structural-versus-cyclical diagnostic. But the 2012 MLR authors judged the post-2009 outward shift 'in all likelihood largely temporary'. They warned against reading it directly as a higher natural rate.
candidates.evidence_quote: "one has to be very careful when trying to translate the measured shift" (MLR 2012)

candidates.name: CPS reason for unemployment: permanent job losers; long-term unemployed share
candidates.who_uses_it: BLS Employment Situation tables; FRED LNS13026638 (permanent job losers, from 1994-01), LNS13023653 (temporary layoff, from 1967) and LNS13025703 (share unemployed 27+ weeks, from 1948).
candidates.definition: Unemployed people by reason: job losers (temporary layoff or permanent), job leavers, re-entrants, new entrants. Recomputed permanent-loser share of all unemployed (LNS13026638 / UNEMPLOY): 17.7% (Dec 2000), 30.9% (Nov 2001), 44.0% (Oct 2009), peak 44.8% (Nov 2009), 41.4% (Dec 2010), 23.8% (Jul 2024), 25.3% (Aug 2026). Long-term share: 36.6% (Oct 2009), peak 45.5% (Apr 2010), 27.0% (Aug 2026).
candidates.data_source: BLS CPS monthly, first-Friday release. October 2025 is missing in the series (not collected; shutdown).
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. Both shares jump in ordinary recessions, so a structural-looking mix does not isolate AI.
candidates.evidence_quote: "Data for October 2025 were not collected due to the federal government shutdown" (BLS)

candidates.name: BLS AI exposure categories (Employment Projections, Aug 2026)
candidates.who_uses_it: BLS Employment Projections program; page last modified 27 Aug 2026. No third-party adoption was found (absence not provable).
candidates.definition: Each of 831 detailed occupations gets one of four categories: Low, Moderate, High or Very high. The inputs are percentile ranks on five indices: Felten-Raj-Seamans; Eloundou-Manning-Mishkin-Rock; Eisfeldt-Schubert-Taska-Zhang; Massenkoff-McCrory (Anthropic); and Tomlinson-Jaffe-Wang-Counts-Suri (Microsoft). BLS takes median ranks separately across the theoretical and observed sources, then clusters occupations into the four groups.
candidates.data_source: BLS page and XLSX 'AI exposure categories and 2025–35 employment projections' (/emp/ind-occ-matrix/ai-exposure-categories.xlsx). A plain download returned HTTP 403 and was not bypassed, so employment by category is not verified. The researcher's 'next projections in 2027' is not verified.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Not by itself. It is an official exposure map that can be joined to CPS data by occupation to compare High or Very high with Low exposure. BLS says it is not a forecast, and the OECD's cyclical-sensitivity warning applies, so pair it with an output-recession exclusion.
candidates.evidence_quote: "An exposure category is not a forecast of employment growth or decline" (BLS)

candidates.name: CPS employment and unemployment by occupation (Table A-13 monthly; cpsaat11 annual detail)
candidates.who_uses_it: BLS Employment Situation (Table A-13) and CPS annual averages (Table 11).
candidates.definition: A-13: employed and unemployed people by major occupation group, not seasonally adjusted, monthly. Aug 2026 unemployment rates: management and professional 2.9% (2.7% in Aug 2025); sales and office 3.7% (4.5%). cpsaat11: employment by detailed occupation, annual; 2025 is an 11-month average excluding October.
candidates.data_source: BLS CPS monthly (A-13) and annual (cpsaat11). Detailed-occupation monthly figures need CPS microdata (not verified).
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Only when combined with an exposure map; the published monthly groups are too coarse.
candidates.evidence_quote: "Employed and unemployed people by occupation, not seasonally adjusted" (Table A-13)

candidates.name: BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS)
candidates.who_uses_it: BLS; annual estimates for about 830 occupations.
candidates.definition: Employment and wage estimates by occupation, industry and area. Each set pools six semi-annual panels over three years, about 1.1 million establishments.
candidates.data_source: BLS OEWS, annual; May 2025 data released 15 May 2026.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: No. BLS discourages time-series use of OEWS, so it is a poor trigger base, though usable for weights.
candidates.evidence_quote: "does not encourage the use of OEWS data for time-series analysis" (BLS)

candidates.name: Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS): core AI-use question
candidates.who_uses_it: US Census Bureau (tables every two weeks, America Counts story May 2026, CES working papers). CES WP 26-25 says lessons from BTOS inform plans to add AI questions to other core surveys such as the AIES.
candidates.definition: Two core AI questions since Sep 2023: use in the last two weeks, and expected use in the next six months. The wording changed from 'producing goods or services' to 'any business function' from 17 Nov 2025. Firm-weighted use rose from 3.5% to 10% before the revision and reached 18% after, a discrete jump. CES attributes it to the new wording, adoption during the funding lapse (when no data were collected), and the second AI supplement. National use was 17-20% from 14 Dec 2025 to 3 May 2026, and 37% at firms with 250+ employees.
candidates.data_source: Census BTOS, about 1.2M businesses in six panels (about 200k each), representative of employer businesses excluding farms. Collection every two weeks; estimates reflect conditions about four weeks earlier.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Adoption only; the core questions carry no employment attribution. Usable as a 'widespread adoption' condition, not as evidence of displacement.
candidates.evidence_quote: "Data collection will occur every two weeks" (Census BTOS page)

candidates.name: Census BTOS AI supplement: AI-driven employment change (Question 28)
candidates.who_uses_it: Census Bureau: CES Working Paper 26-25 (Bonney, Breaux, Dinlersoz, Foster, Haltiwanger and Pande, April 2026). The first supplement is covered in Bonney et al. (2024a,b).
candidates.definition: AI-using firms are asked how AI affected the business's total employment: increased, decreased or no change. 2025-26 supplement (all six panels, 17 Nov 2025 to 8 Feb 2026): decreased 2.0% firm-weighted (2.4% employment-weighted); increased 2.3% (3.7%); no change 95.7% (93.9%). The authors call this very similar to the first supplement (Dec 2023–Feb 2024).
candidates.data_source: Two supplements so far; each topical supplement runs for one 12-week cycle. There is no fixed schedule.
candidates.attributes_to_ai: Yes. It is the only official US statistic found in which firms attribute employment change to AI. But it covers AI users only and runs irregularly, so it cannot resolve on known dates unless Census commits to a schedule.
