rec.answer_to_owner:
No. The model's trigger was invented for this model. It fires when the US 12-month average unemployment rate is at least 7.3% (the 2025 average plus 3 points) while real GDP is at or above its previous peak. No statistical agency, central bank, academic paper, bill or forecasting platform I found uses it. None of them publishes any pre-stated rule that says "an AI labour shock has started".

What does exist falls into three groups:

1. **Established cycle rules that ignore cause.**
   - The Sahm rule (FRED SAHMREALTIME). It is written into bill S.2312, and Sahm designed it in 2019 to trigger automatic cash payments.
   - NBER recession dates.
   - The "two consecutive quarters of falling GDP" convention. I read this wording in Kalshi's KXRECSSNBER contract this session.
   - Hamilton's GDP-based recession index.
   - Unemployment-insurance Extended Benefits triggers.

2. **Established ways of measuring AI exposure, with no threshold.** Anthropic (Massenkoff and McCrory, March 2026), the Yale Budget Lab, Stanford's canaries tracker, EIG and SIEPR all track unemployment or employment in AI-exposed versus unexposed occupations. None sets a trigger. The only benchmark is Anthropic's statement that "differential increases in unemployment on the order of 1 percentage point would be detectable" (I read this in the saved page text).

3. **Things close in spirit but not operational.**
   - Anthropic's June 2026 Economic Policy Framework makes the unemployment rate the "primary trigger", with tiers at about 5%, about 10% and "exceeding historical peaks". It names no series, window or test.
   - H.R.10044 would let Treasury exclude non-AI unemployment at its discretion.
   - The Manifold market the model uses (23%) resolves on the creator's judgment.

**Why the current rule misfires.** In my backtest the baseline fired in five US recession recoveries: 1976-77, 1981, 1983-85, 1992-93 and 2011-13 (plus a short 2021 spell in current-vintage data). It also fired often in other countries.

**What I recommend instead: Option A below.** Unemployment's 12-month average must be at least 3 points above its lowest level of the previous three years. Real GDP must never have fallen more than 1% below its previous peak since that low. The rule is judged once GDP for that quarter is published.

- In the historical data it has never fired: not in the US since 1951, and not in any of the ten countries (395 country-years).
- These results are from my backtest only. The rule is built from established parts, but nobody has adopted it as a whole.

options.name: Baseline: current bespoke rule (level 7.3% with GDP at its peak)
options.rule: US: in month t, the 12-month average of BLS U-3 is at least 7.3%, and the latest published real GDP quarter (BEA GDPC1) is at or above every earlier quarter. Each other country uses its own series and fixed level, 2025 average plus 3 (dashboard/src/countries.js): GBR 7.9, CAN 9.9, DEU 6.7, FRA 10.7, ESP 13.5, BRA 8.9, KOR 5.8, JPN 5.5, AUS 7.2.
options.established_components: Only the data sources are established: BLS U-3, BEA real GDP, OECD harmonised unemployment and national GDP series. The 2025 baseline, the 3-point level and the 'GDP at peak in the latest quarter' test were all invented for this model.
options.backtest:
Method: current-vintage data. A GDP quarter counts as known from the month after it ends; this removes a look-ahead in an earlier verifier's run, which started firing in Oct 1975.

US, current vintage (judged 1948-11 to 2026-08): fires 1976-01..1977-09, 1981-04..06, 1981-10..12, 1983-07..1985-07, 1992-07..1993-06, 2011-01..03, 2011-07..09, 2012-01..2013-12 and 2021-04..05. That is 5 episodes in 78 years.

US, real-time GDP (ALFRED vintages, 1992 on): fires 1992-10..1993-06, 2011-01..06, 2011-10..2012-12 and 2013-02..12. 2021 does not fire.

Relative version (a 3-point rise above the 36-month low, same GDP test), US: 1976-01..08, 1983-07..10, 2011 and 2021-04..06.

Other countries, literal levels:
- GBR: 1983-11..1984-06, 1985-01..09, 1986-01..1989-04, 1993-10..1997-02
- CAN: 1984-01..1986-03, 1986-07, 1993-07..1995-04
- DEU: intermittently 1994-07..2002-12, then 2005-07..2008-06
- FRA: 1994-08..10, 1996-06..1998-11, 1999-04..05
- ESP: 1996-04..1999-12, 2017-01..2020-03
- BRA (IBGE PNAD, 2012 on): 2022-07..2023-02
- KOR: 1999-07..2000-03
- JPN: never
- AUS: 1984-01..1985-12, 1986-04..06, 1986-10..1988-12, 1991-02..03, 1992-07..1995-03, 1995-07..1999-06

Relative version across all ten countries: 10 episodes in 401 country-years.
options.false_positive_risk:
High, and the evidence is direct. Every US firing is an ordinary recession recovery: unemployment lags output, so GDP regains its peak while the 12-month average is still high.

With fixed levels, it also fires for years whenever a country's normal unemployment rate was higher than in 2025 (Germany 1994-2008, Spain, the UK in the 1980s).

The historical non-AI firing rate is about 0.064 a year in the US. That implies a non-AI firing chance of about 24% by the end of 2030 and 45% by the end of 2035.
options.attributes_to_ai: No. It has no cause test, and its GDP test does not tell a recovery apart from a jobless expansion.
options.resolution:
Unemployment comes from the BLS Employment Situation release (first Friday of the following month; FRED UNRATE). GDP comes from the BEA advance estimate, about 4 weeks after the quarter ends.

It is ambiguous in two ways:
- The rule does not fix which GDP vintage counts. Real-time and current-vintage data disagree about 1992-07..09, parts of 2011 and 2021.
- October 2025 was never collected, so the 12-month average must be defined for a missing month.
options.fit_with_priors:
Not a fair prior. The market-anchored prior prices only an AI shock, but this rule also fires on ordinary recessions.

Combining the model's AI prior with the historical non-AI rate, 1-(1-AI)(1-bg), the rule's actual chance of firing is:
- 0.17/0.20/0.26 by 2028
- 0.32/0.38/0.45 by 2030
- 0.56/0.63/0.71 by 2035
- 0.71/0.77/0.84 by 2040
- 0.86/0.91/0.95 by 2050

The prior's modes are 0.08, 0.18, 0.33, 0.43 and 0.55. Raising the prior would not fix this: a firing would then put ordinary recessions through the model's AI-shock endorsement rates. The rule needs to change.

options.name: Option A (recommended): 3-point rise with output held within 1% of its peak
options.rule:
US, month t:
(1) Compute the 12-month average of U-3, averaging whichever months are published (so October 2025, never collected, is skipped).
(2) Find m0, the month with the lowest 12-month average in t-36..t-1.
(3) The trigger fires if the 12-month average at t is at least 3.0 points above its value at m0, AND every quarter of real GDP (GDPC1) from the quarter containing m0 through the quarter containing t is at least 99% of the highest earlier quarter.

The month is judged once the BEA advance estimate for the quarter containing t is out, using that day's GDP vintage (checkable later on ALFRED). The trigger date is month t.

Other nine countries: the same rule on the series the model already uses (FRED LRHUTTTT..M156S; IBGE PNAD table 6381 for Brazil; national real GDP series in research/trigger). Each is judged when the national GDP for t's quarter is published.

A strict variant with no 1% allowance was also tested.
options.established_components:
- The rise is measured the Sahm way: a moving average compared with its recent low (Sahm rule, FRED SAHMREALTIME; the same construction is written into S.2312). The window (12-month average against a 36-month low) and the 3.0 threshold are mine, not Sahm's (3-month, 12-month, 0.5).
- The size, 3 points, matches the model's own definition of the event ('about 3 pp') and the '3 percentage points' in the Manifold market the model uses.
- The output test is peak-relative real output: the model's own current GDP test, and the MacAskill-Moll bet's 'over its previous peak' rule (Kalshi KXAIGROWTHBET, whose text I read). Here it is applied to every quarter since the rise began.
- The 1% allowance is my parameter.
- Nobody has adopted this combination as a whole.
options.backtest:
US, current vintage (1951-10 to 2026-06): never fires at 3 points. Window variants: never with W=60 either.

US, real-time ALFRED vintages from 1992: never fires at 3 or 2 points with the strict test, or at 3 points with the 1% allowance.

All ten countries: never fires at 3 points, 0 episodes in 395 country-years (378 with W=60).

Looser thresholds (with the 1% allowance):
- X=2: USA 2003-08..2004-01 (also in real time), CAN 1971-02..05 and 1978-04..07, FRA 1994-01..12.
- X=1.5: USA 2002-06..2004-07.

Safety margin, the largest rise ever reached while the output test held:
- US 2.06 (2003-10), CAN 2.44 (1978-04), FRA 2.32 (1994-07)
- ESP 1.80, DEU 1.50, AUS 1.38, GBR 1.12
- KOR 0.62, JPN 0.10, BRA -0.03

Every one of the 15 rises of 3 points or more in the data came with an output decline. They were: US 1975, 1982, 2009, 2020; GBR 1992; CAN 1958, 1982, 1992, 2020; ESP 1993, 2008; BRA 2016; KOR 1998; AUS 1983, 1991. The output test could not be checked for CAN 1958 and ESP 1993, which predate the GDP series.

Synthetic forward paths (my construction, onset Sep 2026):
- +4 points over 36 months with GDP growing: fires at month 35.
- Same with two -0.3% quarters: month 35.
- Same with one -0.1% quarter: month 35 (the strict variant: month 50).
- +5 points in 12 months: month 13.
- +3.5 points over 72 months: never.
- Deep recession and jobless-recovery paths: never.

Status now: US 12-month average 4.30, 0.75 above its 36-month low (3.55, Aug 2023); it would need 6.55.
options.false_positive_risk:
Low on the evidence available, but the evidence is thin.

Why low:
- Zero firings in 75 US years and 395 country-years.
- The point estimate of the non-AI chance of firing is 0.5% by the end of 2030 (pooled, Jeffreys), with a 95% upper bound of 3%. On US data alone the upper bound is 16%.
- The safety margin is at least 0.9 points everywhere; the best near-miss is Canada's 2.44.

Why thin:
- Zero false positives only shows specificity against the 13 rises where the output test could be checked, all of them recessions.
- There has never been a true positive, so sensitivity cannot be tested.

Other causes of jobless rises: at a 2-point threshold it fires in Canada 1971 and 1978, France 1994 and the US 2003 jobless recovery. I did not verify what caused those.

False negatives:
- It vetoes an AI shock that itself pulls output more than 1% below peak.
- It also vetoes one that overlaps an unrelated recession. 38% of all US 3-year windows are blocked.
- It misses very slow rises (under about 1 point a year).
- Outside a recession, the strict variant blocks 17% of US 3-year windows; the 1% allowance blocks 0%.
options.attributes_to_ai: Only by exclusion. It rules out the cyclical explanation (an output recession) and captures 'jobless growth', the pattern AI displacement would produce. But any structural cause of rising unemployment with steady output would also qualify. It is not AI-specific; Option D adds attribution.
options.resolution:
Unambiguous if the vintage and missing-month rules are written down.

US data:
- BLS U-3 (FRED UNRATE), monthly, first Friday; the September 2026 figure is due 2 October 2026 per FRED.
- BEA GDPC1 advance estimate, about 4 weeks after quarter end.

Timing: month t resolves on the advance-GDP release for t's quarter, about 1 to 4 months after t. Anyone can recompute it from FRED and ALFRED.

Other countries: the OECD harmonised rates on FRED lag 1 to 3 months (the UK's latest is May 2026), and national GDP lags vary (not verified country by country). Brazil's history comes from IBGE SIDRA table 6381 (from 2012-03). The repo's br_unemp.json holds only 24 months.
options.fit_with_priors:
It is the right kind of event for a market-anchored AI prior, because the non-AI background is near zero. But the numbers need two changes.

(1) Timing. The GLOBALS comment calls the prior the date a shock 'has started'. The engine uses that date as the date the trigger is met, which I confirmed in engine.js. A 3-point rise in a 12-month average arrives 13-35 months after onset in my synthetic paths.

(2) The veto. Multiply by the chance the shock comes without output falling more than 1% below peak. 38% of US 3-year windows are blocked by recessions from any cause, and AI-caused dips add to that, so k is about 0.5-0.6 (judgment).

Also, the 2028 anchor (ACX: a 'visible break', including positive ones) is weak. Firing by the end of 2028 needs the 12-month average near 7.2% within 27 months, and the Sahm reading is -0.07 (Aug 2026).

Illustrative re-based prior, low/mode/high, with d = 1.5 years and k = 0.6 (the inputs are judgment; the outputs are computed):
- by 2028: 0.008/0.016/0.030
- by 2030: 0.033/0.063/0.110
- by 2035: 0.102/0.171/0.252
- by 2040: 0.154/0.240/0.338
- by 2050: 0.204/0.319/0.436

The results JSON has the other d and k combinations. Alternatively, keep the current prior but relabel it as 'shock started', and add an explicit lag and no-recession factor in the engine.

options.name: Option B: 3-point rise with no two consecutive quarters of falling GDP
options.rule: As in Option A, except for the output test. The output test here: there must be no two consecutive quarterly declines in real GDP from 4 quarters before m0's quarter through t's quarter. The month is judged when GDP for t's quarter is published, using that day's vintage. Other countries use their own GDP series in the same way.
options.established_components:
- The rise is Sahm-style, as in Option A.
- The output test is the widely used 'two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth' convention. I read it verbatim in Kalshi KXRECSSNBER-26 and -27: 'two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth ... according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis'.
- This has the most familiar wording of the options, but the combination is not adopted anywhere.
options.backtest:
At 3 points: never fires in the US (1951-10 to 2026-06), in current vintage or in real time (1992 on). Never fires in any of the other nine countries: 0 in 395 country-years, and 0 in 377 with W=60.

At 2 points:
- US 2003-08..2004-01 in current vintage, but never in real time. As published on 2003-11-05, 2001 had three straight quarterly declines; they were later revised away.
- CAN 1971-02..05
- FRA 1994-01..12

At 1.5 points: US 2002-06..2004-07 in current vintage; 2004-04..07 in real time.

If judged on the jobs-report date, before GDP for t's quarter exists, it would misfire in US 2020-06 (at 2 points) and ESP 2008-12 (at 3 points). That is why the rule waits for GDP.

Synthetic paths: +4 over 36 months fires at month 35. With two -0.3% quarters it never fires. With one -0.1% quarter it fires at month 35. A fast +5 fires at month 13. Recession paths never fire.
options.false_positive_risk:
Low: the same zero-firing record and safety margins as Option A (US maximum 2.06 while the test held).

It has more false negatives than Option A:
- Any two tiny or first-print declines close the guard. As published in Aug and Nov 2022 (ALFRED), US GDP fell in 2022Q1 and Q2; that was later revised away. Germany's 2025Q2-Q3 declines were -0.02% and -0.03%.
- It currently blocks the UK (2023Q3-Q4) and Germany (2022Q4-2023Q2) for rises measured from their 2023 lows.
- Unconditionally it blocks 37% of US 3-year windows, 65% in Germany and 55% in Japan.
- It vetoes an AI shock that comes with a mild demand dip.
options.attributes_to_ai: By exclusion only, as in Option A. Not AI-specific.
options.resolution: Same sources and timing as Option A. It is more sensitive to GDP revisions, because a sign flip of a tiny quarter can change the verdict. So the vintage must be fixed: the advance-estimate day for t's quarter.
options.fit_with_priors:
The same conclusion as Option A: the right kind of prior, but it must be shifted later by about 1-2 years and scaled down. The scaling factor k should be a little lower than for Option A (about 0.45-0.6, judgment), because the guard closes more often, including on revised first prints.

The market does price the veto risk directly: Kalshi KXRECSSNBER-27 (two negative quarters from Q4 2026 through Q4 2027) is bid 0.19 / ask 0.20 (read this session).

options.name: Option C: 3-point rise outside an officially dated recession (NBER, or the Hamilton GDP index) - US only
options.rule:
As in Option A, except the output test is one of two:
(C-NBER) no NBER recession month (FRED USREC) from 12 months before m0 through t; or
(C-Ham) Hamilton's GDP-based recession index (FRED JHGDPBRINDX) below 67 in every quarter from 4 quarters before m0's quarter through t's quarter, judged once t's quarter's index is out.

For the other nine countries the only comparable published series were the OECD-based recession indicators (xxxRECM on FRED). They were discontinued and their data end in 2022. The irregular national committees (CEPR-EABCN, CODACE, ESRI, C.D. Howe) have no schedule.
options.established_components:
These are the most established cycle classifiers:
- NBER business-cycle dates.
- Hamilton's index on FRED. FRED says values are never revised, and above 67 is a reliable recession signal.
- The OECD recession indicators (historical only).
options.backtest:
C-NBER: never fires at 3, 2 or 1 points (1951-10 to 2026-08). NBER dates are final-vintage, so this carries look-ahead by construction.

C-Ham, judged once the index covers t's quarter: never fires at 3, 2, 1.5 or 1 points (1968-11 to 2026-03). If judged on the jobs-report date instead, it misfires at 2 points in 2020-06..07, and at 1.5 points in 2009-01 and 2020-05..07. An earlier verifier found a 2003-10 firing at 1.5 points, but that used a different window (8 quarters before through 4 after the month).

C-OECD, other nine countries: never fires at 3 or 2 points, through 2022.

The largest rise ever reached while each guard held: 0.79 (2026-06) for NBER and 0.78 (2026-03) for Hamilton.
options.false_positive_risk:
The lowest of the options: none at any threshold down to 1 point.

The false-negative risk is the highest. NBER weights payroll employment and real income heavily, so an employment-led AI shock could itself be dated a recession and veto the trigger (an inference from the NBER description the official verifier read).

The Hamilton index uses output only, which avoids that problem, but it is US-only.
options.resolution:
Poor for NBER. Announcements are irregular, 4-21 months after turning points (announcement dates the official verifier read), so the prior's dates cannot be matched to known resolution dates.

Hamilton: resolves about 7 months after t's quarter, because the index for a quarter comes out with the next quarter's GDP (the latest value, 2026Q1, was updated 30 Jul 2026).

Other countries: cannot resolve going forward.
options.fit_with_priors: The same adjustments as Option A (shift by about 1-2 years, scale by about 0.5-0.6). But the event date and the date anyone can confirm it differ by up to 1-2 years, which undermines falsifiability for NBER. Hamilton is usable as a US cross-check on Option A, not as the model's rule for ten countries.

options.name: Option D: 3-point rise concentrated in AI-exposed occupations (US attribution path; E-A in the script)
options.rule:
US, month t: the 3-point rise from Option A must hold, AND either:
(i) Option A's output test holds, or
(ii) the AI-exposure gap has widened by at least 1.0 point over m0..t.

The gap is the rise in the 12-month-average unemployment rate of AI-exposed occupation groups minus the rise for low-exposure groups.
- Exposed groups (FRED LNU04032216, 17, 20, 21): management, business and financial; professional; sales; office and administrative support.
- Low-exposure groups (LNU04032218, 24, 25, 26): service; construction and extraction; installation, maintenance and repair; production, transportation and material moving.
- Both are unweighted means of the published, not seasonally adjusted group rates (BLS Table A-13).

For the other countries I found no monthly published unemployment by occupation-exposure series. They would use Option A alone.
options.established_components:
The design, unemployment of AI-exposed versus unexposed occupations in the CPS, is the one used by Anthropic (Massenkoff and McCrory 2026), EIG, SIEPR and the Yale Budget Lab.

The 1-point threshold is Anthropic's detectability benchmark (quote verified in the saved page text).

The group mapping is my coarse approximation. It is consistent with Anthropic's examples: customer service reps and data entry keyers are highly exposed, while cooks, bartenders and motorcycle mechanics have zero coverage. The BLS AI exposure categories (Aug 2026) would be the official mapping, but the XLSX returned 403, and BLS publishes no monthly unemployment by category.
options.backtest:
Data start in 2000. The combined rule never fires at 3 points (1951-10 to 2026-06; the gap path exists only from 2000). At 2 points it fires 2003-08..2004-01, through the output path.

Gap path alone with the aggregate rise (D2):
- Never fires at 3, 2, 1.5 or 1 points with a 1.0 gap (2000-12 to 2026-08).
- Fires 2012-05 at 1 point with a 0.5 gap, and 2012-05..07 at 0.5 or 0.25 points.

In every recession rise the gap moved the other way: 2001-03 -1.06, 2008-09 -1.85, 2020 -1.41.

The gap alone, without the aggregate-rise condition, is at least 1.0 in recoveries: 2011-11..2015-11, 2019-05..09, 2022-07..2024-01. So it cannot be used on its own.

Now (Aug 2026): exposed +0.65, low +0.62, gap +0.03 against the 36-month low. On a 24-month basis I get +0.07; the academic verifier got +0.10 with a different handling of the missing October 2025.

Synthetic paths, assuming exposed groups rise 1.5x the aggregate and low groups 0.5x (an assumption):
- It fires at month 35 even with two -0.3% quarters.
- With a 1-point aggregate threshold, the gap path alone fires at month 14.
- It never fires in the recession paths.
options.false_positive_risk:
Specific in the only history available: 26 years and 3 recessions, with a 95% upper bound of 39% by 2030 on that sample alone.

It is untested against a non-AI white-collar downturn, such as a finance-led bust. In 2001-03 low-exposure unemployment still rose more.

The Yale synthetic-DiD authors warn that the lower cyclicality of exposed occupations (1994-2019) has not held in recent years. The OECD (2026) warns that exposed occupations sit in rate-sensitive sectors.

Its sign has depended on the exposure measure in other work (EIG).
options.attributes_to_ai: Yes, by design: it is the only option that looks for an AI signature instead of ruling out a recession. It lets an AI shock that causes its own recession count, provided the exposed groups bear it.
options.resolution:
The group rates come out on the jobs-report day (BLS Table A-13; FRED LNU040322xx), not seasonally adjusted, monthly, from 2000.

The gap is my arithmetic from published series, so the mapping and weights must be fixed in advance. SOC reclassifications could break continuity (not verified).

US only.
options.fit_with_priors:
Closest to what the market anchors intend. The cited 23% Manifold market requires AI to be responsible for at least 3 points, and the gap is the mechanical stand-in for that judgment. Because the gap path does not veto AI-caused recessions, k is higher (about 0.7-0.9, judgment).

The timing shift of about 1-2 years is still needed. Also, the 23% market requires unemployment above 10%, a bigger event than a 3-point rise from 4.3%, so the anchor remains an approximation.

rec.recommendation:
Adopt Option A as the model's trigger for all ten countries. Publish the exposure gap from Option D next to it for the US, and re-base the US timing prior.

**The recommended rule, in plain terms.** The shock counts as started when two things are both true:

1. The average unemployment rate over the last 12 months is at least 3 points above its lowest point of the previous three years.
2. Over that same stretch, the economy has never shrunk more than 1% from its best level. Check this using the GDP figures published for the quarter in question.

**Why this one:**

1. **It fixes the reviewer's problem.** The current rule fired in five US recession recoveries (1976-77, 1981, 1983-85, 1992-93, 2011-13) and in many other countries. Option A has never fired:
   - in the US since 1951, on today's data or on data as first published (checked from 1992);
   - in any of the ten countries (395 country-years).

   Every one of the 15 historical 3-point rises came with an output fall; the output test could be checked in 13 of them. The closest near-miss was a 2.44-point rise (Canada 1978), which leaves a safety margin.
2. **It is built from recognised parts.** The rise is measured the way the Sahm rule measures it (against a recent low), with its own window and threshold. The output test is peak-relative, like the model's current GDP test and the MacAskill-Moll bet. Only the 1% allowance is my choice, and it matters in both directions:
   - without it, a single tiny quarterly dip blocks the trigger, which happens in 17% of non-recession US windows;
   - with it, small dips and first estimates that are later revised away do not block it (the US 2022 first-print dip was about -0.6%).
3. **Anyone can check it on known dates from official figures.** It uses BLS unemployment and BEA GDP (or each country's equivalents). A month is settled on the day the first GDP estimate for its quarter comes out, 1 to 4 months later. Write two things into the rule: use that day's GDP figures, and average whichever months exist (October 2025 was never collected).

Option B, using the familiar "two quarters of shrinking" wording, is a fine second choice. But it gets blocked by tiny or later-revised dips (the US 2022 first print, Germany 2025) and by mild AI-caused slowdowns.

The NBER version (Option C) settles on no known date and cannot be used outside the US. Option D's AI-specific gap has only 26 years of history, so use it as the US evidence that the rise is AI-related. Let it override the output test only if the owner wants AI shocks that cause their own recession to count.

**What to change in the prior:**

- Relabel GLOBALS from "shock has started" to "trigger met".
- Move it about 1-2 years later. A 12-month average takes 13-35 months to rise 3 points in plausible paths.
- Scale it by about 0.5-0.6 for shocks the output test would block. Recessions from any cause touch about 38% of US 3-year windows.

Illustration with a 1.5-year shift and a factor of 0.6 (low/mode/high):

| By end of | Low | Mode | High |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2028 | 0.8% | 1.6% | 3.0% |
| 2030 | 3.3% | 6.3% | 11.0% |
| 2035 | 10% | 17% | 25% |
| 2040 | 15% | 24% | 34% |
| 2050 | 20% | 32% | 44% |

The current prior's modes are 8%, 18%, 33%, 43% and 55%.

- Every firing date above comes from my own backtest: repo CSVs copied read-only, plus FRED, ALFRED and IBGE series fetched today.
- The synthetic paths and the occupation mapping are my constructions.
- Real-time GDP vintages were checked for the US only.
